title: Message capacity and claim wording set the transition points of collective truth-finding in language-model networks
summary: Whether human or large language model (LLM), an agent in a discussion reads only a few of the others' contributions, bounded by cognition, context, or cost. LLM collectives can settle on a wrong consensus even when a majority starts out correct; we ask how far that reading bound alone decides the outcome. We model the bound with one number, the message capacity, which sets how many of the others' messages an agent reads, and generate the communication network from it. Over 31,824 randomized queries, we found that an 8-billion-parameter model's judgment of a claim effectively reduces to a logistic function of a weighted sum of its inbox, the update rule of a stochastic binary neuron with divisively normalized weights. From these weights and the network's degree statistics alone, the wrong consensus should become unreachable from any start once agents read, on average, fewer than 6.4 of their 31 sources. In 1,414 episodes with assigned starts the prediction failed: the correct side won in fewer than 50% of episodes from every start, and in only 28-45% when 75% of agents started correct. The failure traces to the field, the threshold that a claim's wording sets for the agent's answer before any message is read: the experimental claims' fields lay below the calibration mean, and with each claim's own field the same weights reproduce the outcomes. Reversing the wording showed that the threshold follows what a claim asserts, not whether it is true. On a second 8B model the pipeline predicts claim-dependent bistability; transition points appeared where computed, and an eight-claim calibration matched in 15 of 16 conditions. At 70B the assertion bias is not detected. Thus a collective's fate is largely set by two single-agent measurements: the threshold a claim's wording sets, and the message capacity that sets the transition point.

AI.tldr: A stochastic binary neuron model derived from LLM behavior shows that collective consensus outcomes in multi-agent discussions are largely determined by two factors: the cognitive threshold set by claim wording and the message capacity (how many messages agents read).
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand why LLM collectives can settle on wrong consensus even when a majority starts correct, and to determine how reading limitations (message capacity) alone affects outcomes in multi-agent discussions.
AI.method: The researchers modeled discussion with a stochastic binary neuron framework where agents' judgments reduce to logistic functions of weighted sums of their inbox. They conducted 31,824 randomized queries with an 8-billion-parameter LLM, generating communication networks based on message capacity, and analyzed 1,414 discussion episodes with various starting conditions.
AI.result: 1) Agents' judgments reduce to a logistic function of weighted inbox sums, similar to stochastic binary neurons. 2) Wrong consensus should theoretically be unreachable when agents read <6.4 of 31 sources on average, but experiments showed wrong consensus prevailed even with 75% correct starts. 3) The discrepancy traces to "field" thresholds set by claim wording. 4) Assertion bias (threshold following what claim asserts rather than truth) was detected in 8B models but not in 70B models.
AI.conclusion: Collective outcomes in LLM discussions are largely predetermined by two single-agent measurements: the cognitive threshold set by claim wording (assertion bias) and the message capacity that determines network transition points. The wording of claims, not just their truth value, critically shapes consensus formation through individual cognitive processing.

title: CC-OPI: Online Distributed Task Allocation for UAV Swarms under Communication Constraints
comment: 26 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables, including 6 pages of supplementary material. Code and data: https://github.com/bdathe-lb/CC-OPI-Exp
summary: In multi-robot missions such as post-disaster search and rescue, a short communication range fragments a swarm of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) into transient information islands. Under such intermittent connectivity, the prevailing "allocate-then-execute" paradigm--which requires global consensus before any physical movement--breaks down. This paper proposes the Communication-Constrained Online Performance Impact (CC-OPI) algorithm, an event-driven method that interleaves task negotiation with physical execution. CC-OPI replans only at discrete physical and topological events and integrates two further elements. The first is a pair of cost-evaluation metrics adapted to dynamic topologies--one with a spatial locality penalty that promotes regionalized operation, the other with a deadline-aware urgency term--complemented by a non-preemptive state lock that shields each UAV's ongoing action. The second is a decentralized fault-tolerance layer that pairs version-based state synchronization with a global-time-driven emergency pool. We establish that CC-OPI terminates in finite time, free of stale-completion deadlock and of unbounded reassignment within the mission horizon. In simulations at a 250 m communication radius, CC-OPI sustains a task completion rate of about 0.80: it leads a matched online execution of the unmodified Performance Impact (PI) and Consensus-Based Bundle Algorithm (CBBA) rules by about seven percentage points, exceeds the naively transferred static baselines by roughly 20 points, and remains within several points of PI and CBBA under full connectivity. Within the tested settings, CC-OPI degrades gracefully as connectivity weakens and absorbs packet loss, terrain occlusion, and runtime task arrival. The price is more messages and some redundant travel--a deliberate trade-off of efficiency for robustness.

AI.tldr: CC-OPI is an event-driven algorithm for multi-UAV task allocation under intermittent connectivity that interleaves negotiation with execution, achieving robust performance with 80% task completion despite limited communication.
AI.motivation: In post-disaster search and rescue missions, UAV swarms face fragmented communication due to short ranges, creating transient information islands. The traditional "allocate-then-execute" approach requiring global consensus before movement breaks down under intermittent connectivity.
AI.method: CC-OPI interleaves task negotiation with physical execution, replanning only at discrete physical/topological events. It uses: 1) cost-evaluation metrics adapted to dynamic topologies (spatial locality penalty and deadline-aware urgency) with non-preemptive state locks, and 2) decentralized fault-tolerance with version-based state synchronization and global-time-driven emergency pools.
AI.result: At 250m communication radius, CC-OPI achieves ~80% task completion rate, outperforming PI and CBBA by ~7 percentage points, beating static baselines by ~20 points, and staying close to full-connectivity performance. It degrades gracefully with weaker connectivity and handles packet loss, terrain occlusion, and dynamic task arrivals.
AI.conclusion: CC-OPI provides a robust solution for UAV task allocation under intermittent connectivity by trading some efficiency (more messages, redundant travel) for robustness, proving finite-time termination without deadlock or unbounded reassignment while maintaining competitive performance.

title: Reputation as Community Memory for the Agentic Web
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, The 22nd IEEE International Conference on eScience
summary: Agents can now externalize experience into memory, consolidating historical traces into semantic knowledge and procedural shortcuts that persist between sessions. Such memory is typically private to a single agent. We argue that agentic memory benefits from being collective, because trustworthy knowledge of the shared environment---the data sources, services, and tools agents depend on---cannot be established by any single agent, only corroborated across many independent observers. We present Cairn, a community reputation platform that captures collective knowledge, allowing agents to query the community's opinion of a resource before use and to submit evidence-backed ratings afterward. Cairn aggregates observations via a time-decayed Beta model with confidence shrinkage and supports semantic discovery over reviewer rationales. We evaluate Cairn's reputation engine under adversarial simulation (e.g., lying, collusion, camouflage), benchmark its retrieval performance, and report a case study of rating heterogeneous agents in production.

AI.tldr: Cairn is a community reputation platform that enables AI agents to share and query collective knowledge about resources, with adversarial-resistant reputation aggregation and semantic discovery capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current agent memory systems are typically private to single agents, but trustworthy knowledge about shared environments (data sources, services, tools) requires corroboration across many independent observers rather than individual agents.
AI.method: Cairn uses a time-decayed Beta model with confidence shrinkage to aggregate observations from multiple agents, supports semantic discovery over reviewer rationales, and provides a reputation engine resilient to adversarial attacks.
AI.result: The system was evaluated under adversarial simulations (lying, collusion, camouflage), benchmarked for retrieval performance, and tested in a case study of rating heterogeneous agents in production environments.
AI.conclusion: Collective agentic memory through community reputation platforms like Cairn provides more trustworthy and reliable resource assessment than individual agent memory systems.

title: Position: It is Time to Virtualize Foundation Models with a Self-evolving Operating System Layer
summary: AI applications have shifted from single, monolithic foundation models (FM) to compound agentic systems. Yet today's stacks remain fragmented: even as protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) ease tool/agent connectivity, each framework embeds an implicit runtime for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails, making behavior non-portable and governance brittle. It mirrors computing before operating systems, when every program re-implemented basic services. This position paper argues that the field now needs a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS) -- a system layer that virtualizes FM interactions analogous to how virtual machines abstract physical hardware, giving applications the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities. Internally, the FMOS orchestrates knowledge across memory tiers, model selection and resource allocation, and verification and policy enforcement. Like the human brain switching between fast intuition and slow deliberation, the FMOS learns when to intervene and when to let inference proceed directly and continuously adapting its policies based on operational experience.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS) as a system layer that virtualizes foundation model interactions, addressing the fragmented nature of current AI stacks by providing standardized runtime services for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails.
AI.motivation: Current AI applications are shifting from single foundation models to compound agentic systems, but today's stacks remain fragmented with each framework implementing its own implicit runtime for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails. This leads to non-portable behavior and brittle governance, similar to computing before operating systems when every program had to re-implement basic services.
AI.method: The paper proposes a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS) that virtualizes foundation model interactions analogous to how virtual machines abstract physical hardware. FMOS provides applications with the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy foundation model instances with effectively unbounded capabilities. Internally, it orchestrates knowledge across memory tiers, model selection and resource allocation, and verification and policy enforcement.
AI.result: The FMOS concept enables applications to seamlessly interact with foundation models without worrying about underlying runtime complexities. Like the human brain switching between fast intuition and slow deliberation, the FMOS learns when to intervene and when to let inference proceed directly, continuously adapting its policies based on operational experience.
AI.conclusion: The field needs a Foundation Model Operating System to standardize and virtualize foundation model interactions, addressing the fragmentation in current AI stacks and enabling more portable, governable, and efficient compound agentic systems by providing a system layer that abstracts runtime complexities.

title: Regularized Emphatic Temporal-Difference Learning: Stability under Constant Stepsizes
summary: Emphatic temporal-difference learning (ETD) stabilizes the expected off-policy TD update and changes its projection geometry, but neither property determines constant-stepsize sampled dynamics. We construct an ergodic two-state counterexample in which the ETD mean map contracts while the sampled product has a positive top Lyapunov exponent. Regenerative-cycle analysis separates this sign from the infinite variance of the follow-on trace. We introduce regularized emphatic TD (RETD), a normalized first-order post-shock repair that leaves the trace and importance ratios unchanged, stores the emphatic TD signal in a leaky scalar state, and releases a delayed correction. RETD's raw equilibrium is an affine shift of the ETD equilibrium; single- and two-regularization readouts recover the ETD fixed point exactly. We prove almost-sure convergence for harmonic diminishing stepsizes and a conditional constant-stepsize moment-contraction result from a Markovian random-product bound. RETD has certified negative exponents on the two-state construction and one Baird point, whereas the positive Baird ETD sign remains numerical. Paired 10,000-run experiments validate both separations, fixed-point recovery, a nonmonotone stability region, and task dependence. RETD changes post-shock dynamics; it does not reduce the shared follow-on-trace variance.

AI.tldr: RETD (Regularized Emphatic TD) fixes ETD's instability issues by normalizing the emphatic TD signal with leaky scalar state storage and delayed correction, providing certified convergence while preserving ETD's fixed point.
AI.motivation: ETD stabilizes off-policy TD learning theoretically but has practical instability issues in sampled dynamics, creating a disconnect between theoretical stability guarantees and actual implementation performance.
AI.method: Introduces RETD with normalized first-order post-shock repair: stores emphatic TD signal in leaky scalar state, releases delayed correction, maintains original trace and importance ratios unchanged, and provides multiple regularization readouts.
AI.result: RETD achieves almost-sure convergence with harmonic diminishing stepsizes, certified negative Lyapunov exponents on test cases (including Baird point where ETD had positive sign), recovers ETD fixed point exactly, and demonstrates stability through extensive experimental validation.
AI.conclusion: RETD successfully addresses ETD's practical stability issues while preserving its theoretical fixed points, providing a practical solution for off-policy TD learning with certified convergence properties.

title: Generative Query Suggestion via Intent Coverage and Query-Level Credit Assignment
summary: Generative query suggestion aims to enhance user engagement by anticipating user intents and recommending relevant follow-up queries. A central challenge is to generate slates whose individual queries are useful while the slate covers distinct intents. We propose an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization. First, intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. Second, query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to the corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate. Experiments on a large-scale production dataset, including online A/B testing and offline evaluation, show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

AI.tldr: A dual-stage optimization framework for generating diverse query suggestions that balance individual query quality with intent coverage across the entire slate.
AI.motivation: The main motivation is to improve user engagement in search systems by generating query suggestions that anticipate user intents. The key challenge is creating suggestion slates where individual queries are useful while the entire slate covers diverse intents comprehensively.
AI.method: The method proposes an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization: 1) Intent-aware diversity modeling that constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. 2) Query-level credit assignment that routes individual quality signals to corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the entire slate.
AI.result: Experiments on a large-scale production dataset show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage. Both online A/B testing and offline evaluation demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-stage optimization framework successfully addresses the challenge of generating query suggestions that balance individual query usefulness with slate-level intent diversity, leading to improved user engagement and search experience.

title: Agentic AI Networking for Heterogeneous Unmanned Aerial Systems in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks
summary: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) are emerging as a key infrastructure for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems that support concurrent services within a shared three-dimensional airspace. Their coexistence creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared network resources, while heterogeneous services impose distinct and time-varying requirements. These interactions naturally form a dynamic non-cooperative game in which both operating conditions and coordination objectives evolve over time. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture for low-altitude wireless networks that uses an outer LLM loop to adapt game objectives and an inner MARL loop to execute decentralized policies, enabling autonomous adaptation to changing service requirements without retraining.
AI.motivation: Low-altitude wireless networks support heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems with distinct time-varying requirements, creating dynamic non-cooperative games. Conventional controllers with predefined objectives cannot autonomously adapt to changing service requirements and resource priorities.
AI.method: Hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture with dual-loop structure: outer adaptation loop uses LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret requirements and reconfigure objectives/priorities; inner loop executes decentralized parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game.
AI.result: The framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services in a logistics-monitoring case study, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical LLM-MARL architecture enables autonomous adaptation in LAWNs, with discussion of key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic low-altitude wireless networks.

title: BioPhys-Bridge: A Benchmark for Interdisciplinary Scientific Reasoning in Physics-Grounded Biological Research
comment: Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026, 11 pages, 3 figures
summary: Language models face unique challenges in analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature. In biophysics research, faithful answers require grounding observed data in source evidence, interpreting it through a quantitative physics model, and linking it to a biological mechanism. To address this challenge, we introduce BioPhys-Bridge, a novel benchmark dataset for evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature. Each case contains evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for question answering (QA) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The initial release contains 500 cases, 1,517 agent-facing tasks, and covers six biological domains and nine physical model families, including three sparse families reserved for future expansion. We enforce strict quality gates for all cases in schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license, duplicate, unit-normalization, with domain expert review and annotation for 81 cases. Preliminary evaluations show that DeepSeek-V4-Flash obtain the highest evidence-ID $F_1$ score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294). BioPhys-Bridge is an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future works will increase the size and complexity of the dataset and perform comprehensive evaluations. Code and data are available in the GitHub repository and on Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: BioPhys-Bridge is a new benchmark dataset for evaluating language models' ability to perform evidence-grounded scientific reasoning in biophysics literature, requiring grounding in source evidence, quantitative physics models, and biological mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Language models struggle with analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature, particularly in biophysics where faithful answers require grounding observed data in source evidence, interpreting through quantitative physics models, and linking to biological mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors introduce BioPhys-Bridge, a benchmark dataset containing evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for QA and RAG. They enforce strict quality gates including schema validation, evidence-integrity checks, quantitative-grounding verification, source-license compliance, duplicate detection, and unit-normalization.
AI.result: Initial release contains 500 cases with 1,517 agent-facing tasks across six biological domains and nine physical model families. Preliminary evaluations show DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieved the highest evidence-ID F₁ score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294).
AI.conclusion: BioPhys-Bridge serves as an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future work will expand the dataset's size and complexity and perform comprehensive evaluations.

title: Layer-wise Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Compression
comment: Accepted by the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2026
summary: In this paper, we introduce layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression. The proposed method facilitates the knowledge transfer from the teacher model to the student model, utilizing a curriculum learning approach that begins with easier optimization tasks and progressively tackles harder ones. In order to adopt the layer-wise learning in LLM compression, we partition the whole model into multiple segments consisting of layers, thereby enabling more computationally efficient knowledge transfer for LLMs. Based on our theoretical analysis of cumulative error phenomenon, layer-wise curriculum learning accelerates convergence while stabilizing the knowledge transfer process. In addition, we present a feature caching method with a multi-threading strategy to efficiently address feature misalignment across layers, maximizing GPU utilization. Consequently, our method exhibits advanced model compression performance, as well as high computational efficiency in terms of minimized memory usage and short training hours. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50\% on BERT and GPT-2. Moreover, it outperforms the other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under the same training hours, with a lower GPU memory footprint.

AI.tldr: Layer-wise curriculum learning method for LLM compression that partitions models into segments, uses easier-to-harder task progression, and employs feature caching to achieve efficient knowledge transfer with reduced memory and training time.
AI.motivation: Need for efficient LLM compression methods that can transfer knowledge from teacher to student models while addressing computational challenges like high memory usage and long training times.
AI.method: Proposes layer-wise curriculum learning that partitions LLMs into layer segments, uses curriculum learning approach (easier to harder tasks), incorporates theoretical analysis of cumulative error, and implements feature caching with multi-threading for GPU efficiency.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets, reduces GPU memory usage and training hours by over 50% on BERT and GPT-2, outperforms other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models with same training hours and lower memory footprint.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise curriculum learning is an effective approach for LLM compression that combines accelerated convergence, stabilized knowledge transfer, and high computational efficiency through feature caching and segment partitioning.

title: Replan, Repair, or Edit? A Unified Empirical Evaluation of Travel Agents for Itinerary Revision under Resource Disruptions
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables
summary: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance because of flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Revising these itineraries involves full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision, whose differing task formulations and evaluation protocols hinder comparison. We conduct a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases, including feasible and infeasible instances, and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. We compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens. The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: Travel-planning agents face disruptions requiring itinerary revision; this study systematically compares full replanning, hierarchical repair, and local-revision approaches on effectiveness, stability, and cost.
AI.motivation: Existing travel-planning agents generate itineraries that can become infeasible due to disruptions, but revision methods have differing formulations and evaluation protocols that hinder comparison and selection.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study using 500 single-disruption cases and 200 compound-disruption cases from TREK-derived benchmarks, comparing LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost metrics.
AI.result: LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved highest compound-disruption success; IPyHOPPER nearly matched single-disruption success while preserving more of the original itinerary; successful repairs made fewer edits and retained more commitments than full replanning; computational profiles differed significantly across methods.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost, showing trade-offs between different revision approaches for travel-planning systems.

title: What Do We Expect from LLMs? Mapping the Design of LLM Benchmarks
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Data and code: https://github.com/xxcg322/LLM-Bench-Map
summary: Benchmarks are central to how progress in large language models (LLMs) is assessed and communicated. Yet model rankings alone reveal little about how evaluation requirements themselves are changing. The expanding variety of benchmarks offers another perspective: what researchers expect LLMs to do, and what they count as successful performance. We systematically map 14,767 papers introducing or updating evaluation resources from arXiv submissions between January 2022 and August 2026. Using staged screening and automated full-text coding, we examine changes in target systems and domains, evaluation materials and conditions, and scoring mechanisms. The collection shows growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications, while established and newer design elements frequently coexist. Model participation also develops unevenly: LLM-based scoring grows within both agent and non-agent groups, whereas model-generated materials show no comparable sustained increase in recent cohorts. These findings illuminate how public research translates capability expectations into concrete tests and criteria for success. As AI participates in constructing tests, performing tasks, and judging responses, they also raise a question: does expanding evaluation provide more independent evidence, or risk reproducing the preferences and blind spots of its participating models?

AI.tldr: A systematic analysis of 14,767 papers shows how LLM benchmark evolution reveals shifting evaluation requirements toward action/interaction tasks and professional applications, while raising questions about whether expanded evaluation provides independent evidence or reproduces model biases.
AI.motivation: While benchmarks are central to assessing LLM progress, model rankings alone don't reveal how evaluation requirements themselves are changing. The authors aim to understand how researchers' expectations of LLMs and definitions of successful performance evolve through benchmark development.
AI.method: Systematic mapping of 14,767 papers introducing or updating evaluation resources from arXiv submissions (Jan 2022-Aug 2026) using staged screening and automated full-text coding. Examined changes in target systems/domains, evaluation materials/conditions, and scoring mechanisms.
AI.result: The collection shows: 1) Growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications; 2) Established and newer design elements frequently coexist; 3) Uneven model participation - LLM-based scoring grows in both agent/non-agent groups, but model-generated materials show no comparable sustained increase in recent cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The findings illuminate how public research translates capability expectations into concrete tests and success criteria. However, as AI increasingly participates in constructing tests, performing tasks, and judging responses, there's a critical question: does expanding evaluation provide more independent evidence, or risk reproducing the preferences and blind spots of participating models?

title: Block Parallelism For Efficient Distributed Long-Context Diffusion Language Model Training
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures
summary: Block diffusion language models (BDLMs) combine autoregressive dependencies across blocks with parallel denoising within blocks, but long-context training is constrained by distributed attention communication and activation memory. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, communicating shared clean K/V together with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients. We observe that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks. We introduce block parallelism (BP), a new distributed parallelism dimension that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank. To scale BP to long contexts, we introduce context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP), which also shards the shared clean sequence across those ranks. CSBP keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics. On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context, CSBP improves throughput over the best baseline by 1.18-1.45x for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 speculative-decoder training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite. Code: https://github.com/ScalingIntelligence/Turbo-dLLM

AI.tldr: CSBP (Context-Sharded Block Parallelism) is a novel distributed training method for Block Diffusion Language Models that improves training throughput for long contexts by combining block and context parallelism, achieving significant speedups over existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Training Block Diffusion Language Models (BDLMs) with long contexts is challenging due to distributed attention communication overhead and activation memory constraints. Existing context parallelism approaches communicate both clean and corrupted key-value pairs, leading to inefficiencies.
AI.method: The paper introduces Block Parallelism (BP) that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank, leveraging the BDLM objective's separation over target blocks. To scale to long contexts, they propose Context-Sharded Block Parallelism (CSBP), which also shards the shared clean sequence across ranks while keeping corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoiding replicated clean prefixes.
AI.result: CSBP achieves 1.18-1.45x throughput improvement for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for autoregressive-to-BDLM conversion on 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite at every checkpoint.
AI.conclusion: CSBP is an effective distributed parallelism strategy for training BDLMs with long contexts, providing significant performance improvements while maintaining training semantics and reducing memory overhead compared to conventional approaches.

title: FINSKILLOPS: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for SEC Filing QA
summary: Financial QA systems are typically improved before deployment through better retrieval, prompting, or agent coordination, leaving their reliability behavior fixed thereafter. In practice, new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods can turn failures into new behaviors, but offer limited control over where a correction should apply or which previously correct answers it may break. We therefore frame post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance: recurring failures should become scoped skill patches, and each patch should earn deployment with- out introducing regressions. We instantiate this view in FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent system for SEC filing QA. FINSKILLOPS derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement. Across six financial QA benchmarks, a single frozen skill registry achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among the evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on our enhanced benchmark. In a separate 12-round operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%. These results establish controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management as the foundation for reliable self-improvement.

AI.tldr: FINSKILLOPS introduces a multi-agent system for controlled behavioral maintenance in financial QA, using scoped skill patches with rigorous validation to fix failures without causing regressions, achieving improved correctness and reduced error rates.
AI.motivation: Financial QA systems have fixed reliability post-deployment, with new SEC-filing questions repeatedly exposing heterogeneous errors. Existing self-improvement methods lack control over correction scope and risk breaking previously correct answers.
AI.method: FINSKILLOPS is a multi-agent system that frames post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance. It derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement/retirement.
AI.result: Across six financial QA benchmarks, FINSKILLOPS achieves highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on enhanced benchmark. In 12-round operational study, only 6 of 33 proposed skills are promoted, reducing monitoring non-correct rate from 20.0% to 12.5%.
AI.conclusion: Controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management establish the foundation for reliable self-improvement in financial QA systems, enabling scoped patches that fix failures without introducing regressions.

title: Randomized SVD Approximations for Spectral Co-Clustering of Word-Document Matrices
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA)
summary: Spectral co-clustering is a useful tool for discovering latent structure in word-document matrices, but its reliance on singular value decomposition (SVD) can make standard formulations expensive on high-dimensional data. This paper presents two randomized approximations for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data when the numbers of document and word clusters may differ. The first method uses randomized SVD through random projection, while the second combines partial SVD with element-wise random sampling. Across real-world and synthetic datasets, both methods reduce runtime relative to the full-SVD baseline, but their behavior depends on matrix sparsity. The random projection method is the more reliable approximation across the tested settings, whereas the sampling-based method is most useful on denser matrices and provides limited benefit on already sparse text data. These results show that randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be selected according to the underlying structure of the data.

AI.tldr: Randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering can reduce computational costs while maintaining performance, with random projection being more reliable across settings and sampling-based methods working best on denser matrices.
AI.motivation: Spectral co-clustering is computationally expensive on high-dimensional data due to its reliance on SVD, creating a need for efficient approximations that can handle different numbers of document and word clusters.
AI.method: Two randomized approximations: 1) randomized SVD through random projection, and 2) combination of partial SVD with element-wise random sampling, for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data with potentially different cluster counts.
AI.result: Both methods reduce runtime compared to full-SVD baseline. Random projection is more reliable across settings, while sampling-based method works best on denser matrices but provides limited benefit on sparse text data.
AI.conclusion: Randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be selected based on the underlying data structure - random projection for general reliability and sampling-based methods for denser matrices.

title: LearnActCoder: Role-Aware Error Memory for Adaptive Clinical Coding Agents
summary: Clinical coding agents repeatedly encounter the same failure modes, including unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. We introduce Learn-Then-Act, an inference-time adaptation framework that converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB). False-negative lessons are routed to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons are routed to a precision-oriented Judge. We instantiate the framework in LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge clinical coding pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available. On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, structured MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories remain near the no-memory baseline; the ICD-9 improvement is not significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the same memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintains a stable ICD operating point, providing scale/stability evidence. Overall, the results are consistent with structured, feedback-derived error memory being useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow. Absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system is evaluated retrospectively rather than in clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: A Learn-Then-Act framework converts coding errors into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database to adapt clinical coding behavior, showing improvements in CPT coding but mixed results for ICD codes.
AI.motivation: Clinical coding agents frequently encounter the same types of errors (unsupported codes, missed conditions, specificity errors, procedure-coding mismatches). There's a need to improve coding accuracy by learning from past mistakes without requiring weight updates or workflow changes.
AI.method: Learn-Then-Act framework converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database. False-negative lessons go to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons go to a precision-oriented Judge. Instantiated as LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III notes: MistakeKDB improved CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories had little effect; ICD-9 improvement was not significant. On MIMIC-IV: memory shifted ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at recall cost, with stable F1. On 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes: maintained stable ICD operating point, showing scale/stability.
AI.conclusion: Structured, feedback-derived error memory is useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or workflow changes. However, absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system needs prospective clinical deployment evaluation.

title: What Do Current Systematic Generalization Tasks Miss? A Reasoning-Centered Analysis
comment: Preprint. Under review
summary: Systematic generalization, the ability to solve novel problems by recombining known atomic elements, is central to human intelligence but difficult to study rigorously under controlled settings. Existing studies therefore rely on simplifications such as approximately linear action composition, productivity-based tests, and action-explicit goals, which make systematic generalization easier to study but omit some essential aspects of this capability. To characterize what these simplifications miss, we adopt a reasoning-centered lens and introduce TranSGrid, a testbed that brings deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning together within a unified task. Experiments with seven Transformers on 4,800 TranSGrid instances show that all models perform much worse on TranSGrid than on a held-out test set: the largest model solves 79.6% of the test set, but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% of the hardest subset. The gap remains within the training length range, showing that productivity alone is not sufficient to evaluate systematic generalization. Additionally, we reintroduce the other two simplifications into TranSGrid: one variant makes actions compose almost linearly (reducing the inductive demand), the other makes goals action-explicit (reducing the abductive one). In both, solve rates return to roughly the test set level, showing that either simplification alone is enough to reduce TranSGrid to an ordinary held-out test set. Together, our results show that existing tasks reduce either or both of the inductive and abductive demands, and that comprehensively measuring systematic generalization requires a task that involves all three forms of reasoning.

AI.tldr: TranSGrid is a new testbed that combines deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning to better measure systematic generalization in AI models, revealing that existing benchmarks oversimplify by reducing inductive/abductive demands.
AI.motivation: Current studies of systematic generalization rely on simplifications like linear action composition, productivity-based tests, and action-explicit goals, which omit essential aspects of this capability. There's a need for more comprehensive evaluation that captures what existing simplifications miss.
AI.method: Introduced TranSGrid testbed that integrates deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning within a unified task. Tested seven Transformers on 4,800 TranSGrid instances and compared performance against held-out test sets. Created variants of TranSGrid to reintroduce the simplifications: one with almost-linear action composition (reducing inductive demand) and one with action-explicit goals (reducing abductive demand).
AI.result: Models performed much worse on TranSGrid than on held-out test sets: largest model solved 79.6% of test set but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% of hardest subset. When simplifications were reintroduced (linear action composition or action-explicit goals), solve rates returned to test set levels, showing each simplification alone reduces the challenge. The performance gap remained within training length range, indicating productivity alone isn't sufficient for systematic generalization evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Existing tasks reduce either inductive or abductive demands, making systematic generalization appear easier than it is. Comprehensive measurement requires a task involving all three forms of reasoning (deductive, inductive, abductive). TranSGrid reveals gaps in current evaluation practices and provides a more rigorous benchmark for assessing true systematic generalization capabilities.

title: Radio-Frequency Convolutional Neural Networks
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary Information: 50 pages, 31 figures, 1 table
summary: Running artificial intelligence (AI) models directly on edge devices such as smartphones, wearables, and drones offers low latency, pervasive scalability, and data privacy, but these devices rarely carry the computing capability that modern neural networks demand. Edge accelerators have been developed in response, yet each adds computing hardware to devices already constrained in size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). An alternative lies in what these devices already carry: the frequency mixer in every wireless radio multiplies signals in time, natively performing convolution in the frequency domain. Here we introduce radio-frequency convolutional neural networks (RF-CNNs), which repurpose existing communication hardware for CNN inference. Multi-channel convolutions are mapped onto frequency tones for a passive mixer to execute in a single pass. We experimentally demonstrate that RF-CNN runs deep CNNs up to 26.4 million parameters and nine layers from classification of wireless signals and images to controllable image generation, close to full-precision performance. Because the weights arrive over the air and the analog hardware is shared with communication, the edge device spends energy only on data preparation and readout-down to 0.72 femtojoules per multiply-accumulate, two orders of magnitude less than it would cost on an added digital processor. These results suggest that deployed wireless infrastructure can bring efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference to the billions of devices it already connects.

AI.tldr: Repurposing wireless radio frequency mixers for convolutional neural network inference, enabling energy-efficient AI on edge devices without additional hardware.
AI.motivation: Edge devices have limited computing capabilities for AI models, while adding specialized accelerators increases SWaP-C (size, weight, power, cost). Existing wireless radios already contain hardware that can perform mathematical operations needed for neural networks.
AI.method: Propose radio-frequency convolutional neural networks (RF-CNNs) that map multi-channel convolutions onto frequency tones, using the frequency mixer in wireless radios to perform convolution in the frequency domain. The system leverages existing communication hardware rather than adding new accelerators.
AI.result: Experimental demonstration of RF-CNNs running deep CNNs up to 26.4M parameters and 9 layers for various tasks including wireless signal classification, image classification, and controllable image generation, achieving near full-precision performance with only 0.72 femtojoules per multiply-accumulate operation.
AI.conclusion: Existing wireless infrastructure can enable efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference on billions of edge devices by repurposing communication hardware, eliminating the need for additional AI accelerators and dramatically reducing energy consumption.

authors: Henrique Curi de Miranda e Lourenço Alves Pereira
title: A Proposal for an Agentic AI Architecture to Support Multi-Domain Decision-Making in the Brazilian Armed Forces
comment: This paper was accepted for publication in the XXVIII SIGE (Simpósio de Aplicações Operacionais em Áreas de Defesa)
summary: The growing complexity of multi-domain operational environments (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum) has increased the volume and velocity of data reaching command-and-control (C2) centers, straining the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems currently employed in defense are, in general, reactive and isolated tools that still rely heavily on human operators to integrate information, assess scenarios, and formulate courses of action. This paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture for AI systems that can plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously and audibly, aimed at supporting decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, and Air Force). Four application fronts are discussed (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion), as well as the data and sensor access requirements and the security and permission safeguards necessary for responsible employment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

AI.tldr: Proposes an Agentic AI architecture for defense C2 systems that can plan, access data, execute tools, and act autonomously to support decision-making across Brazilian Armed Forces.
AI.motivation: Growing complexity of multi-domain operations (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, EM spectrum) has overwhelmed traditional C2 centers with data volume/velocity, straining the OODA decision cycle. Current AI defense systems are reactive, isolated tools requiring heavy human integration.
AI.method: Proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture that enables AI systems to: plan, access various data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously with auditability. The architecture is designed to support decision-making across three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, Air Force).
AI.result: Identifies four application fronts: decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion. Also discusses data/sensor access requirements and security/permission safeguards necessary for responsible employment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI architecture can enhance decision-making in complex multi-domain defense environments by moving beyond reactive, isolated tools to create autonomous, auditable systems that support human operators across all levels of military operations while maintaining security and responsibility safeguards.

title: Characterizing Web Search by Conversational LLM Agents: From Search Decisions and Strategies to Results and Responses
summary: Conversational LLM agents increasingly rely on Web search, yet the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search remains poorly understood. We present the first study of Web search across four major conversational platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and DeepSeek), combining real-world user interactions (invivo) with controlled experiments using the same platform's models by their APIs (invitro). We investigate the quality of agentic decisions to invoke Web search, their strategies to formulate queries, the potential domain preferences in the search results they receive, and the choices they make when transforming search results into grounded responses. We find that Web-search decisions vary substantially across platforms and models, while more frequent Web-search invocation does not necessarily yield better response quality. We further show that conversational agents employ different complex querying strategies and that platform specific search engines return search results from their preferred domains. Finally, although responses are largely grounded in search results, some claims rely on uncited search results, raising concerns about attribution and reliability. Our findings have important implications for the design of future AI agents and Web search tools optimized for conversational retrieval.

AI.tldr: First comprehensive study of how conversational AI agents use web search across four major platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek), revealing platform-specific behaviors, search quality issues, and attribution problems.
AI.motivation: Conversational LLM agents increasingly rely on web search, but there's poor understanding of the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search decisions and behaviors across different platforms.
AI.method: Combined real-world user interactions (invivo) with controlled experiments using platform models via APIs (invitro) across four major conversational platforms. Investigated search invocation decisions, query formulation strategies, domain preferences in results, and result transformation into responses.
AI.result: Web-search decisions vary substantially across platforms; frequent search invocation doesn't guarantee better response quality. Agents use different complex querying strategies; platform search engines favor their preferred domains. Responses are largely grounded but some claims rely on uncited results, raising attribution and reliability concerns.
AI.conclusion: Findings have important implications for designing future AI agents and web search tools optimized for conversational retrieval, highlighting the need to address platform biases and improve attribution transparency.

title: Learning-Induced Dynamical Transition in Recurrent Neural Networks
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: Learning in recurrent neural networks can fundamentally reshape their underlying dynamics, transforming initially chaotic activity into stable task-dependent behavior. We develop a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory(DMFT) to describe this transition during learning. We show that a slow feedback-driven learning process generates an evolving effective feedback strength that drives the network through a transition from chaotic to stable dynamics defined by a bifurcation of the DMFT solution. By deriving the two-time correlation function throughout learning, we identify a critical feedback strength and a corresponding learning rate dependent critical time separating these regimes. The transition arises from the progressive deformation of an effective dynamical landscape by the growing learned feedback structure. Starting from the untrained state, the theory predicts the time evolution of the network output during training and shows quantitative agreement with numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: A non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory explains how recurrent neural networks transition from chaotic to stable dynamics through learning-driven feedback evolution.
AI.motivation: Recurrent neural networks initially exhibit chaotic activity that transforms into stable task-dependent behavior through learning. There's a need to understand this transition theoretically, specifically how learning reshapes network dynamics from chaos to stability.
AI.method: Developed a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to describe the learning transition. Derived the two-time correlation function throughout learning, identified critical feedback strength and learning-rate-dependent critical time separating chaotic and stable regimes.
AI.result: The theory shows that slow feedback-driven learning generates an evolving effective feedback strength that drives the network through a bifurcation of the DMFT solution. The transition arises from progressive deformation of an effective dynamical landscape by growing learned feedback structure.
AI.conclusion: The DMFT approach successfully predicts the time evolution of network output during training, showing quantitative agreement with numerical simulations, and provides a theoretical framework for understanding learning-induced transitions from chaotic to stable dynamics in recurrent neural networks.

title: Language-model groups overstate consensus when replaying human deliberation on a reasoning task
comment: 37 pages, 4 figures. Preregistration: https://osf.io/5jp7s . Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21318346
summary: Full-consensus rates are often treated as indicators of collective cognition, yet depend on how participation and final states are operationalized. We replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scoring agents and people with the same code. Across human scoring definitions, estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%; about one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual in two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses: the submit-based comparison (n = 98) yielded gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points for chat and reasoning modes, and the participation-matched comparison (n = 45) yielded gaps of 34.1 and 44.4 points. These complementary routes reduced different measurement asymmetries yet converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under a reparameterization removing the memorizable answer; reasoning-mode groups then agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution in this setting. These analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

AI.tldr: LLM agent groups show much higher consensus rates than human groups in Wason task discussions, but this artificial consensus doesn't correlate with accuracy and provides biased estimates of human collective outcomes.
AI.motivation: Full-consensus rates are often used as indicators of collective cognition, but these metrics depend heavily on how participation and final states are operationalized. The researchers want to understand how LLM agent groups compare to human groups in deliberative settings, particularly regarding consensus formation.
AI.method: Researchers replayed 100 held-out human Wason task groups with matched LLM agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer. They used the same scoring code for both agents and humans, conducted post-unblinding sensitivity analyses including submit-based (n=98) and participation-matched (n=45) comparisons, and tested robustness under different conditions including removal of early stopping and reparameterization.
AI.result: Human consensus estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0% depending on scoring definitions, with about one fifth of participants never posting. Agent groups showed much higher consensus rates with gaps of 34.0-44.4 percentage points depending on comparison method. Even after removing memorizable answers, reasoning-mode LLM groups agreed nearly unanimously but mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent groups with belief-anchored agents are biased estimators of human group outcome distributions in deliberative settings. The artificial consensus shown by LLM groups doesn't correspond to accuracy, highlighting the importance of scoring-explicit approaches when using simulated groups to estimate human deliberative outcomes.

title: Do AI Agents Understand Computer Architecture?
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: Agents are increasingly asked to design hardware, and increasingly reported to succeed. Such reports establish that a design improved; they cannot establish why. An agent that improves an accelerator may be reasoning about the machine, or may be searching competently over knobs whose meaning it never recovers -- and only the first transfers to the next architecture. Existing evaluations cannot tell the two apart, because they vary the agent while holding the framing of the problem fixed. We do the opposite. AutoTuring hands the same agent the same 15-dimensional accelerator space twice: once as named architectural knobs with simulator counters, once as anonymous variables on [0,1], with the evaluator, the legal space and the reachable optima held identical, so that the only thing that varies is whether the problem means anything. The gap between the two is the measurement. On a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket, meaning pays: the architect beats a modeled H200 by 5.4% and its blind counterpart by 12.3% on average, with 70.1% fewer simulator calls. It does not pay uniquely: a critic loop recovers most of that gap for the blind agent and buys the architect nothing, so architectural knowledge and structured critique behave as substitutes rather than as complements. We report these as preliminary findings -- five to six runs per condition on a single modeled accelerator -- and take the comparison itself, not the accelerator, to be the contribution.

AI.tldr: A novel evaluation method called AutoTuring tests whether AI agents designing hardware actually understand architecture vs. just optimizing blindly. By comparing the same agent optimizing with architectural knowledge vs. anonymous variables, the study finds architectural meaning improves performance but can be substituted with structured critique.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations can't distinguish whether AI agents improving hardware designs are actually reasoning about architecture or just competently searching over optimization knobs without understanding. The latter wouldn't transfer to new architectures, making this distinction crucial for assessing true architectural reasoning.
AI.method: AutoTuring uses the same 15-dimensional accelerator space with the same agent twice: once with named architectural knobs and simulator counters (meaningful representation), and once as anonymous variables on [0,1] (blind optimization). All other factors are held identical, allowing isolation of the value of architectural understanding.
AI.result: Architectural meaning provides significant benefits: the architect-aware agent outperforms a modeled H200 by 5.4% and its blind counterpart by 12.3% on average, with 70.1% fewer simulator calls. However, adding a critic loop to the blind agent recovers most of the performance gap, suggesting architectural knowledge and structured critique are substitutes rather than complements.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is the comparative evaluation method itself, not the specific accelerator design. The study demonstrates that meaning matters in hardware design optimization, but structured critique can partially substitute for architectural knowledge, revealing important insights about how AI agents approach hardware design problems.

title: Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Privacy-Preserving Modeling of Heterogeneous Distributed Systems
summary: We present Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes (pFedHGP) for probabilistic regression and classification when data are distributed across heterogeneous clients. Each client's latent function decomposes into (i) a shared global component, (ii) a client-specific deviation that shares the global kernel structure, and (iii) a flexible local residual. Sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference keep raw data local while the server synchronizes only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component. Full predictive distributions support uncertainty-aware decisions. In application studies, pFedHGP attains perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using 13.77% of labeled cycles and recovers geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series. An Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output Gaussian processes for correlated sensors.

AI.tldr: pFedHGP is a personalized federated hierarchical Gaussian process method for probabilistic regression/classification that decomposes client functions into shared global, client-specific deviation, and local residual components while keeping data local through federated variational inference.
AI.motivation: To address probabilistic regression and classification in federated learning settings where data is distributed across heterogeneous clients, requiring methods that handle client heterogeneity while maintaining data privacy and supporting uncertainty-aware predictions.
AI.method: Each client's latent function decomposes into three components: (1) shared global component, (2) client-specific deviation sharing global kernel structure, and (3) flexible local residual. Uses sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference to keep raw data local while synchronizing only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component via server.
AI.result: In press tonnage monitoring, achieves perfect fault classification using only 13.77% of labeled cycles. Recovers geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series. The Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output Gaussian processes for correlated sensors.
AI.conclusion: pFedHGP provides an effective federated probabilistic framework that handles client heterogeneity, maintains data privacy, supports uncertainty quantification, and demonstrates practical utility in real-world applications with significantly reduced labeling requirements and successful pattern discovery.

title: COIN-GP: Cooperative Online Learning in Networked Distributed Systems with Partial Measurements via Gaussian Process Regression
summary: In this paper, we tackle the problem of jointly estimating the system states and partially unknown dynamics within distributed sensor-equipped networks, particularly in scenarios where only partial state observations are available. To address this issue, we propose an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework incorporating online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression, which enables accurate estimation despite incomplete in measurements and deficient GP models. In addition, a novel data collection strategy is introduced, with theoretical conditions ensuring feasible data acquisition. Moreover, we also derive an error upper bound encompassing state estimation and model estimation, leveraging the deterministic error bounds of GPs. Empirical simulations demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to existing distributed GP-based methods.

AI.tldr: A distributed observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework using online Gaussian Process regression for joint state and partially unknown dynamics estimation in sensor networks with partial observations.
AI.motivation: Distributed sensor networks often face challenges in jointly estimating system states and partially unknown dynamics, especially when only partial state observations are available, leading to incomplete measurements and deficient models.
AI.method: Proposes an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework incorporating online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression, along with a novel data collection strategy with theoretical conditions for feasible data acquisition.
AI.result: Theoretical error upper bound encompassing both state estimation and model estimation derived using deterministic GP error bounds; empirical simulations show superiority over existing distributed GP-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables accurate state and dynamics estimation in distributed networks with partial observations, with theoretical guarantees and demonstrated practical superiority over existing approaches.

title: MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs
summary: LLM coding agents now generate complex programs at a scale that makes thorough human review increasingly difficult, raising the risk of safety and security failures. Common approaches, including fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier, can detect many failures but struggle to cover all possible edge cases. Formal verification addresses this by providing machine-checkable guarantees over specified properties, but traditionally demands substantial manual specification and proof engineering. We introduce a unified multi-agent framework, MAGS, that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees, using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation where safety properties can be mechanically checked. MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back into executable code. We evaluate MAGS on 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. Across all 220 examples, it achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations further show strong performance across all three domains, while revealing failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the target behavior.

AI.tldr: MAGS is a multi-agent framework that automatically generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees by using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation, achieving 100% success rate on safety verification across 220 diverse examples.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code poses safety and security risks at scale, making human review increasingly difficult. Existing approaches (fuzz testing, static analysis, LLM-as-a-Verifier) have coverage limitations, while formal verification requires substantial manual effort.
AI.method: MAGS uses a unified multi-agent framework that: 1) formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs/safety requirements, 2) translates generated code into Dafny (verification-aware IR), 3) repairs violations using verifier feedback, and 4) compiles verified programs back to executable code.
AI.result: Evaluation on 220 examples (100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, 20 robotic-arm tasks) shows 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees. Independent evaluations confirm strong safety and functional performance across domains.
AI.conclusion: MAGS successfully bridges the gap between automated code generation and formal verification, providing machine-checkable safety guarantees without extensive manual proof engineering. However, limitations remain when auto-formalized semantics don't fully capture target behavior.

title: How to Guide Your Language Flow
summary: We introduce a new method to guide flow matching models. Our approach, which we call probe guidance, uses the frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. This works using a similar principle as autoguidance, but eliminates the need for an additional forward pass at inference time and provides a reliable path to ensure that the weak and strong model share similar dynamics. We apply and benchmark this method on continuous diffusion language models, where probe guidance sets a new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, probe guidance consistently improves on multiple choice question answering benchmarks. Using our probes, we study the traditional autoguidance setting where the strong model is a weak checkpoint, and find that the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training. These findings both provide a practical way to improve diffusion language models and shed light on the actual mechanism behind autoguidance, which is currently poorly understood.

AI.tldr: Probe guidance uses frozen internal states of existing diffusion models to create guidance signals, eliminating extra inference-time computations while improving performance on language generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Current guidance methods for flow matching models like autoguidance require additional forward passes at inference time and suffer from dynamics mismatch between weak and strong models. There's also poor understanding of how autoguidance actually works mechanistically.
AI.method: Probe guidance extracts guidance signals from frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to guide flow matching models. This approach maintains similar dynamics between weak and strong models and avoids extra inference-time computations.
AI.result: Probe guidance achieves SOTA on unconditional generation with continuous diffusion language models. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, it consistently improves performance on multiple choice QA benchmarks. The study also reveals that for effective autoguidance, weak models must come from low-entropy training regions.
AI.conclusion: Probe guidance provides both a practical improvement for diffusion language models and illuminates the underlying mechanisms of autoguidance, showing that successful guidance requires weak models from low-entropy training phases.

title: Closed-World Resolution Against Tool Hallucination in LLM Agents
summary: Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents fail in a way no tool-selection or tool-security method addresses: they call tools that do not exist and pass arguments no schema declares. Existing defenses either pick the right tool (selection) or constrain what an agent may do with real tools (gating), both of which presuppose the emitted call refers to a real tool at all. We show this is a structural blind spot: a hallucinated call is by construction not a decision any gate made, so no gate can reject it. This paper is primarily a measurement and benchmark study. We give a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5) and, as a reference point, the Resolution Rung: a training-free, closed-world resolver (registry membership plus a signature check) whose interest is where it must sit, not what it computes. We prove hallucination defense must precede any causal gate, and characterize the one irreducible residue (borrowed arguments schema-indistinguishable from a valid call). Across ten hosted models under two invocation surfaces we measure 322 genuine hallucinations; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on the unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3), and model scale does not help (a 675B model matches a 7-8B one). We then extend to the Model Context Protocol, where merging several servers into one namespace creates hallucination surfaces a single registry cannot express (a second taxonomy, M1-M5); on the live MCP surface we measure 154 hallucinations, including from frontier models that were clean on the single-registry surface, because collisions and shadowing are structural to the merge. We release the versioned Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) so any resolver is comparable across submissions.

AI.tldr: LLM agents hallucinate tool calls to non-existent tools with undeclared arguments, creating a structural blind spot that existing tool-selection/gating methods cannot address, requiring pre-gate hallucination defense.
AI.motivation: Current tool-augmented LLM agents suffer from a fundamental security gap: they can hallucinate calls to tools that don't exist with arguments not defined in schemas, and existing defenses (tool selection/gating) can't detect these hallucinations because they presuppose the tool exists.
