AI.method: 1) Create five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5); 2) Develop Resolution Rung as training-free closed-world resolver with registry membership + signature check; 3) Prove hallucination defense must precede causal gates; 4) Measure hallucinations across 10 models on two invocation surfaces; 5) Extend to Model Context Protocol (MCP) with second taxonomy (M1-M5); 6) Create Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) for reproducibility.
AI.result: Found 322 genuine hallucinations across models; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on raw-JSON surfaces (34 vs 3); model scale doesn't help (675B matches 7-8B). On live MCP surface, found 154 hallucinations including from frontier models that were clean on single-registry surfaces, due to structural namespace collisions and shadowing in merged environments.
AI.conclusion: Tool hallucination is a structural blind spot requiring pre-gate defenses, as hallucinations bypass existing security gates by definition; merging multiple tool registries (as in MCP) creates new hallucination surfaces; benchmark provides standardized measurement framework.

title: Smart Insole Human Activity Recognition for Continuous Monitoring in Elderly Care
summary: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. This paper presents a wireless smart insole platform and machine-learning workflow for recognizing sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking from plantar-pressure and inertial signals. Each insole integrates 16 active pressure-sensing locations and a six-dimensional IMU stream consisting of tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity. Data were collected from 15 healthy adults at 80~Hz and segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and candidate model families were first screened with stratified 10-fold cross-validation; the primary performance estimate was then obtained with participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation, ensuring that all windows from a participant remained in a single fold. Under this protocol, Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 and 0.959 for the left and right feet, respectively, and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. A compact 1D-CNN evaluated with the same participant-independent folds did not significantly outperform HGB ($p=0.0625$). The results show that low-profile footwear sensing can infer activity state from pressure and IMU measurements for participants unseen during training, establishing a basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care.

AI.tldr: A smart insole system using plantar pressure and IMU data with machine learning achieves high accuracy in recognizing sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking activities, enabling participant-independent activity monitoring for fall prevention in elderly care.
AI.motivation: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions, highlighting the need for continuous activity monitoring systems to enable early intervention and fall prevention in elderly care settings.
AI.method: Developed a wireless smart insole platform with 16 pressure sensors and 6D IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope) per insole. Collected data from 15 healthy adults at 80Hz, segmented into overlapping windows. Used stratified 10-fold cross-validation for initial screening, then participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation to ensure generalization to unseen participants. Compared machine learning models including Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) and compact 1D-CNN.
AI.result: HGB achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 (left foot), 0.959 (right foot), and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. The 1D-CNN did not significantly outperform HGB (p=0.0625). The system demonstrated effective participant-independent activity recognition.
AI.conclusion: Low-profile footwear sensing with plantar pressure and IMU measurements can accurately infer activity states for participants unseen during training, establishing a practical basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care applications.

title: The syntax and semantics of goals
comment: To appear in Topics in Cognitive Science, special issue on Goal-Centric Perspectives in Cognitive Science
summary: In both cognitive science and computer science, goals are conceptualized as cognitive states that flexibly combine with world knowledge to organize and specify purposeful behavior. In this way, goals are compositional representations whose content relates to rational behavior. We here draw attention to goals as representations and their content because it highlights a parallel with other areas in cognitive science - in particular, the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic - while also foregrounding foundational questions about the expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations. For example, goals are typically taken as fixed and imposing constraints on desirable behaviors, but we can also identify constraints on goal representations themselves, such as whether a particular goal language is sufficiently expressive to capture behaviors of interest, or whether different goal representations capture the same behavior. Here, we synthesize work that aims to characterize the properties of different goal representations and suggest these are points of a broader design space. We close by discussing how distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can elucidate the implicit assumptions we make about goals, inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals.

AI.tldr: Goals are cognitive representations that combine with world knowledge to organize purposeful behavior, with parallels to syntax-semantics in linguistics, highlighting questions about expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations.
AI.motivation: To examine goals as cognitive representations and highlight parallels with syntax-semantics interfaces in linguistics/logic, foregrounding foundational questions about expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations.
AI.method: Synthesizing existing work to characterize properties of different goal representations and identify them as points in a broader design space.
AI.result: Establishes that goals have both form (syntax) and meaning (semantics), leading to questions about whether goal languages are sufficiently expressive to capture behaviors of interest, and whether different representations capture the same behavior.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing form and meaning of goals can elucidate implicit assumptions about goals, inform study of higher-level cognition-motivation interactions, and isolate axes of variation for different goal conceptions.

title: Stiefel Attention: When the Geometry of Transformer Projection Matrices Dominates Optimizer Choice---and When It Does Not
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures
summary: The query and key projections $\WQ,\WK$ in attention are almost always trained by Euclidean optimizers with no constraint on their geometry. We constrain them to the Stiefel manifold and optimize them there with a Riemannian Adam that carries one scalar second moment per frame, caps its step by a trust region, and retracts polarly. Four propositions prove this update is steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale, well conditioned, and exactly $\mathrm{O}(d)$-equivariant, each certified numerically in \texttt{float64}. A fifth supplies the mechanism: weight decay has \emph{identically zero} Riemannian gradient on $\St(d,r)$, since $W = W I_r$ lies in the normal space, so the learned attention geometry survives the collapse cycles that decay drives through the rest of the model. On modular arithmetic grokking, a single run holds $97.0\%$ validation accuracy at epoch 20\,000 against the baseline's $61.1\%$---an unstable endpoint we report as evidence for the mechanism rather than as an effect size. On CIFAR-10 patches the same rule gains $\mathbf{+8.98}$\,pp over 12 paired starts ($t{=}60.6$, $12/12$), and the gap widens with data rather than eroding. The step rule earns this: a fixed-step Riemannian update is degree one in the gradient, so it moves $24$--$40\times$ less per step than an identically shaped AdamW matrix---its frames barely leave their initialization, and freezing them outright costs only $0.28$\,pp. An ablation credits the whole gain to making the step scale free, and nothing measurable to the projector or to equivariance. A negative result sharpens the account: gauge removal cannot motivate the method, because a direction along which the loss is invariant carries no gradient at all.

AI.tldr: Constraining attention query/key projections to the Stiefel manifold with Riemannian optimization prevents weight decay from destroying learned attention geometry, improving stability and performance.
AI.motivation: Standard attention query/key projections are trained with Euclidean optimizers without geometric constraints, allowing weight decay to collapse learned attention geometry during training cycles.
AI.method: Constrain WQ, WK to Stiefel manifold St(d,r), optimize with Riemannian Adam that uses one scalar second moment per frame, caps step size with trust region, and uses polar retraction.
AI.result: On modular arithmetic grokking: 97.0% validation accuracy vs baseline 61.1% at epoch 20,000. On CIFAR-10 patches: +8.98 percentage points improvement over 12 paired starts. Gains attributed to step scale-free property, not projector or equivariance.
AI.conclusion: Constraining attention projections to Stiefel manifold preserves learned geometry against weight decay collapse, with performance gains coming from making optimization step scale-free rather than from projection or equivariance properties.

title: Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training
summary: Compositional reasoning is critical for real-world problem solving: since training data is necessarily limited, models must generalize by composing learned skills in new ways. While post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the reasoning abilities of language models (LMs), their effects on compositional reasoning remain less well understood. We propose a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning, yielding three levels of compositionality with increasing complexity. Empirically, we instantiate this framework with data-structure tasks, which provide deterministic reward computation and clear compositional structure. We find a consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. We provide theoretical explanation for this asymmetry, and further evaluate compositional generalization under length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to tasks requiring unseen skills. Finally, we present a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks, showing preliminary evidence that the decomposed-to-composed asymmetry can extend to practical settings.

AI.tldr: Post-training methods like RL improve language model reasoning, but compositional generalization remains limited, showing a decomposed-to-composed training asymmetry where composed training transfers better than decomposed training.
AI.motivation: Compositional reasoning is essential for real-world problem solving since training data is limited, but the effects of post-training methods like reinforcement learning on compositional generalization are not well understood.
AI.method: Proposed a dependency-graph framework with three levels of compositionality, instantiated with data-structure tasks that provide deterministic rewards and clear compositional structure. Evaluated through decomposed vs. composed training experiments, theoretical analysis, and tests on length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to unseen skills.
AI.result: Found consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training doesn't reliably transfer to composed tasks, but composed-task training transfers more readily to decomposed tasks. Also showed preliminary evidence that this asymmetry extends to practical tool-calling benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Compositional reasoning in language models exhibits fundamental training asymmetries, with composed-task training providing better generalization than decomposed-skill training, suggesting important implications for how to structure training for better real-world problem-solving capabilities.

title: Machine-Learning Assessment of the Predictive Value of Inflammatory Biomarkers for Cognitive Impairment in an Older Hispanic Adult Cohort
summary: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is often impractical and ensemble models can be difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility. Using data from the Panama Aging Research Initiative--Health Disparities (PARI-HD) cohort (n=165), we implemented a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier. Within every training fold, each continuous predictor was reduced to a supervised chi-square-derived state, while income entered the model through a categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats. The demographic baseline achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.630 +/- 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110, with paired DeLong tests yielding p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the pre-specified primary analysis, I-309 produced a fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with robustness assessed across 200 random partitions, where the median p-value was 0.0011. Within the exploratory family of 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved a Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions, whereas no other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value. Because the fitted model is an inspectable table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities, these results identify I-309/CCL1 as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation.

AI.tldr: BNB/CNB classifier identifies I-309 (CCL1) as the most predictive biomarker for cognitive impairment in small clinical datasets, providing interpretable threshold-based models while addressing statistical vs. predictive utility issues.
AI.motivation: Small clinical tabular datasets need interpretable ML since deep learning is impractical and ensemble models are hard to inspect; statistical significance doesn't guarantee predictive utility in biomarker discovery.
AI.method: Implemented leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes classifier; used supervised chi-square-derived states for continuous predictors; employed repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats; tested 18 candidate markers on PARI-HD cohort (n=165).
AI.result: I-309 (CCL1) increased AUC by 0.110 from baseline 0.630, with p<0.05 in 100% of repeats; achieved fixed-partition p=0.0018 and median p=0.0011 across 200 random partitions; had BH-adjusted q=0.032 while no other marker showed reliable predictive value.
AI.conclusion: I-309/CCL1 is an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment; the inspectable threshold-based model offers transparency for small clinical datasets, pending external validation.

title: Safety Beyond the Interface: Detecting Harm via Latent States in Large Language Models
summary: Autonomous systems increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) yet the safety infrastructure surrounding these models introduces latency and compute overhead. This limits utility in resource-constrained, time-critical deployments. Existing external guardrail models remain blind to the model's internal workings, creating a fundamental assurance gap. We ask: does the model already know when the content is harmful? We extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0, our probes achieve F1 scores of 99%, 83%, and 84%, respectively competitive with 1000x larger guard models while cutting latency and compute costs.

AI.tldr: Lightweight MLP probes trained on LLM activations can detect harmful prompts with high accuracy, matching performance of much larger guardrail models while reducing latency and compute costs.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems using LLMs face safety vs. efficiency trade-offs: traditional external guardrails introduce latency and compute overhead, limiting deployment in resource-constrained, time-critical scenarios. Existing safety approaches are blind to the model's internal workings, creating an assurance gap.
AI.method: The authors extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (only 12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts directly from the model's internal representations, asking "does the model already know when the content is harmful?"
AI.result: Probes achieve impressive F1 scores: 99% on WildJailbreak, 83% on Beavertails, and 84% on AEGIS 2.0. These results are competitive with guard models that are 1000x larger, while significantly reducing latency and compute costs.
AI.conclusion: LLMs already encode knowledge about harmful content in their internal activations, enabling lightweight probing approaches that match large external guardrails' safety performance while being much more efficient - addressing the latency/compute bottleneck for safety-critical autonomous systems.

title: FCx: An algorithm for finding Feasible Counterfactual Explanations
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures
summary: Counterfactual (CF) explanations identify changes that alter an input's classification. While existing methods produce realistic and low-cost CFs, they often fail to ensure feasibility, by suggesting non-constructive modifications or incompatible with future changes (e.g., changing an individual's race to secure a job offer). We introduce a refinement of CF explanations that explicitly enforces feasibility. Our approach is the first to efficiently generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost and feasible. We accommodate both hard feasible constraints, specified by domain knowledge users, and soft feasible constraints, inferred automatically via causal inference from the dataset. Our method, Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), is based on a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. We measure the cost of a change based on the absolute change in values (proximity) as well as the number of features changed (sparsity) while realism is measured based on the LOF for density estimation, guaranteeing that CFs reside in densely populated regions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that our approach matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

AI.tldr: FCx introduces a novel counterfactual explanation method that guarantees feasibility by incorporating both hard domain constraints and soft causal constraints, while maintaining realism and low cost through a modified VAE architecture.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods often fail to ensure feasibility by suggesting non-constructive modifications or changes incompatible with future realities (e.g., changing immutable characteristics like race). There's a need for counterfactuals that are not only realistic and low-cost but also actually feasible to implement.
AI.method: Proposes Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx) based on a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. The approach accommodates both hard feasible constraints (specified by domain experts) and soft feasible constraints (inferred automatically via causal inference from datasets). Uses proximity (absolute value changes) and sparsity (number of features changed) to measure cost, and Local Outlier Factor (LOF) for density estimation to ensure realism.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that FCx matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility of generated counterfactuals.
AI.conclusion: FCx represents the first approach to efficiently generate counterfactual explanations that are simultaneously realistic, low-cost, and feasible, addressing a critical limitation of existing methods by incorporating both explicit domain knowledge and data-driven causal constraints.

title: QVAC Genesis III: A Large-Scale, High-Quality Open Synthetic STEM Corpus for Efficient Language Model Pre-Training
summary: High-quality pre-training data is a critical bottleneck for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment where token budgets are tightly constrained. While major organizations train ever-larger models on private corpora, the open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models. To address this gap, we introduce QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token, STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across several difficulty levels and different educational styles. QVAC Genesis III is built via a dual generation strategy that performs targeted teacher distillation using a weak edge-scale student model as signal: the student's failures are converted into corrective explanations, while its successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. We further introduce an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks both accuracy and answer validity. To validate the effectiveness of our QVAC Genesis III data, we conduct controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models, showing that models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform both models trained with the open-source synthetic corpus Cosmopedia-v2 and the publicly released Cosmo-1B model across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks, achieving up to +28.57% on ARC-E and +21.35% on ARC-C, while reaching a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45%.

AI.tldr: QVAC Genesis III introduces a 191.43B-token STEM-focused synthetic corpus using a novel dual generation strategy and demonstrates its effectiveness by outperforming existing open-source synthetic datasets in training small models for edge AI deployment.
AI.motivation: There's a critical bottleneck in high-quality pre-training data for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment. The open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models with constrained token budgets.
AI.method: The authors introduce QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across difficulty levels and educational styles. It's built via a dual generation strategy using targeted teacher distillation: student model failures are converted into corrective explanations, while successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. They also introduce an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers and tracks both accuracy and answer validity.
AI.result: Models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform both models trained with Cosmopedia-v2 and the publicly released Cosmo-1B model across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks. They achieve up to +28.57% on ARC-E and +21.35% on ARC-C, while reaching a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45% in controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models.
AI.conclusion: QVAC Genesis III addresses the critical gap in STEM-focused synthetic pre-training data for small models, demonstrating superior performance over existing open-source alternatives through its innovative dual generation strategy and comprehensive evaluation methodology.

title: Improving Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning via Selective Reward Stimulation
summary: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn policies that reach specified goals, but remains challenging in offline settings with sparse rewards and long-horizon dependencies. In such settings, goal-completion information can be temporally distant from the early decisions that enable success, while offline value estimation introduces additional error. We study this issue from a reward-propagation perspective and show, in a stylized delayed-goal setting, how goal-directed value separation can become small relative to local estimation error. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Reward Stimulation Implicit Q-Learning (RSIQL), a simple non-hierarchical method that introduces additional reward signals at progress-making intermediate states in offline trajectories. RSIQL uses an auxiliary goal-conditioned value function to identify intermediate states estimated to make progress toward the goal and applies reward stimulation to provide less-delayed training supervision. Unlike hierarchical methods, RSIQL does not learn a separate high-level subgoal policy. Experiments on D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks and OGBench show that RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and achieves performance competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods, while retaining a simple flat policy structure.

AI.tldr: RSIQL improves offline goal-conditioned RL by adding reward signals at progress-making intermediate states identified by an auxiliary value function, outperforming baseline methods without requiring hierarchical policy structure.
AI.motivation: Offline goal-conditioned RL struggles with sparse rewards and long-horizon dependencies where goal-completion information is temporally distant from early decisions. Value estimation errors further complicate learning, as goal-directed value differences can become small relative to local estimation errors.
AI.method: RSIQL (Reward Stimulation Implicit Q-Learning) introduces additional reward signals at intermediate states estimated to make progress toward the goal, using an auxiliary goal-conditioned value function to identify these states. Unlike hierarchical methods, it maintains a simple flat policy structure without learning separate high-level subgoal policies.
AI.result: Experiments on D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks and OGBench show RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and achieves performance competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods.
AI.conclusion: RSIQL effectively addresses delayed reward propagation in offline goal-conditioned RL through intermediate reward stimulation, achieving strong performance while maintaining simplicity compared to hierarchical approaches.

title: LLM-as-an-Improver: Turning Verification into Better Candidates
summary: Verifier-based selection improves LLM performance by generating multiple candidate solutions and using a verifier to select the most promising one. However, existing methods typically treat verification only as a ranking step and discard its feedback once a fixed candidate pool has been evaluated. In this paper, we ask whether verification can also improve the candidate set itself. To this end, we introduce LLM-as-an-Improver and propose Verify--Repair--Reselect (VRR), which uses verification feedback to generate and reselect improved candidates. VRR retains the initial winner while conditionally generating three complementary alternatives: repaired versions of the winner and runner-up, and a solution based on a new approach. It filters invalid and duplicate candidates using only inference-time information and then reselects the final answer under the original evaluation criteria. Across diverse models and code-generation and reasoning benchmarks, VRR improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection in many settings and can recover correct solutions even when all candidates in the initial pool are incorrect. These results highlight a broader role for LLMs as improvers: verification feedback can not only select among existing solutions but also construct stronger candidates beyond the initial pool.

AI.tldr: VRR introduces a verification-based improvement framework where LLMs use verification feedback to repair and generate better candidates, going beyond just selecting from a fixed pool.
AI.motivation: Existing verifier-based selection methods only use verification as a ranking step and discard feedback after evaluating a fixed candidate pool. The authors question whether verification can also improve the candidate set itself.
AI.method: Verify-Repair-Reselect (VRR) framework: uses verification feedback to generate three complementary alternatives (repaired winner, repaired runner-up, and new approach solution) while retaining the initial winner. Filters invalid/duplicate candidates using only inference-time information and reselects final answer under original criteria.
AI.result: VRR improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection across diverse models and benchmarks (code-generation and reasoning). It can recover correct solutions even when all initial candidates are incorrect.
AI.conclusion: Verification feedback can construct stronger candidates beyond the initial pool, highlighting LLMs' broader role as improvers rather than just selectors.

title: Bayesian Optimization with Rich Auxiliary Information via LLMs
summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely used for optimizing expensive black-box functions, yet many real-world optimization problems contain substantially richer information than function evaluations alone. Examples include training curves in hyperparameter optimization, expert notes and images in scientific experimentation, and prior knowledge about where optima may lie. We show that large language models (LLMs) can effectively leverage such rich auxiliary information to guide optimization. Motivated by these findings, we develop three methods for incorporating auxiliary information into BO using LLMs. Across hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a real-world nuclear fusion optimization task, our methods consistently outperform both standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization approaches. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of LLMs for leveraging rich auxiliary information in BO.

AI.tldr: Large language models (LLMs) can effectively leverage rich auxiliary information (like training curves, expert notes, images) in Bayesian Optimization (BO) to outperform standard BO and existing LLM-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Real-world optimization problems often contain richer information beyond simple function evaluations (e.g., training curves in hyperparameter optimization, expert notes in scientific experiments, prior knowledge about optimal regions), but standard BO doesn't effectively utilize this auxiliary information.
AI.method: Developed three methods for incorporating auxiliary information into Bayesian Optimization using large language models (LLMs) to process and leverage rich contextual data.
AI.result: Across hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a real-world nuclear fusion optimization task, the LLM-enhanced BO methods consistently outperform both standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization approaches.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are effective for leveraging rich auxiliary information in Bayesian Optimization, demonstrating superior performance over conventional methods in both benchmark and real-world applications.

title: An Architecture for Long-Horizon Agents: Levels, Ticks and Cascaded Intelligence
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out work spanning days or weeks, such as an operations remediation or a research programme. Such a task outlives any context window, any process and any interval at which a person can attend. In this paper, we argue that a long-horizon agent must run continually without forgetting before it can learn continually. This ability lies in the harness around the model rather than in the model itself. We derive seven bottlenecks from the long-horizon setting and answer them with a hierarchical architecture of three parts: (i) levels indexed by time scale, each keeping a bounded file summarising the level below; (ii) a clocked tick as the unit of autonomous action; and (iii) cascaded intelligence, where work is escalated to a more capable model only after failing review. We report on a ten-day campaign in which an agent built on this architecture reproduced a published reinforcement-learning result with a human attending once a day, and show (1) the agent kept the thread across every context reset and session boundary of the campaign, (2) operating knowledge written early changed later behaviour with no change to model weights, and (3) where learned components would enter such a system. Overall, our experience suggests continual learning for these agents needs a substrate outliving every context and process, and the checks the harness already runs are where a learner belongs.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical architecture for long-horizon language-model agents enables continual operation across extended timeframes (days/weeks) by maintaining memory beyond context windows and using escalation mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents need to perform tasks spanning days or weeks, which exceeds context window limitations and human attention intervals. Current systems can't maintain continuity over long horizons without forgetting.
AI.method: Three-part hierarchical architecture: (1) time-scale indexed levels with bounded file summaries, (2) clocked tick as autonomous action unit, (3) cascaded intelligence with escalation to more capable models after review failure.
AI.result: In a 10-day campaign, the agent reproduced a published RL result with daily human attendance, demonstrating: (1) continuity across context resets and sessions, (2) early-written operational knowledge influencing later behavior without weight changes, (3) identification of where learned components could integrate.
AI.conclusion: Continual learning for long-horizon agents requires a substrate that outlives context and processes; the review mechanisms in the architecture provide natural insertion points for learning components.

title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) Improves Classification Accuracy of Bacterial Raman Spectral Data Enabling Portable Diagnostics
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the ICLR 2024 Workshop on Practical ML for Low Resource Settings (PML4LRS)
summary: Antimicrobial resistance is expected to claim 10 million lives per year by 2050, and resource-limited regions are most affected. Raman spectroscopy is a novel pathogen diagnostic approach promising rapid and portable antibiotic resistance testing within a few hours, compared to days when using gold standard methods. However, current algorithms for Raman spectra analysis 1) are unable to generalize well on limited datasets across diverse patient populations and 2) require increased complexity due to the necessity of non-trivial pre-processing steps, such as feature extraction, which are essential to mitigate the low-quality nature of Raman spectral data. In this work, we address these limitations using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to enhance model generalization across a diverse array of hyperparameters in clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks. We demonstrate that SAM achieves accuracy improvements of up to 10.5% on a single split, and an increase in average accuracy of 2.7% across all splits in spectral classification tasks over the traditional optimizer, Adam. These results display the capability of SAM to advance the clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy tools.

AI.tldr: SAM optimizer improves Raman spectroscopy classification for antimicrobial resistance testing, achieving up to 10.5% accuracy boost over Adam optimizer on bacterial isolate data.
AI.motivation: Antimicrobial resistance is a global crisis claiming 10 million lives annually by 2050, especially in resource-limited regions. Raman spectroscopy offers rapid antibiotic resistance testing (hours vs days) but current AI algorithms suffer from poor generalization on limited datasets and require complex preprocessing steps.
AI.method: The authors use Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to enhance model generalization for clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks. SAM works by optimizing for flat loss landscapes rather than just low loss values, improving generalization across diverse hyperparameters and patient populations.
AI.result: SAM achieves accuracy improvements of up to 10.5% on a single split and an average accuracy increase of 2.7% across all splits in spectral classification tasks compared to the traditional Adam optimizer. This demonstrates SAM's capability to improve Raman spectroscopy AI tools.
AI.conclusion: Sharpness-Aware Minimization significantly advances the clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy for antimicrobial resistance testing by improving model generalization on limited, diverse datasets without requiring complex preprocessing steps.

title: EconSkills: Studying Skill Transfer and Retrieval for Web Agents on Live Economic Data
summary: Web agents often revisit the same sites, yet most evaluations discard the procedures learned in earlier successful interactions. We introduce EconSkills, a skill library and evaluation framework that distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures for retrieving live economic data. Each skill records its scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps while replacing source-instance values with placeholders. EconSkills separates two questions: whether a known relevant procedure transfers to a held-out task, and whether an agent can retain that benefit when selecting from a library. In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes, while abstraction is substantially more effective than replaying raw trajectories. At library scale, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and performs best on directly covered tasks; coverage-stratified outcomes show that approximate matches on uncovered tasks offset these gains. Browser trajectories further identify when procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation and when semantic verification remains necessary. These results establish that reusable economic web procedures can transfer across task instances and provide a concrete design target for coverage-aware selection and context delivery.

AI.tldr: EconSkills introduces a skill library framework that distills verified web trajectories into reusable procedures for economic data retrieval, enabling transfer across tasks and evaluating skill selection effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Web agents frequently revisit similar sites but existing evaluations discard learned procedures from successful previous interactions, wasting accumulated knowledge and requiring agents to relearn navigation patterns each time.
AI.method: Create EconSkills library with parameterized procedures extracted from EconWebArena trajectories, including scope, navigation steps, site guidance, verification checks, and recovery. Replace specific values with placeholders. Evaluate through controlled transfer experiments (matched skills vs no-skill) and library-scale retrieval testing.
AI.result: Matched skills improve success rates over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps. Parameterized abstraction outperforms replaying raw trajectories. Library retrieval is competitive with baseline overall, best on directly covered tasks. Approximate matches on uncovered tasks partially offset gains. Browser analysis shows when procedural guidance helps and when semantic verification is still needed.
AI.conclusion: Reusable economic web procedures can effectively transfer across task instances. The framework provides concrete design targets for coverage-aware skill selection and context delivery in web automation systems.

title: Enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network by Domain Knowledge
summary: Accurate prediction of nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from agriculture is important for assessing environmental impacts and supporting sustainable farming. However, prediction remains difficult because N2O emissions result from complex interactions among soil properties, climate, biochemical processes, and management practices, while high-quality observations are limited. Deep learning models can capture nonlinear relationships but often lack physical interpretability and may generalize poorly across environmental conditions. We propose the Knowledge-enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network (KAINN), a hybrid neural-mechanistic framework that extends the Agriculture-informed Neural Network by incorporating domain knowledge about fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity. We evaluate KAINN using CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures across multiple growing seasons and input-feature configurations. The results show that KAINN generally provides lower root mean square error and mean absolute error and higher R-squared values than purely data-driven models and the original AINN. Analysis of the learned interfaces also shows smoother and more physically consistent parameter trajectories with reduced uncertainty. These findings demonstrate that incorporating environmental knowledge into neural networks can improve the reliability, interpretability, and generalization of agricultural N2O-emission predictions.

AI.tldr: KAINN: A hybrid neural-mechanistic framework that combines deep learning with agricultural domain knowledge to improve prediction of nitrous oxide emissions from farming.
AI.motivation: Accurate N2O emission prediction is important for environmental assessment and sustainable farming, but remains difficult due to complex soil-climate-biochemical-management interactions and limited high-quality observations. While deep learning can capture nonlinear relationships, it often lacks physical interpretability and generalizes poorly across environmental conditions.
AI.method: Proposed Knowledge-enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network (KAINN), extending the Agriculture-informed Neural Network by incorporating domain knowledge about fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity. Evaluated with CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures across multiple growing seasons and input-feature configurations.
AI.result: KAINN generally provides lower root mean square error and mean absolute error, and higher R-squared values than purely data-driven models and the original AINN. Learned interfaces show smoother, more physically consistent parameter trajectories with reduced uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating environmental knowledge into neural networks can improve reliability, interpretability, and generalization of agricultural N2O-emission predictions.

title: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems
summary: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified framework for assessing AI trustworthiness across eight dimensions, connecting technical evaluation with governance requirements while ensuring interpretability and preventing critical failures from being masked by aggregate scores.
AI.motivation: Current benchmark scores provide incomplete assessment of AI trustworthiness. LLMs, agentic systems, and multimodal models require different assessment approaches, but evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight.
AI.method: Proposes a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. Includes system-specific metrics mapped to common performance bands with uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. Adds a meta-evaluation layer examining evaluation validity, reliability, and reproducibility. Provides safety-critical overrides to prevent masking critical failures.
AI.result: Framework provides structured basis for assessing system performance and evaluation credibility. It preserves system-specific metrics while enabling unified assessment. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and EU regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs.
AI.conclusion: The framework addresses limitations of benchmark-only assessment by providing comprehensive, interpretable trustworthiness evaluation across AI system types. Empirical validation across deployment contexts is identified as essential next step for practical implementation.

title: Search at the Cost of Sampling: Nearly-Instant Latent Space Bayesian Optimization
summary: Generative models are increasingly central to many de novo discovery pipelines, in which designs are generated at scale and filtered through virtual screens to determine a set of candidates to experimentally validate. While Bayesian optimization (BO) is a natural fit for this setting, as it uses past evaluations to guide future proposals, the computational overhead required for its sequential decision-making becomes a bottleneck when virtual screens are relatively cheap. We make BO practical in this regime by exploiting the unique combination of a linear model constrained to a spherical domain where high-dimensional latents concentrate. We build off recent work justifying the use of linear surrogates, while deriving nearly closed-form solutions to the surrogate modelling and acquisition problems that exploit spherical symmetry. The result is at least a 100x speedup over state-of-the art baselines, with matching or improved performance across molecular and image generation benchmarks. Altogether, our method makes BO a practical drop-in for de novo pipelines where it was previously too slow to consider.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a highly efficient Bayesian optimization method for generative models that achieves at least 100x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines by exploiting linear models on spherical domains where high-dimensional latents concentrate.
AI.motivation: Generative models are central to de novo discovery pipelines, but Bayesian optimization (BO) becomes a computational bottleneck when virtual screens are relatively cheap. Current BO methods have excessive computational overhead that makes them impractical in this regime.
AI.method: The method exploits the unique combination of linear models constrained to spherical domains where high-dimensional latents concentrate. It builds on recent work justifying linear surrogates and derives nearly closed-form solutions to both surrogate modeling and acquisition problems by exploiting spherical symmetry.
AI.result: The method achieves at least 100x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines while maintaining matching or improved performance across molecular and image generation benchmarks. This makes BO practical for de novo pipelines where it was previously too slow.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method transforms BO from being computationally prohibitive to a practical drop-in solution for de novo discovery pipelines, enabling efficient guided exploration in generative model applications where cheap virtual screens are available.

title: Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search
summary: Coding agents can recursively modify their own implementations, forming a loop of self-improvement. While prior work shows this can boost performance on coding benchmarks, existing approaches are costly and compute-intensive. We introduce a simple, sample-efficient self-improvement framework that significantly improves coding performance under strict budget constraints. We identify evaluation of candidate self-modifications as the main runtime bottleneck since prior approaches estimate their effectiveness by re-running a subset of benchmark tasks with the modified agent, which is time-consuming. We introduce Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search (SIFT), which augments these downstream task evaluations with an LLM-as-a-judge signal that performs pairwise comparisons between candidate patches, where the win-loss record is aggregated with a regularized Bradley-Terry model, and the resulting strength scores drive rank-based parent sampling inside a lightweight disaggregated tree search. Expensive downstream task evaluations are reserved only for the most promising nodes. Using a fully disaggregated tree search pipeline, the judge scores provide intermediate signal to guide exploration on promising candidate patches without being bottlenecked by slow evaluation runs. SIFT outperforms existing tree-search based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in terms of CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.

AI.tldr: SIFT is a cost-effective self-improvement framework that uses LLM-as-judge pairwise comparisons and regularized Bradley-Terry scoring to guide tree search, reducing expensive benchmark evaluations and outperforming existing methods on Polyglot with lower resource requirements.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improvement approaches for coding agents are expensive and compute-intensive, with evaluation of candidate modifications being the main runtime bottleneck since they require re-running benchmark tasks.
AI.method: SIFT uses LLM-as-a-judge to perform pairwise comparisons between candidate patches, aggregates win-loss records with regularized Bradley-Terry model, and uses strength scores to drive rank-based parent sampling in lightweight disaggregated tree search. Expensive evaluations are reserved only for most promising nodes.
AI.result: SIFT outperforms existing tree-search based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in terms of CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective self-improvement for coding agents under strict budget constraints by addressing the evaluation bottleneck through intelligent search guided by inexpensive LLM judgments.

title: Sample Count Is Not Enough: Candidate-Generation Strategy Shapes the Energy and Performance of LLM Test-Time Scaling
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Experiments evaluate Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on GSM8K and SciQ using NVIDIA A100 and V100 GPUs. Studies LLM test-time scaling, candidate-generation scheduling, latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and GPU-device energy
summary: Test-time scaling can improve large language model reasoning by generating and combining multiple candidate responses. In sampling-based methods, the inference budget is often described by the number of generated candidates, N. However, N tells us how many candidates are generated, not how they are executed. The same candidate budget can be produced in one batched generation call or split across several sequential calls with smaller batch sizes. We first study the effect of increasing N on reasoning accuracy using Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 500 GSM8K prompts. As expected, increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4 percentage points for Phi-3-mini and 18.4 points for Qwen2.5-1.5B. However, accuracy alone does not show the systems cost of using a larger candidate budget. We therefore fix N = 8 and compare four generation schedules: 1x8, 2x4, 4x2, and 8x1, where axb denotes a generation calls with b candidates per call. We measure latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy while keeping the total candidate count fixed. On A100 GPUs, eight serial calls use 4.64-4.86x as much gross GPU-device energy and have 5.77-6.12x the P95 latency of one batched call with eight candidates. The same pattern appears across three independently scheduled A100 nodes per model and in short-output SciQ/V100 experiments. These results show that candidate count alone is not enough to describe the systems cost of multi-candidate test-time scaling. When candidates are independent and memory allows it, fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes are more efficient. Evaluations should therefore report not only candidate count and accuracy, but also generation schedule and GPU-level systems metrics.

AI.tldr: Test-time scaling with multiple candidate responses improves reasoning accuracy but the same candidate count (N) can be executed with different generation schedules affecting systems cost significantly - fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes are more efficient.
AI.motivation: Current test-time scaling methods focus on candidate count (N) but ignore how candidates are executed (generation schedule), which significantly impacts systems cost metrics like latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and energy consumption.
AI.method: Study effect of increasing N on reasoning accuracy using Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on GSM8K, then fix N=8 and compare four generation schedules (1x8, 2x4, 4x2, 8x1) measuring latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy on A100 GPUs.
AI.result: Increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4pp for Phi-3-mini and 18.4pp for Qwen2.5-1.5B. With N=8 fixed, eight serial calls use 4.64-4.86x more energy and have 5.77-6.12x higher P95 latency than one batched call with eight candidates.
AI.conclusion: Candidate count alone is insufficient to describe systems cost of multi-candidate test-time scaling. When candidates are independent and memory allows, fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes are more efficient. Evaluations should report generation schedule and GPU-level systems metrics.

title: When Hiring Becomes Agent-Mediated: Evaluating Access and Recurrence in Two-Agent Résumé Screening
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure. Accepted to the REALM Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Hiring is bilateral: employers assess fit, while candidates present and defend evidence of their qualifications. Yet résumé screening, the first gate, is commonly automated as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé-job pair. We study a two-agent alternative in which employer-side and candidate-side agents represent these roles, exchange evidence, and update their judgments before deciding who advances. We compare procedures on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3% to 39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0% to 35.5% for Opus 4.7). Across three runs on the common 191-pair borderline pool, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5% to 26.2% and from 6.5% to 16.1%, respectively. This is not a uniform relaxation: two-agent screening rejects applications one-call advances, changing decisions in both directions. At similar pass volumes, the procedures advance different applications, and no one-call threshold recovers applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Among discovery-selected cases re-executed in fresh runs, two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections, clearly under GPT-5.5 and less certainly under Opus 4.7, while a separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline. As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure, not only the model behind it, shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs.

AI.tldr: Two-agent AI screening (employer and candidate agents) shows higher advancement rates and different decision patterns than traditional one-call résumé screening, with less reliable recurrence for unique selections.
AI.motivation: Current automated résumé screening treats hiring as a static, one-way judgment, ignoring the bilateral nature where employers assess fit while candidates present evidence. This creates an unrealistic screening process.
AI.method: Developed a two-agent system where employer-side and candidate-side agents interact, exchange evidence, and update judgments before decisions. Tested on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7, with three runs on 191 borderline pairs.
AI.result: Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3%→39.3% GPT-5.5; 34.0%→35.5% Opus 4.7). Decision changes occur in both directions, with different applications selected even at similar pass volumes. Two-agent-only selections recur less reliably than shared selections, especially under GPT-5.5.
AI.conclusion: The screening procedure itself, not just the AI model, shapes who reaches human review in hiring. As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the interaction dynamics between agents crucially influence decision reliability and outcomes.

title: LSTM-UT and Recurrent-Depth Transformers on Cellular Automata
summary: Recurrent-depth Transformers apply shared computation repeatedly, but differ in how they retain information across steps. We compare a Block Universal Transformer (BUT), which carries only its current hidden state; CoTFormer, which also retains an expanding attention cache; and a new LSTM Universal Transformer (LSTM-UT) with bounded gated memory. On Rule 30 cellular automata, BUT extrapolates to unseen recurrent depths more reliably than CoTFormer, although its accuracy eventually degrades. State and cache interventions show that CoTFormer's failure depends on their interaction: correcting the current state can temporarily restore accuracy, while retained history can undermine that correction. In a delayed-recall task, BUT also outperforms CoTFormer despite lacking direct access to past states; CoTFormer does not reliably select the requested cached representation. LSTM-UT improves both depth extrapolation and delayed recall over these baselines. The results support bounded gated memory as an effective inductive bias for repeated computation and later retrieval in these tasks.

AI.tldr: Recurrent-depth transformers with bounded gated memory (LSTM-UT) outperform both block universal transformers (BUT) and CoTFormers in depth extrapolation and delayed recall tasks, showing bounded gated memory is an effective inductive bias for repeated computation and retrieval.
AI.motivation: To understand how different recurrent-depth transformers retain information across computational steps and compare their performance on tasks requiring repeated computation and later retrieval.
AI.method: Compare three architectures: Block Universal Transformer (BUT) with only current hidden state, CoTFormer with expanding attention cache, and new LSTM Universal Transformer (LSTM-UT) with bounded gated memory. Test on Rule 30 cellular automata depth extrapolation and delayed-recall tasks. Conduct state and cache interventions to analyze failure modes.
AI.result: BUT extrapolates to unseen recurrent depths more reliably than CoTFormer, though accuracy eventually degrades. CoTFormer's failures stem from interaction between state and cache - correcting state temporarily helps but retained history undermines corrections. BUT also outperforms CoTFormer in delayed recall despite lacking direct past state access. LSTM-UT improves both depth extrapolation and delayed recall over both baselines.
AI.conclusion: Bounded gated memory (as in LSTM-UT) is an effective inductive bias for repeated computation and later retrieval, outperforming both minimal-state (BUT) and expanding-cache (CoTFormer) approaches in the tested tasks.

title: Compressed Active Subspaces for Scalable Bayesian Inference
summary: Active subspace methods provide a framework for quantifying predictive uncertainty in high-dimensional models by identifying and performing inference along parameter directions that have the greatest influence on the model output. However, the construction of active subspaces requires storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases. We address this limitation by proposing Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS), a scalable approach that first maps the model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding and then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization. Our approach substantially reduces the memory required for active subspace construction and enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical. We demonstrate the scalability of CAS on neural networks of increasing size while maintaining predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates.

AI.tldr: Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS) enables scalable uncertainty quantification for high-dimensional models by constructing active subspaces in compressed parameter spaces, overcoming memory limitations of traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional active subspace methods require storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive for large models due to memory constraints. This limits their applicability to modern high-dimensional models like large neural networks.
AI.method: CAS first compresses model parameters using structured isometric embeddings, then constructs active subspaces within this reduced parameterization. This significantly reduces memory requirements while preserving key information for uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: The method demonstrates scalability on neural networks of increasing size while maintaining predictive performance and providing robust uncertainty estimates, enabling Bayesian inference for large models where standard approaches become impractical.
AI.conclusion: CAS provides a practical solution for scalable uncertainty quantification in high-dimensional models by bridging the gap between active subspace methods' theoretical advantages and practical computational constraints.

title: Continual Enterprise World Model Discovery in Dynamic Systems
summary: In an enterprise system, updating one field can set another, create a record, or start an approval. These effects are produced by business rules that are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent working in such a system cannot predict the result of its own actions without knowing these rules. We study continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts without knowledge of these business rules and discovers them by interacting with records and observing the outcomes. From those observations it builds a world model, which it revises as the rules change. To evaluate this, we introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, built on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules and 600 evaluation actions. It presents four versions of the same enterprise world, with the tables and records held fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, so that discovery, revision, extension and retirement are each tested in turn. Our Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds such a model and carries it from one world to the next. It predicts the effects of the hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question, the approach taken by prior work, by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.

AI.tldr: An agent discovers and continually updates business rules in enterprise systems by interacting with records, building world models that outperform direct rule lookups by 8.98 IoU points.
AI.motivation: Enterprise systems contain hidden, organization-specific business rules that determine field updates, record creation, and approval workflows. Agents cannot predict action outcomes without knowing these rules, which constantly evolve as organizations revise them over time.
AI.method: Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) approach where agents start without knowledge of business rules and discover them through interaction with records and outcome observation. Built EnterpriseWorldShift benchmark on live ServiceNow environment with 9 tables, 25 hidden rules, 600 evaluation actions across four rule-changing versions.
AI.result: CDA predicts hidden rule effects more accurately than direct lookup approaches used in prior work, achieving up to 8.98 IoU point improvement. The agent can answer queries using its own learned model without querying the live system.
AI.conclusion: Continual world model discovery enables agents to effectively learn and adapt to evolving business rules in enterprise systems, outperforming static lookup methods and enabling autonomous operation without constant system queries.

title: FedFIbOS: Fisher Importance based Optimal Submodelling for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures
summary: Heterogeneous federated learning requires clients with diverse computational capacities to collaboratively train a global model, where each client trains a capacity-constrained submodel. Existing methods select submodel parameters using heuristic importance measures---most prominently parameter magnitude---without theoretical justification for why these measures support convergence. We identify a fundamental gap: existing parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding in the convergence framework, partial client participation introduces additional estimation effects in the Fisher scores. We propose \textbf{FedFIbOS}: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling for heterogeneous federated learning, using Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. %We formally establish when magnitude selection is equivalent to Fisher selection fail under non-IID heterogeneous federated learning. We theoretically formulate submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate and show that the raw Fisher top-$k$ rule implemented by FedFIbOS solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition. The resulting method retains the convergence structure of the underlying masked federated optimization bound. Fisher scores are efficiently estimated from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves ${\approx}10\%$ higher accuracy than the state of the art, with improvements becoming more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: FedFIbOS is a theoretically-grounded heterogeneous federated learning method that uses Fisher information for principled submodel parameter selection, achieving ~10% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods under various non-IID settings.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous federated learning methods use heuristic importance measures (like parameter magnitude) without theoretical justification for convergence. There's a fundamental gap: current parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding, and partial client participation introduces estimation effects in Fisher scores.
AI.method: Proposes FedFIbOS: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling. Uses Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. Theoretically formulates submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate, showing that raw Fisher top-k selection solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition. Fisher scores are efficiently estimated from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves ~10% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. Improvements become more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: FedFIbOS provides a theoretically-grounded approach to submodel selection in heterogeneous federated learning using Fisher information, maintaining convergence structure while enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead, significantly outperforming existing methods.

title: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
comment: COLM 2026 Learning from Situated and Embodied Interaction Workshop
summary: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only what people need in the moment, but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. We introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on SimLife, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding: the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks or months of everyday observations. The benchmark contains 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, and 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints. Evaluating frontier models and architectures, we find that current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change. These findings suggest that long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

AI.tldr: SimLife is a simulation platform and benchmark (SimLife-BP) for evaluating AI models' ability to understand long-term behavioral patterns in household settings from weeks/months of observation.
AI.motivation: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer routines, why they repeat, and when they change. Current AI struggles with comprehensive pattern understanding from extended observations.
AI.method: Built the SimLife platform with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues. Created SimLife-BP benchmark with 106 episodes (average 15.49 hours, 38.57 days) and 1,439 QA pairs testing direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning with varying rule hints.
AI.result: Current frontier models achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.
AI.conclusion: Long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens research opportunities for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in human-AI interaction.

title: The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability
summary: Complexity measured from generated code is failure-dependent: a difficult prompt can yield a short failing program and be assigned low output complexity. We introduce a six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation and kept separate from correctness. We select 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater rubric. Four out-of-panel LLM raters rescore the locked prompts, giving 19,997 score rows; composite inter-rater reliability is ICC = 0.872 on the 4,998 prompts with all four ratings. We evaluate 21 models per prompt, yielding 105,000 generations. In the unadjusted mean-pooled analysis, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 13.75, with 79.9% at or below and 87.6% above. This is not a universal failure cutoff. Task-type fixed effects shift the breakpoint to 10.75 and cut the regime gap from 7.6 to 2.1 points. A construction-frame control shifts it to 8.50 with a raw gap of -3.5 points, and neither frame alone reproduces the pooled +7.6-point change. Model-specific fits include 16 upward and five downward changes. A 365-prompt audit-clean extension matches the original five-model estimates at bins 15 and 16 but adds only 14 prompts above bin 16. Among zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity, 28.5% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity at most 10. Human agreement is moderate and rater-dependent on a disagreement-enriched calibration set; paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve score ordering. Overidentification tests reject the joint restrictions on the six dimensions, so we treat the composite as an index and make no causal interpretation of the 2SLS estimates. The contribution is a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes.

AI.tldr: Researchers introduce a six-dimension prompt-side structural complexity index that's scored before code generation, finding a nonmonotonic relationship between prompt complexity and code generation success rates across 21 models.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity measures based on generated code output are failure-dependent, meaning difficult prompts can yield short failing programs and be assigned low complexity scores. This creates a need for prompt-side complexity measurement that's independent of generation correctness.
AI.method: Develop a six-dimension structural complexity index for prompts, score 5,000 Python prompts across complexity bands using LLM raters, evaluate 21 models per prompt (105k generations total), analyze pass rates relative to complexity scores with statistical modeling and fixed effects.
AI.result: Found nonmonotonic breakpoint at complexity 13.75 with 79.9% pass rate below and 87.6% above. Task-type fixed effects shift breakpoint to 10.75 and reduce gap to 2.1 points. Model-specific fits show varied complexity effects, with 28.5% of zero-pass generations having high prompt complexity but low output complexity.
AI.conclusion: Provides a pre-generation complexity measurement framework, shows reliability varies by complexity regime, rejects causal interpretation of dimension effects, contributes bounded observational analysis with moderate human agreement on scoring.

title: From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

AI.tldr: A benchmark for evaluating LLM safety decisions in vehicle voice assistants, revealing that even top-performing models still make dangerous false executes, necessitating independent safety enforcement layers.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants, creating safety-critical authorization problems where systems must decide whether to execute, refuse, or modify commands. Prior evaluations don't isolate pre-action decisions across key factors like speaker role, authentication, vehicle state, and tool availability.
AI.method: Created a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions using a seven-class taxonomy. Evaluated two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics, with controlled ablations comparing structured authorization policies against baselines.
AI.result: Alignment ranges from 40.1% (Llama 3.2 3B) to 89.1% (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview). API models score 83.2-89.1% with no significant differences, but still produce 2-3 False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios. Structured policies improve alignment but don't eliminate False Executes.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM decisions are insufficient as standalone safety mechanisms for vehicle voice assistants. Deployment requires independent enforcement layers to verify tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before function invocation.

title: A Policy Profile for Croissant: Refusal as a Property of the Dataset
comment: 23 pages. Reference implementation and conformance corpus archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22018156 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.22016112
summary: Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets: JSON-LD over schema.org. Since version 1.1 it also carries data use conditions, recommending DUO and ODRL for them. What no version specifies is how any of them is evaluated: no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no outcome for a condition an implementation cannot evaluate, no record of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority. We supply that half.
