An additive profile lets a dataset declare the operations it admits and the conditions under which it admits them, over a closed set of five operators whose decision procedure is given in full, so a gate decides from the descriptor alone and records what it checked. Two corpora evaluate it and their evidence is kept apart. Three descriptors that gated a real nf-core pipeline give the deployment result: decisions from a profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record, stripping the layer leaves a valid Croissant document, and the added cost is 11.7 $μ$s against a 119 $μ$s decision. A corpus generated from the profile's grammar gives the breadth, covering every operator, refusal class and conformance clause. Across its valid cases, 552 complete decision records agree three ways -- native descriptor, profile terms, and the same policy as ODRL in usageInfo. The carrier is therefore not the contribution; the evaluation semantics is. Finally, caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.

AI.tldr: Croissant ML dataset descriptors lack evaluation mechanisms for data use conditions; this work adds an additive profile with five operators having complete decision procedures, enabling automated evaluation with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Croissant, the standard machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets, carries data use conditions but lacks specifications for how to evaluate them: no decision procedures, no bounds on evaluation cost, no outcomes for unevaluable conditions, no records of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority.
AI.method: Developed an additive profile that lets datasets declare admitted operations and conditions using a closed set of five operators with fully specified decision procedures. Gates can decide from the descriptor alone and record what was checked. Evaluated with two corpora and deployed in a real nf-core pipeline.
AI.result: The profile adds only 11.7 μs to a 119 μs decision cost. Valid Croissant documents remain after stripping the profile layer. Across 552 valid cases, decision records agree three ways: native descriptor, profile terms, and ODRL usageInfo policies. Caller-bound and data-bound policies don't overlap in permission sets.
AI.conclusion: The carrier (Croissant format) is not the main contribution; the evaluation semantics is. The additive profile provides practical evaluation mechanisms for data use conditions while maintaining compatibility and minimal overhead.

title: Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs
summary: Reinforcement learning now trains language-model agents that act over dozens of steps in live environments. The gains are large, and they are read as better decision-making. An agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs. Each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so the states it meets late in an episode are partly of its own making. An SFT checkpoint and an RL checkpoint are then scored from different states, even on identical tasks. Endpoint success mixes two changes: where the agent arrives, and what it does once it is there. Restricting the comparison to states both policies reach does not separate them. That restriction selects on an outcome, and in our data it flips the sign of the effect. We introduce checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another, with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH and SOLVE. REACH is how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE is how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher by solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction. Handoff asks only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion beside endpoint success.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces checkpoint handoff, a method to separate RL agent performance into REACH (ability to reach promising states) and SOLVE (ability to complete tasks from those states), showing RL improves both components compared to SFT.
AI.motivation: Current RL evaluation conflates two effects: where agents arrive in state space and what they do once there. Comparing RL and SFT checkpoints is problematic because they visit different states in closed-loop environments, making it hard to isolate whether gains come from better state reaching or better task completion.
AI.method: Checkpoint handoff: clones a state that one checkpoint (e.g., RL) reached and hands it to another checkpoint (e.g., SFT) without retraining. By crossing reacher role (policy that reaches states) and solver role (policy that completes from those states), they decompose performance into REACH (frequency of arriving at states close to success) and SOLVE (frequency of completing from identical cloned states).
AI.result: Across two benchmarks and two pipelines, RL improves both REACH and SOLVE compared to SFT. RL histories are more valuable to RL solvers than to SFT solvers. On ALFWorld, the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. The interaction between REACH and SOLVE gaps predicts overall performance differences.
AI.conclusion: Checkpoint handoff provides a clean decomposition of RL agent performance, revealing that RL gains come from both better navigation through state space and better task completion from given states. This evaluation protocol enables more fine-grained analysis of long-horizon agent capabilities.

title: CoRe: Coherence and Relational Alignment for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Direct forecasting has become a standard paradigm for multivariate time-series forecasting because it predicts the full future horizon in a single pass. However, its training objective is often still decomposed into pointwise errors such as MSE. Such objectives provide stable supervision, but they do not explicitly preserve the structure of the future trajectory: temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables can both be weakened. We propose CoRe, a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate forecasting. CoRe replaces pointwise supervision with two output-space constraints: a frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra, and a low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The resulting objective introduces no trainable parameters and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings overall consistently.

AI.tldr: CoRe: A model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate forecasting that replaces pointwise errors with frequency coherence and relational graph constraints to preserve trajectory structure.
AI.motivation: Direct forecasting models predict full future horizons in one pass but use pointwise errors (like MSE) that don't explicitly preserve the structure of future trajectories, weakening temporal coherence within variables and relational consistency across variables.
AI.method: CoRe introduces two output-space constraints: 1) frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra, and 2) low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. It's model-agnostic, adds no trainable parameters, and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss.
AI.result: Experiments on standard benchmarks show CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings consistently.
AI.conclusion: CoRe provides a simple yet effective alternative to pointwise objectives for direct multivariate forecasting by explicitly preserving trajectory structure through frequency coherence and relational consistency constraints, offering consistent improvements without architectural changes.

title: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
summary: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/

AI.tldr: ScientistTwo is a fully autonomous multi-agent AI framework that independently conducts end-to-end scientific research, generating publishable papers and executable codebases that outperform human state-of-the-art work.
AI.motivation: The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research where AI can independently navigate scientific landscapes, identify bottlenecks, and expand knowledge frontiers without human intervention. Current AI tools are mostly assistive rather than autonomous.
AI.method: ScientistTwo is a multi-agent framework that takes initial problems as input, establishes baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, coordinates specialized agents for end-to-end discovery cycles, conducts experiments with diverse datasets/metrics, performs automated ablation studies, and validates findings through simulated peer-review rebuttal engines.
AI.result: ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level publishable papers and fully verified executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents when benchmarked against top-tier conference papers (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS).
AI.conclusion: ScientistTwo demonstrates capability as an autonomous scientific pioneer rather than just an assistive tool, showing AI can independently push frontiers of human discovery by conducting complete research cycles from problem formulation to peer-review validation.

title: Conservation Buys Stability and Factoring Buys Counterfactuals in Physical World Models
summary: A learned simulator can reproduce its training conditions accurately yet fail in two distinct ways once those conditions change. Over long rollouts, small errors accumulate until the trajectory drifts away from physically plausible behavior; under an intervention on a physical parameter, the model may continue to follow the law seen during training rather than the intervened one. We show that these two failures require different structural remedies. Evolving a learned energy with a symplectic integrator preserves the geometry of the conservative dynamics and keeps rollouts bounded and physically meaningful for up to $100\times$ the training horizon, while equal-capacity predictors, an energy-regularized predictor, and a tuned neural ODE diverge. By contrast, encoding the physical coupling through an explicit linear factorization enables the model to follow a never-seen sign of that coupling, whereas an unrestricted parameterization remains locked to the training law. Crucially, the two mechanisms are separable: removing the structure responsible for long-horizon stability leaves counterfactual transfer intact, while removing the factorized coupling destroys counterfactual transfer without eliminating stability. This double dissociation, established with matched controls that remove or replace one structural component at a time, persists beyond the headline three-body system and remains visible when the physical state must be inferred from pixels rather than provided directly. The result is a concrete design principle for physical world models: long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments, and each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that learned physics simulators fail in two distinct ways outside training conditions, requiring different structural remedies: symplectic integration for long-horizon stability and explicit linear factorization for counterfactual generalization.
AI.motivation: Learned simulators can accurately reproduce training conditions but fail in two distinct ways when conditions change: accumulating small errors over long rollouts causes divergence from physical plausibility, and failing to adapt to interventions on physical parameters causes the model to continue following training laws rather than intervened ones.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate that these failures require different structural remedies: using symplectic integrators with learned energy for long-horizon stability preserves conservative dynamics geometry, while encoding physical coupling through explicit linear factorization enables adaptation to never-seen parameter interventions. They establish a double dissociation through matched controls that remove or replace one structural component at a time.
AI.result: Symplectic integrators keep rollouts bounded and physically meaningful for up to 100× the training horizon, while explicit linear factorization enables models to follow never-seen coupling signs. The two mechanisms are separable - removing long-horizon stability structure leaves counterfactual transfer intact, and vice versa. This double dissociation persists beyond three-body systems and when physical state must be inferred from pixels.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments in physical world models. Each can be deliberately imposed without requiring the other, providing a concrete design principle for building robust learned simulators.

title: Opinion Dynamics-based Coalition Formation for Federated Learning in Heterogeneous IoT Systems
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving, on-device training across heterogeneous Internet-of-Things (IoT) deployments such as smart-city water-metering networks, where each smart meter observes a household-specific consumption time series. Under such statistical heterogeneity, the standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) aggregation averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that may fail to capture client-specific patterns. We address this by forming client coalitions directly in the local-weight space and aggregating at the coalition level. Extending a prior weight-driven coalition-formation scheme, we model coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on the local weights, and develop variants of the HK interaction based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting with local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models and evaluated against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg with Euclidean-distance or cosine-similarity coalition formation. Experiments on a real smart-metering dataset of water consumption show that the proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations, incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg, and reduces the average MAE by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).

AI.tldr: Federated learning framework using Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics for client coalition formation improves water consumption forecasting accuracy over standard FL methods.
AI.motivation: Standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) fails to capture client-specific patterns under statistical heterogeneity in IoT deployments like smart-metering networks, where each client observes household-specific consumption time series.
AI.method: Form client coalitions directly in local-weight space using Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence opinion dynamics with Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria, applied to local LSTM models for water consumption forecasting.
AI.result: HK-based coalition formation produces stable coalition structures within 10 iterations, incurs no additional computation/communication overhead, reduces average MAE by up to 54% vs FedAvg, 39% vs FedProx, 24% vs Per-FedAvg, and achieves highest global accuracy (83-85%).
AI.conclusion: Weight-driven coalition formation via HK opinion dynamics effectively handles statistical heterogeneity in FL, significantly improving forecasting accuracy for real-world smart-metering applications without increasing client-side costs.

title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

AI.tldr: When2Think is a post-training framework that dynamically allocates computation to hybrid reasoning models based on problem difficulty, improving efficiency without sacrificing accuracy on hard problems.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have systematic inefficiency: they overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches like uniform length penalties or rigid routing methods trade accuracy on hard instances for reduced computation on easy ones, creating an "efficiency tax."
AI.method: When2Think formulates efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem. It introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that uses pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. The method combines verifier-based rewards with batch-wise standardized advantages, enabling stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries.
AI.result: On mathematical benchmarks, When2Think shows improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: On AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model. On AIME25, it achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming both compression and routing-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: When2Think effectively learns when to use System 1 (NoThink, direct answering) for easy instances versus System 2 (Think, extended reasoning) for hard instances, enabling LRMs to achieve better efficiency-accuracy trade-offs through instance-adaptive computation allocation.

title: Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling: A Specification and Design Guide for Contrast-Based Multi-Armed Bandits
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables in the main text; 2 figures and 3 tables in the supplement. Reference implementation at https://github.com/sulgik/orts
summary: Batched multi-armed bandits update on a service's own schedule, and the usual implementation carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level moves between batches, that memory goes stale even though the comparisons between arms may not have. Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS) instead carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and fits the common level afresh in every batch, marginalizing it out. This paper specifies that update, places it inside a Bayesian bandit agent with two controls, decay for how much past evidence survives an update and aggressiveness for how sharply belief becomes allocation, and evaluates it against absolute-rate memory. Across 86 public A/B series the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In prespecified synthetic environments a moving level costs absolute-rate memory five times the regret and leaves the best arm below a majority of traffic in 7 of 20 runs, against none for OR-TS. In a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments, where the contrasts are too small to resolve, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 of them, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often. Where the contrasts themselves move, the bet fails, and that case is reported too.

AI.tldr: OR-TS (Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling) is a Bayesian bandit method that tracks log-odds contrasts rather than absolute reward rates, with better performance when the shared baseline level varies between batches.
AI.motivation: Traditional batched multi-armed bandits remember each arm's absolute reward rate between updates. This approach fails when the shared baseline level changes between batches, making the stored rates stale even though relative differences between arms may remain valid.
AI.method: OR-TS maintains a joint posterior over log-odds contrasts (differences between arms) rather than absolute rates. It fits the common baseline level fresh in each batch and marginalizes it out. The method includes two controls: decay (how much past evidence survives updates) and aggressiveness (how sharply beliefs translate to allocations).
AI.result: In 86 public A/B tests, baseline levels varied about 25x more than contrasts. In synthetic environments with moving baselines, absolute-rate memory suffered 5x higher regret and failed to give the best arm majority traffic in 7/20 runs (vs. 0/20 for OR-TS). In 71 real experiments with small contrasts, expected-click differences stayed within 0.1% for 58 cases, but OR-TS still ended on the better arm more than twice as often. However, OR-TS fails when contrasts themselves move.
AI.conclusion: OR-TS provides superior performance for batched bandits in environments where baseline levels vary significantly between batches, outperforming absolute-rate memory methods. The approach is particularly valuable when relative arm performance is stable but absolute metrics fluctuate.

title: Learn Your Own Thoughts: Abstract Token Curriculum
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable reasoning capabilities by utilizing chain-of-thought (CoT) as a scratchpad for intermediate stages of thinking. However, CoT techniques require explicit supervision on thinking tokens, which requires rich, task-specific data. In this work, we propose Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC), a novel curriculum learning framework that elicits effective continuous intermediate representations without direct supervision or manual scratchpad design. ATC gradually increases problem complexity through a sequence of distributions, training the model to develop internal abstract ``thoughts'' in the continuous representation space. This paper provides both theoretical and experimental evidence for the benefits of ATC and its advantages over previous methods for training continuous thoughts. Theoretically, we show that for learning parity functions with single-layer softmax attention using ATC, attention naturally focuses on the CoT tokens in the context that provide the ``easiest path'' to predicting the next token. Experimentally, we show ATC's effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks.

AI.tldr: ATC is a curriculum learning framework that trains LLMs to develop internal abstract continuous representations for reasoning without explicit supervision or manual scratchpad design.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought (CoT) techniques require explicit supervision on thinking tokens and task-specific data, which limits their applicability. There's a need for methods that can elicit effective intermediate representations without such direct supervision.
AI.method: Proposes Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC), a curriculum learning framework that gradually increases problem complexity through a sequence of distributions. It trains models to develop internal abstract "thoughts" in continuous representation space without direct supervision or manual scratchpad design.
AI.result: Theoretical: For learning parity functions with single-layer softmax attention using ATC, attention naturally focuses on CoT tokens that provide the "easiest path" to predicting next tokens. Experimental: ATC shows effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: ATC provides a novel approach to elicit effective continuous intermediate representations for reasoning in LLMs without explicit supervision, offering advantages over previous methods for training continuous thoughts.

title: Alliance Beats Isolation: Unifying Heterogeneous Allied Datasets Improves Classifier Performance
summary: In many application domains, such as student dropout, insurance fraud, loan approval, and machine failures, several labelled public datasets are available where (i) data is about the same type of objects but the set of actual underlying objects are disjoint; and (ii) the class labels are same; and (iii) the feature spaces of the datasets are largely distinct (heterogeneous), with a few shared features. We call such datasets as allied. A single classifier cannot be trained on both datasets together, and one classifier trained on one dataset cannot be tested on the other. In this paper, we propose a method to merge the feature-spaces into a single feature-space for a pair of given allied heterogeneous datasets. We then use a matrix completion method to create a unified dataset based on the merged feature-space. The hypothesis is that the merged representation facilitates the transfer of classification knowledge from one dataset to another. We conduct experiments on several pairs of allied, heterogeneous datasets and several classifiers to demonstrate that any classifier trained on the unified representation always outperforms classifiers separately trained on the constituent allied datasets on several pairs of allied datasets. This work provides an easy way to substantially improve classifier performance by unifying and using multiple allied datasets together.

AI.tldr: A method to merge feature-spaces from disjoint but related datasets to create unified representations that improve classifier performance across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Many real-world applications have multiple labeled datasets that are about the same type of objects but have disjoint object sets, same class labels, and largely distinct (heterogeneous) feature spaces with only a few shared features. These "allied" datasets cannot be used together with standard classifiers since each dataset has different features, preventing knowledge transfer between them.
AI.method: The paper proposes: 1) A method to merge feature-spaces from a pair of allied heterogeneous datasets into a single unified feature-space. 2) Using matrix completion to create a unified dataset based on the merged feature-space representation, enabling classifiers to leverage information from both datasets.
AI.result: Experiments on several pairs of allied, heterogeneous datasets show that any classifier trained on the unified representation always outperforms classifiers separately trained on the constituent allied datasets. The approach provides substantial performance improvements across various classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables effective knowledge transfer between allied datasets by creating unified representations, offering an easy way to substantially improve classifier performance by utilizing multiple related datasets together rather than treating them separately.

title: AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection
summary: LLM agents have recently shown promise in automating machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback. Data, however, remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. We frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features, i.e., lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity. We introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms. Unlike prior data mixture methods that optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, AutoData searches a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically by iteratively refining algorithms with validation feedback from a proxy model. Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on this small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE. These results suggest that data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

AI.tldr: AutoData is an LLM agent that automates pre-training data selection by searching over executable algorithms, outperforming human-designed curation pipelines and showing transferability to larger scales.
AI.motivation: While LLM agents have shown promise in automating model and training code optimization, data engineering has remained largely outside this agentic loop. Current data mixture methods only optimize weights over fixed domains, lacking the ability to discover richer feature interactions and selection rules automatically.
AI.method: AutoData frames data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features (lexical stats, categorical labels, perplexity). It searches directly over executable selection algorithms in a rich program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules. The agent iteratively refines algorithms using validation feedback from a proxy model.
AI.result: Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on a small proxy model, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream CORE metric.
AI.conclusion: Data engineering can be effectively treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data domain. This approach enables automatic discovery of complex feature interactions and selection strategies.

title: OceanMoE: Structured Conditional Sparse Computation for Long-Horizon Multivariate Ocean Forecasting
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Yishun Zhu and Jian Wang contributed equally to this research
summary: Multivariate ocean forecasting must exploit shared evolution in a coupled ocean system while adapting to the heterogeneous statistical and dynamical characteristics of different prediction variables and locations. Fully shared models may lack the flexibility to handle this heterogeneity, whereas fully independent models discard the common ocean context shared across variables. The key question is how to retain shared context in a unified model while allowing computation to specialize according to the prediction target and local state. We propose OceanMoE, a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework that combines sharing and specialization for multivariate ocean forecasting. OceanMoE fuses cross-variable information to construct target-specific local representations and uses them to perform content-conditioned sparse routing at each spatial location, with the number of active experts adapted to router confidence. In the decoder, routing is augmented with a learned geographic bias parameterized by spherical-harmonic spatial bases, while shared residual and seasonal pathways provide common cross-variable and month-dependent context. Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show that OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error in both evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than the corresponding baselines over most later rollout months. Routing analyses further show that expert allocation varies with prediction targets and spatial locations. These results support structured conditional computation as a modeling strategy for balancing shared ocean context with adaptive specialization.

AI.tldr: OceanMoE: A Mixture-of-Experts framework for multivariate ocean forecasting that balances shared ocean context with target-specific specialization using conditional sparse routing and spherical-harmonic spatial bases.
AI.motivation: Multivariate ocean forecasting needs to exploit shared evolution in coupled ocean systems while handling heterogeneous statistical/dynamical characteristics of different variables and locations. Fully shared models lack flexibility, while fully independent models discard common ocean context.
AI.method: Propose OceanMoE, a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework. It fuses cross-variable information to create target-specific local representations, uses content-conditioned sparse routing adapted to router confidence, and augments routing with learned geographic bias parameterized by spherical-harmonic spatial bases. Includes shared residual and seasonal pathways.
AI.result: Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error in both evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than baselines over most later rollout months. Routing analysis shows expert allocation varies with prediction targets and spatial locations.
AI.conclusion: Structured conditional computation is an effective modeling strategy for balancing shared ocean context with adaptive specialization in multivariate ocean forecasting.

title: Rethinking Multi-Agent Collaboration: When More Is Less
summary: The rapid advancement of large language models and single-agent harnesses has reshaped the landscape of autonomous systems, raising a critical question of when multi-agent collaboration offers genuine value. As individual agent capabilities continue to scale, multi-agent collaboration faces diminishing returns while incurring growing context overhead. Through systematic analysis, we delineate the capability boundaries of multi-agent collaboration relative to single-agent alternatives, showing that it confers systematic benefits specifically in long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent harnesses remain superior in tightly coupled, sequential workflows. Building on these insights, we propose SAIGE, a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism based on Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution. SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph, where nodes are agent instances spawned on demand and edges encode semantic dependencies established through content-based information retrieval. Experiments on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks show that SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance, and that scaling the agent pool or deepening the recursion level does not consistently improve outcomes. Our findings suggest that multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal, and that more agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent.

AI.tldr: SAIGE introduces a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism that shows multi-agent systems are only beneficial for specific task types (long-horizon with sparse dependencies), not universally superior, and scaling agent count doesn't consistently improve performance.
AI.motivation: To determine when multi-agent collaboration genuinely adds value over single-agent systems, as LLM capabilities scale and multi-agent collaboration faces diminishing returns with growing context overhead.
AI.method: Proposed SAIGE (Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution) - a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism that models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph where nodes are agent instances spawned on demand and edges encode semantic dependencies established through content-based information retrieval.
AI.result: SAIGE achieves favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance on long-horizon complex task benchmarks. Scaling agent pool or deepening recursion doesn't consistently improve outcomes. Multi-agent collaboration benefits long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent systems excel at tightly coupled sequential workflows.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal, and more agents don't necessarily make a system more intelligent. The paper establishes clear capability boundaries for multi-agent collaboration vs. single-agent alternatives.

title: PhyRestore: Physics-Structured Latent-Factor Restoration
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is challenging when physically meaningful input factors are noisy or corrupted, particularly because substantial changes are rare relative to the large number of locations exhibiting little change. We study this problem through the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and introduce PhyRestore, a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework. Rather than directly predicting soil-loss change or correcting a degraded physical estimate, PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors and reconstructs temporal change through the known physical relationship. We evaluate PhyRestore in a watershed-scale bitemporal raster setting under isolated and simultaneous corruption of rainfall erosivity and cover management, comparing it with the degraded RUSLE estimate and Direct RF, XGBoost, MLP, and CNN models. Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when the corrupted factors remain identifiable, but its advantage weakens under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside the training support.

AI.tldr: PhyRestore: A physics-structured framework that restores corrupted soil-loss factors using latent variables and reconstructs change through known physical relationships, outperforming direct ML approaches in factor recovery but weakening under extreme conditions.
AI.motivation: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is challenging when physical input factors are noisy/corrupted, especially because substantial changes are rare compared to locations with little change. This requires robust methods to handle factor degradation in soil loss estimation.
AI.method: Introduces PhyRestore, a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework that restores corrupted physical factors (like rainfall erosivity and cover management) rather than directly predicting soil-loss change. Uses Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) physical relationship to reconstruct temporal change from restored factors.
AI.result: PhyRestore improves high-magnitude recovery when corrupted factors remain identifiable, outperforming degraded RUSLE estimates and Direct RF, XGBoost, MLP, and CNN models. However, advantages weaken under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside training support.
AI.conclusion: Physics-structured factor restoration is effective for soil-loss estimation when factors are corrupted but identifiable, though limitations exist for extreme cases and joint corruption scenarios. The approach leverages physical relationships for more robust change estimation.

title: TorchCraft: Unified binder design by inverting an all-atom structure predictor
summary: All-atom structure predictors model diverse molecular interactions, but using their learned structural priors for binder design remains challenging. Here we present TorchCraft, a unified binder-design framework that optimizes sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor. Implemented in TorchFold, TorchCraft combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization procedure for minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins. Using pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, TorchCraft generated representative minibinders and VHHs with experimentally measured binding across four targets in each format, without post hoc sequence redesign. Computational benchmarks further demonstrated the framework's applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design. TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, providing a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in design.

AI.tldr: TorchCraft is a unified binder-design framework that optimizes sequences through frozen all-atom predictors like AlphaFold 3, enabling successful generation of various binder formats without post-processing.
AI.motivation: Existing all-atom structure predictors (like AlphaFold 3) capture diverse molecular interactions, but their learned structural priors are underutilized for practical binder design applications, creating a gap between prediction and design capabilities.
AI.method: TorchCraft uses frozen all-atom predictors (specifically AlphaFold 3 weights) and optimizes sequence logits through a framework called TorchFold. It combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization procedure for various binder formats including minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins.
AI.result: TorchCraft successfully generated experimentally validated binders across four targets in both minibinder and VHH formats without needing post hoc sequence redesign. Computational benchmarks also demonstrated applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design.
AI.conclusion: TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, providing a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in design, bridging the gap between structural prediction and practical binder design.

title: Learning-Based Reconstruction of Optical Properties in Bilayered Media from Single-distance Time-Resolved Reflectance Measurements
summary: The inverse problem of reconstructing optical properties, specifically absorption and scattering coefficients, in layered biological media from time-domain reflectance measurements remains a significant challenge for traditional analytical models. Inverse solvers based on the diffusion equation often struggle with structural heterogeneity, frequently yielding poor accuracy for superficial absorption and deep-layers scattering. In this work, we propose a machine learning framework as an alternative approach to reconstruct the optical properties of a bilayered medium, benchmarking its efficiency and accuracy against model-based algorithms. To overcome the intrinsic approximations of diffusion theory and inverse reconstruction, we generated a robust synthetic dataset of forward DTOF using exact Monte Carlo simulations at multiple source-detector distances. A machine learning pipeline was then trained on this dataset and validated against state-of-the-art model-based reconstruction methods. Besides the significant reconstruction speed-up, the machine learning approach achieves higher accuracy than model-based inverse solvers, further providing an estimate of the parameter space dimensionality without requiring any a priori information about the number of layers in the investigated geometry. Further enhancements in the reconstruction accuracy can be expected in future extensions of this work, by training the pipeline over multiple DTOF curves from the same medium, in a joint multi-distance reconstruction approach.

AI.tldr: Machine learning approach outperforms traditional diffusion-based methods for reconstructing optical properties (absorption and scattering coefficients) in layered biological media from time-domain reflectance measurements, providing faster and more accurate reconstructions.
AI.motivation: Traditional analytical models and diffusion equation-based inverse solvers struggle with reconstructing optical properties in layered biological media, particularly with structural heterogeneity, leading to poor accuracy for superficial absorption and deep-layer scattering reconstruction.
AI.method: Proposed a machine learning framework using synthetic datasets generated from exact Monte Carlo simulations of forward DTOF (diffuse time-of-flight) at multiple source-detector distances. Trained ML pipeline on this robust dataset and benchmarked against state-of-the-art model-based reconstruction methods.
AI.result: Machine learning approach achieved significant reconstruction speed-up and higher accuracy than model-based inverse solvers. Additionally provided estimation of parameter space dimensionality without requiring prior information about the number of layers in the investigated geometry.
AI.conclusion: ML framework effectively overcomes limitations of diffusion theory approximations, offering superior performance for optical property reconstruction. Future improvements expected by implementing joint multi-distance reconstruction using multiple DTOF curves from the same medium.

title: Integrating knowledge from case reports: a medical ontology based multimodal information system with structured summary
summary: Published medical case reports serve as a crucial medical information carrier, documenting discoveries in rare diseases, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatments. Despite the wealth of clinical knowledge in millions of case reports in the public medicine literature database (PubMed), accessing relevant information efficiently is hindered by the limitations of traditional keyword-based retrieval tools on unstructured and diverse case reports. To address the above issues, we introduce a comprehensive multimodal information system for case reports integrating structured clinical summaries of patients including medical images and biomedical named entities from 52949 open-access case reports published from 2000 to 2021. The multimodal essential information is organized in a well-structured medical ontology. Also, a powerful interface for searching and browsing case reports is designed to assist junior clinicians in retrieving cases effectively and improving the identification and diagnosis of rare diseases.

AI.tldr: A multimodal information system for medical case reports that extracts structured clinical data from 52,949 open-access case reports, organizing information in a medical ontology with search capabilities to help clinicians diagnose rare diseases.
AI.motivation: Medical case reports contain valuable clinical knowledge, but keyword-based retrieval from unstructured case reports in PubMed is inefficient for accessing relevant information, especially for rare disease diagnosis.
AI.method: Developed a multimodal information system that extracts structured clinical summaries from 52,949 open-access case reports (2000-2021), including medical images and biomedical named entities, organized using a medical ontology with a specialized search/browse interface.
AI.result: Created a comprehensive database integrating multimodal clinical information (text, images, entities) from over 50,000 case reports with a user-friendly interface to assist clinicians in case retrieval.
AI.conclusion: The system improves access to case report knowledge, particularly benefiting junior clinicians in rare disease identification and diagnosis through structured, multimodal information organization and effective search capabilities.

title: DeliveryGym: An RL Environment for Long-Horizon Embodied Agent Planning with Adaptive Curriculum
summary: Executable environments enable LLM agents to learn from the consequences of their actions. For embodied agents, those consequences extend beyond whether the current task succeeds: completing a delivery can consume the time, energy, or money needed for later work. Learning to plan therefore requires environments that preserve these dependencies and turn them into feedback across a complete trajectory. We introduce DeliveryGym, a 3D environment for evaluating and training agents on continuous courier shifts. It couples multimodal tool interaction with persistent world dynamics and computes trajectory rewards from simulator events, making the costs of an agent's decisions available for reinforcement learning (RL). The environment also adapts future training shifts to the policy's observed weaknesses while keeping evaluation fixed. Across six models and 13 city maps, evaluation exposes a gap between reliably executing assigned deliveries and choosing and sequencing work over a shift. On the fixed test suite, RL improves Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3%, showing that learning from complete shifts improves performance under these coupled constraints. Adapting the training environment improves test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at the same rollout budget, indicating that which situations an agent practices also matters. DeliveryGym provides an executable setting for studying how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and preserve resources for later orders within an episode.

AI.tldr: DeliveryGym is a 3D simulation environment for training LLM agents as delivery couriers, focusing on learning to plan complete shifts with resource constraints and sequential dependencies, showing that reinforcement learning with adaptive training improves performance significantly.
AI.motivation: Current executable environments for LLM agents often focus on immediate task success without considering longer-term resource constraints and dependencies between actions. Embodied agents need to learn to manage time, energy, and money across complete trajectories, not just individual tasks.
AI.method: Developed DeliveryGym, a 3D environment with persistent world dynamics and multimodal tool interaction. It computes trajectory rewards from simulator events and adapts future training shifts based on policy weaknesses while keeping evaluation fixed. Tested across six models and 13 city maps with reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Revealed gap between executing individual deliveries versus planning complete shifts. RL improved Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3% on fixed test suite. Adaptive training environment improved test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at same rollout budget, showing practice selection matters.
AI.conclusion: DeliveryGym provides an effective environment for studying how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and manage resources across episodes. Learning from complete trajectories with coupled constraints and adaptive training significantly improves performance, demonstrating the importance of both what agents learn and which situations they practice.

title: Contagion on the Trading Floor: How Adversarial Signals Spread in Multi-Agent Trading Systems
comment: Published in ECML PKDD 2026. 25 pages, including 7 pages of supplementary material
summary: Multi-agent trading systems built on large language models (LLMs) are beginning to appear in quantitative finance, yet their robustness to adversarial inputs is largely unknown. We study the vulnerability of LLM trading stacks to black-box, input-only attacks that enter solely via admissible social-media feeds. We introduce the Generic Multi-Agent Trading System (GMATS), a framework that captures modern multiagent trading architectures and instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers that treat an LLM as a post generator and inject budget-constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. We define contagion metrics that trace how adversarial content propagates through the stack, including belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers and attack-clean deltas on standard backtest metrics. Experiments on a safe offline benchmark with historical market and social data show that even simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles, sharply reducing Sharpe ratios. At the same time, we find that suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts can dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.

AI.tldr: LLM-based multi-agent trading systems are vulnerable to black-box adversarial attacks through social media feeds, with simple attacks able to significantly degrade trading performance, but certain multi-agent architectures and coordinator designs can improve robustness.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent trading systems are emerging in quantitative finance, but their robustness to adversarial attacks is largely unknown, especially attacks that come through legitimate social-media feeds.
AI.method: Developed GMATS framework to model modern multi-agent trading architectures, created black-box poisoning attackers that inject plausibly benign social media content into analyst evidence streams, defined contagion metrics to track adversarial propagation through the stack, and conducted experiments on safe offline benchmarks with historical market and social data.
AI.result: Simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles and sharply reduce Sharpe ratios. However, suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts can dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based trading systems are vulnerable to adversarial attacks through social media channels, highlighting important security concerns, but architectural and prompt engineering choices can enhance system resilience against such attacks.

title: Beyond Flattened Tokens: Structure-Preserving EEG Decoding with Reusable TriDim Blocks
summary: Effective EEG decoding requires representations that preserve organization among channels, local waveform dynamics, and long-range temporal context. Existing EEG architectures often capture these structures using separate specialized modules or collapse them into a single token sequence, making it difficult to maintain their distinct roles and coordinate their interactions throughout the backbone. We propose TriDim, a reusable block that preserves the representation shape and keeps three EEG axes explicit: channel, sample position within each patch, and patch position across the recording. These axes correspond to spatial, short-term temporal, and long-term temporal information, respectively. Each TriDim block applies feed-forward transformations along individual axes and cross-axis attention to coordinate information exchange among them. By stacking TriDim blocks with a multi-level tri-axis readout, we construct TriDimEEG, a standalone EEG decoder. Under strict cross-subject evaluation on eight datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, and emotion recognition, TriDimEEG achieves the best overall performance among fifteen evaluated models, with a 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over the second-best model. Replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models with TriDim blocks yields an average relative improvement of 7.4% in downstream accuracy while reducing parameter counts by 17.0% to 47.3%. These results establish TriDim as an effective and reusable building block and TriDimEEG as a strong standalone EEG decoder. Code and parameters of TriDimEEG are available at https://github.com/ncclab-sustech/TriDim_model.

AI.tldr: TriDimEEG: A novel EEG decoder using TriDim blocks that preserve channel, sample, and patch axes for spatial and temporal information, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple EEG tasks while being parameter-efficient.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG architectures either use separate specialized modules or collapse different EEG structures into a single token sequence, making it difficult to maintain distinct roles (channel organization, local waveform dynamics, long-range temporal context) and coordinate their interactions effectively.
AI.method: Proposes TriDim blocks that preserve EEG representation shape with three explicit axes: channel (spatial), sample position within patch (short-term temporal), and patch position across recording (long-term temporal). Each block applies feed-forward transformations along individual axes and cross-axis attention for coordination. Stacks TriDim blocks with multi-level tri-axis readout to construct TriDimEEG decoder.
AI.result: TriDimEEG achieves best overall performance among 15 models on 8 EEG datasets (clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, emotion recognition) with 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over second-best model. When replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models with TriDim blocks, yields 7.4% average relative improvement in downstream accuracy while reducing parameters by 17.0-47.3%.
AI.conclusion: TriDim is established as an effective and reusable building block for EEG processing, and TriDimEEG serves as a strong standalone EEG decoder that outperforms existing approaches across multiple domains while being more parameter-efficient.

title: Steering Equilibrium Selection in Regularized Self-Play via the Reference Policy
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Companion to arXiv:2606.28308 and arXiv:2607.17543. Fully reproducible: a single self-contained notebook regenerates every number, table, and figure
summary: Regularized self-play -- the family behind DeepNash's Stratego play -- drives a two-player zero-sum policy to a Nash equilibrium by best-responding to a slowly moving, entropy-regularized reference policy $ρ$. When the game has a polytope of value-equivalent equilibria, the regularizer silently breaks the tie: with a uniform reference it selects the maximum-entropy member, the I-projection of $ρ$ onto the Nash set. Can the reference be used to choose the equilibrium on purpose? On five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope, with exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds, anchoring the reference at a target member and refining steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 at median exploitability $5\times10^{-5}$, TOST-equivalent to the request within $\pm0.05$; the anchoring persists through refinement and follows the reference, not the initialization. Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). We report with equal emphasis where the story breaks: fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; stiff or flat families require a smaller mirror step, set by a pre-registered rule; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts where boundary saturation bites (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037) while interior precision is curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps are equivalent within $\pm0.03$ at every target (30 seeds); matched control arms show attention's robust signature is excess seed variance, any systematic shift bounded at 0.018 and not significant. Against a best response the selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate: steering matters only against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents. The recipe -- anchor the reference at the desired member and refine -- reinterprets the KL anchor of RLHF-style RL as a selection knob, not only a stability leash.

AI.tldr: Regularized self-play can steer to specific Nash equilibria by anchoring the reference policy at target members, enabling intentional equilibrium selection rather than just maximum-entropy convergence.
AI.motivation: When games have multiple value-equivalent Nash equilibria, standard regularized self-play selects maximum-entropy members by default. The paper investigates whether the reference policy can be intentionally used to select desired equilibria on purpose.
AI.method: Use regularized self-play with anchored reference policies at target equilibrium members across five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope. Employ exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds, refining steers to follow reach-weighted I-projection.
AI.result: Anchoring at target members successfully steers self-play to desired equilibria with mean coordinate error 0.007 and median exploitability 5×10⁻⁵, equivalent to selection within ±0.05. Selection follows reach-weighted I-projection with slope 0.969. The method works robustly but shows limitations with boundary targets, fixed off-manifold references, and requires careful step size tuning for stiff/flat families.
AI.conclusion: Reference policies can serve as intentional equilibrium selection knobs in regularized self-play, not just as regularization/stability tools. The "anchor and refine" recipe provides a principled way to select desired Nash equilibria, reinterpreting KL anchors in RLHF-style RL as selection mechanisms rather than mere stability leashes.

title: Expected Hypervolume Maximization for Multiobjective Optimization under Uncertainties
summary: The problem of multiobjective optimization under uncertainties is often approached by taking the expectation of each objective. In this work, we propose instead to formulate this as a Bayesian decision problem and to rely on the expected value of the hypervolume, which is to be maximized with respect to a finite set of input points. We show that this can be performed using methods based on gradients in a stochastic optimization framework, provided that care is taken with respect to dominated points. Moreover, in the absence of readily available differentiable code, we propose to use Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogate models, in order to perform the optimization. An additional contribution in this work are some active learning strategies, through acquisition functions which helps construct a surrogate model well-designed for the multiobjective optimization problem at stake. These strategies are compared on simple analytical problems to assess their performances.

AI.tldr: Bayesian approach for multiobjective optimization under uncertainty using expected hypervolume with gradient-based stochastic optimization and Gaussian Process surrogates, enhanced by active learning strategies.
AI.motivation: Traditional multiobjective optimization under uncertainty typically uses expectation of each objective, but this may not fully capture the trade-offs and uncertainties in multiobjective decision-making. The authors propose a Bayesian decision theory approach that better handles uncertainties and dominated points.
AI.method: 1) Formulate multiobjective optimization under uncertainty as Bayesian decision problem maximizing expected hypervolume; 2) Use gradient-based stochastic optimization with careful handling of dominated points; 3) Employ Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogate models when original code isn't differentiable; 4) Develop active learning strategies with acquisition functions to build surrogates specifically designed for multiobjective optimization.
AI.result: The proposed method enables effective multiobjective optimization under uncertainty using gradient-based approaches. Active learning strategies help construct better surrogate models for the multiobjective problem. The methods are validated on simple analytical problems to assess their performance.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian decision framework with expected hypervolume provides a principled approach to multiobjective optimization under uncertainty. Gradient-based optimization with careful handling of dominated points and Gaussian Process surrogates offers practical implementation. Active learning strategies enhance surrogate model construction for better optimization performance.

title: Dual-Axis Policy Optimization for LLM Agents: Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization
summary: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization di- mensions: how environment feedback is exploited within a trajectory, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch. We formulate these dimen- sions as Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution and Inter-Trajectory Objec- tive Aggregation, and introduce BATON (Bayesian Attribution and Trajectory Objective Normalization), a dual-axis policy optimization framework. BATON instantiates the first axis with Bayesian Feedback Attribution, which constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions, and the second with Trajec- tory Mass Normalization (TMN), which assigns equal optimization mass to com- plete trajectories. Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that both axes provide independent gains and that their combi- nation consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across model scales.

AI.tldr: BATON is a dual-axis RL framework for LLM agents that separates intra-trajectory feedback attribution (Bayesian approach) from inter-trajectory objective aggregation (equal mass normalization), achieving consistent performance gains across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization dimensions that are typically conflated: how environment feedback is exploited within individual trajectories, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across batches. The paper aims to address these dimensions separately to improve RL performance for language agents.
AI.method: BATON framework with two main components: 1) Bayesian Feedback Attribution for intra-trajectory optimization - constructs feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions, and 2) Trajectory Mass Normalization (TMN) for inter-trajectory optimization - assigns equal optimization mass to complete trajectories regardless of their lengths or properties.
AI.result: Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA benchmarks show that both axes (intra-trajectory attribution and inter-trajectory aggregation) provide independent performance gains. The combination of both components consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across different model scales.
AI.conclusion: Separating the two optimization dimensions in RL for LLM agents through BATON's dual-axis approach leads to more effective policy optimization. The Bayesian attribution and trajectory normalization components work synergistically, suggesting that treating these dimensions independently is crucial for improving reinforcement learning in language agents.

title: Pretrained Medical Representations for the Practical Screening of Drug Repositioning Candidates
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Representation learning from medical code sequences in electronic health records and medical claims data has been successful in various clinical applications, such as those regarding disease prediction. However, significant challenges remain in extending this approach to the discovery of scientific hypotheses. One reason is that many existing BERT-based models fail to adequately capture the hierarchical structure of medical codes and the complex interactions between diagnoses and treatments. To address these limitations, we propose a new unified pre-training framework that explicitly integrates hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. The proposed model consistently outperformed existing methods on both pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks, including the onset of dementia and hospitalization. We also conducted an in silico drug repositioning case study targeting Alzheimer's disease. In the hypothesis generation step, our approach successfully rediscovered known promising drugs in a data-driven manner without relying on such external knowledge sources as the literature. Subsequently, in the hypothesis prioritization step, we introduced a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to alleviate the over-encoding of historical prescription information within diagnostic vectors, enabling the robust prioritization of generated hypotheses. This study establishes an exploratory screening workflow for hypothesis generation and prioritization based on observational associations. Importantly, this framework is not intended to provide causal evidence, but rather to identify promising candidates for subsequent rigorous causal inference. Overall, this study demonstrates that domain-informed representation learning combined with task-adaptive representation control can enable a practical hypothesis discovery workflow.

AI.tldr: Proposed a unified pre-training framework with hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms for medical code representation learning, enabling practical hypothesis discovery workflows including drug repositioning for Alzheimer's disease.
AI.motivation: Existing BERT-based models fail to adequately capture hierarchical structure of medical codes and complex interactions between diagnoses and treatments, limiting their utility for scientific hypothesis discovery from EHR data.
AI.method: Developed a unified pre-training framework integrating hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. Introduced Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to mitigate over-encoding of prescription information in diagnostic vectors for hypothesis prioritization.
AI.result: Model outperformed existing methods on pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks (dementia onset, hospitalization). Successfully rediscovered known promising Alzheimer's drugs in data-driven hypothesis generation. Task-Adaptive Representation Approach enabled robust hypothesis prioritization.
AI.conclusion: Domain-informed representation learning combined with task-adaptive representation control enables practical hypothesis discovery workflows for exploratory screening of observational associations, identifying candidates for subsequent causal inference rather than providing causal evidence.

title: MetaRTL: Meta-path Attention Enhanced Relational Table Learning
summary: Relational table learning has gained increasing attention with the widespread use of relational databases. Existing methods typically rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, leading to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. We propose MetaRTL, a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning. In the first stage, MetaRTL obtains initial table embeddings via lightweight pre-training. In the second stage, it performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module, MetaAttn. By shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: MetaRTL is a two-stage framework for scalable relational table learning that replaces deep GNN stacks with lightweight pre-training and efficient meta-path aggregation to achieve better performance with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Relational table learning is important but existing methods using deep GNN/HGNN stacks have high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: 1) Lightweight pre-training for initial table embeddings, 2) Non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features aggregated by an attention module (MetaAttn). This shifts computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation.
AI.result: Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MetaRTL, showing it captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency.
AI.conclusion: MetaRTL provides a scalable and expressive approach to relational table learning by balancing computational efficiency with semantic richness through its two-stage meta-path aggregation framework.

title: AURA: Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis for Email Threat Detection
comment: Under review
summary: Email spam and phishing attacks remain a critical security threat. Adversaries increasingly exploit large language models to craft contextually convincing malicious messages, and existing spam detection systems often struggle to keep pace. Generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios is limited, which reduces effectiveness once these systems are deployed in practice. This paper introduces Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis (AURA), a multimodal email threat detection system that analyzes both the content of an email and its embedded URLs. AURA is built around two layers: the first quantifies prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, and only ambiguous messages are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system is evaluated on eight heterogeneous training corpora together with two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns. AURA reaches a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and on NazPhish-Eval and GuenterTrap-Eval it maintains 0.9502 and 0.9436, respectively, which is evidence of robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.

AI.tldr: AURA is a multimodal email threat detection system that combines URL analysis with semantic content analysis using a cascade approach with uncertainty routing to improve generalization against evolving spam and phishing attacks.
AI.motivation: Email spam and phishing attacks remain critical security threats that are increasingly sophisticated due to LLM-generated content. Existing detection systems struggle with generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios, reducing their practical effectiveness.
AI.method: AURA uses a two-layer cascade: 1) Quantifies prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, 2) Only escalates ambiguous messages to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis of email content. Combines URL and content analysis with uncertainty routing.
AI.result: Achieves macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and maintains 0.9502 on NazPhish-Eval and 0.9436 on GuenterTrap-Eval held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns, demonstrating robust generalization under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: AURA's adaptive uncertainty-routed analysis approach provides superior generalization capabilities for email threat detection across diverse attack scenarios and temporal distribution shifts, addressing key limitations of existing systems.

title: A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
comment: Preprint of a manuscript completed in November, 2025
summary: LLM-based GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in digital environments that were designed with human users in mind. These graphical user interfaces were designed to support, but also deliberately steer, the behaviour and decisions of users. While behavioural biases in the textual outputs of LLMs are well-documented, far less is known about how such influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions---and, in particular, whether the reasoning capabilities increasingly built into these agents make them more robust to it. Drawing on Dual-Process Theory, we empirically investigate whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how their reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. In a randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, we found that agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, the reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions, reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening it to reflective social influence nudges. Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect. Exploratory analysis further showed this redirection to be systematically structured by model scale. Beyond establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioural property of agentic AI, the study positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations that delegate decisions to autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to digital nudges designed for humans, with reasoning capabilities not providing robust protection but rather redirecting susceptibility from automatic to reflective nudges.
AI.motivation: GUI interfaces were designed to steer human behavior through digital nudges, but little is known about how LLM-based agents that perceive and act on interfaces are affected by such influence, especially as they incorporate reasoning capabilities that might make them more robust.
