AI.method: The study uses Dual-Process Theory framework to empirically investigate susceptibility of LLM-based GUI agents to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges. Conducted randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents across 21,600 simulations using six frontier models from three providers, testing how reasoning configuration moderates nudge susceptibility.
AI.result: Agents were vulnerable to both automatic and reflective nudges. Reasoning configuration moderated effects in opposite directions: reduced susceptibility to automatic default nudges but increased susceptibility to reflective social influence nudges. Model scale systematically structured this redirection of nudge effects.
AI.conclusion: Extensive reasoning doesn't make agents robust to digital nudges but redirects how choice architecture affects them. Interface design emerges as a governance concern for organizations delegating decisions to autonomous agents, establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioral property of agentic AI.

title: Uni-LaDiR: Latent Diffusion Unifies Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Multimodal reasoning requires models to draw on information from multiple modalities throughout the reasoning process. Yet existing methods often concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, leaving the model to bridge representational differences as it reasons across modalities. We introduce Uni-LaDiR (Unified Latent Diffusion Reasoner), a framework that brings these thoughts into a shared latent space for reasoning. A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve the information needed for later reasoning steps and the final answer or action. Because the same context can support multiple valid next steps, we use diffusion to predict the next block of thought tokens from the input and preceding blocks. Jointly training the encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared model weights encourages thought tokens to be both useful for the task and predictable from the available context. At inference, the model generates these tokens without teacher observations. Across eleven vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks and two vision-language-action (VLA) suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Uni-LaDiR introduces a unified latent diffusion framework for multimodal reasoning that maps thoughts from different modalities into shared latent tokens and uses diffusion to predict reasoning steps, achieving significant performance gains on VLM and VLA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal reasoning methods often concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, forcing models to bridge representational differences across modalities during reasoning, which is inefficient and suboptimal.
AI.method: Unified Latent Diffusion Reasoner (Uni-LaDiR) uses a shared latent space for reasoning: 1) A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, 2) Diffusion predicts next thought token blocks from input and preceding blocks, 3) Joint training of encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared weights encourages both usefulness and predictability of thought tokens.
AI.result: Across eleven vision-language model benchmarks and two vision-language-action suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks over the strongest evaluated baselines.
AI.conclusion: Uni-LaDiR successfully unifies multimodal reasoning in a shared latent space through diffusion-based prediction, demonstrating superior performance on both visual reasoning and robot manipulation tasks by effectively bridging modality-specific representations.

title: Constraint-Safe Graph-Context Scoring for Stable Point-Feature Labels Under Text-Width and Accessibility-Inspired Profiles
summary: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further change label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often collapse these concerns into overlap counts. We present LABELSENSE-Pilot, a reproducible prototype that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects a layout through mixed-integer optimization. The executed scorer is deliberately not described as a graph transformer. Every returned layout is checked for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names spanning 155 countries, with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62 percent of labels with 2.09 percent flicker and zero collisions. Versus a handcrafted-utility integer program, LABELSENSE-Pilot sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57 percent of selected placements. These results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

AI.tldr: LABELSENSE-Pilot is a reproducible prototype for interactive map label placement that uses ML scoring and mixed-integer optimization to achieve high display rates (85.62%), low flicker (2.09%), and zero collisions while handling multilingual and accessibility requirements.
AI.motivation: Current map label placement algorithms often oversimplify complex requirements like geometric validity, display yield, stability during camera motion, and accessibility/multilingual needs (which affect label dimensions). Existing evaluations frequently collapse these concerns into simple overlap counts, failing to address the full complexity of interactive map labeling.
AI.method: Generate eight compass-direction candidates per feature; score candidates using a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries; add previous-placement bonus for stability; select final layout through mixed-integer optimization; verify viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. The system uses 2,500 airport coordinates across 155 countries with various stressors for testing.
AI.result: Achieved 85.62% label display rate with only 2.09% flicker and zero collisions. Compared to handcrafted-utility integer programming, sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display but reduced flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero violations vs. 52.57% violations in standard geometry at 1.5x scale.
AI.conclusion: The approach establishes an auditable engineering trade-off between competing label placement objectives. Results demonstrate effectiveness in handling multilingual and accessibility requirements, though official baselines and participant evidence are still needed before submission. The work presents a reproducible system that addresses practical interactive map labeling challenges beyond simple overlap counting.

title: Online Adaptive Kernel Mixing for Gaussian Process Decision Making
comment: 35 pages, 9 figures. Accepted as a full paper at IFIP Performance 2026
summary: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used as surrogates for black-box functions in sequential decision-making problems such as Bayesian optimization (BO), level set estimation (LSE), and Bayesian active learning (BAL). GP performance critically depends on kernels, and standard kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions under misspecification. To address this, we introduce HACK GPs (Hedge Adaptive Cumulative Kernels), a method that views kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. HACK treats each candidate kernel as a GP "expert" and updates a distribution over experts online using AdaHedge, based on a loss received as a proxy for their ability to fit the function and align with the task objective. We provide two variants of HACK: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling. We establish general guarantees showing that, under a loss-gap condition, the weight concentrates on the best kernel and the resulting acquisition function is close to that of the best expert. Empirically, we observe robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL compared to standard kernels such as Squared Exponential and Matern-5/2, as well as simple ensemble baselines.

AI.tldr: HACK GPs uses online learning to dynamically select optimal kernels for Gaussian Processes in sequential decision-making tasks, outperforming standard kernels through adaptive kernel combinations.
AI.motivation: Standard GP kernels often lead to suboptimal decisions when misspecified in Bayesian optimization, level set estimation, and Bayesian active learning. Kernel selection is critical but challenging, and static kernel choices may not adapt well to evolving information.
AI.method: HACK GPs treats kernel selection as an online learning problem with expert advice. Each candidate kernel acts as a GP "expert," and AdaHedge updates distributions over experts based on task-specific losses. Two variants: Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and categorical sampling.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees show weight concentration on the best kernel under loss-gap conditions, ensuring acquisition functions approximate the best expert. Empirical results demonstrate robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL, surpassing standard kernels (Squared Exponential, Matern-5/2) and ensemble baselines.
AI.conclusion: HACK GPs provides a principled online learning approach to adaptive kernel selection that improves GP performance in sequential decision-making tasks by dynamically selecting or combining kernels based on their empirical performance, offering both theoretical guarantees and practical benefits.

title: Reproducibility is not construct validity: LLM measurement of institutionally situated communication
summary: High annotation reproducibility does not necessarily imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the construct it is intended to measure. We test this distinction using a dataset from the European Commission's AI Act consultation, linking structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders. LLM annotations of consultation submissions are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99), yet show limited convergence with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct they were intended to approximate. Divergence between survey-and LLM-inferred text-based measures varies systematically across stakeholder groups: business associations express greater concern about AI risks in text-based consultations than in survey responses ({g} = +1.0), whereas public authorities and several nonbusiness groups show smaller or negative divergences. Divergences between scores suggest positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating that stakeholders from neighboring countries tend toward more similar text-based stances towards AI safety concerns. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels. These results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence and motivate validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

AI.tldr: High LLM annotation reproducibility doesn't guarantee construct validity, as shown by limited convergence between LLM-inferred text measures and survey-reported measures in AI Act consultation data.
AI.motivation: To examine whether high reproducibility of LLM annotations actually corresponds to valid measurement of intended constructs, distinguishing between reproducibility and construct validity when using LLMs as measurement tools.
AI.method: Using European Commission's AI Act consultation data linking structured survey responses to free-text submissions from same stakeholders. Testing LLM annotation reproducibility (intraclass correlations) and convergence with survey-reported measures of nominal constructs.
AI.result: LLM annotations show high reproducibility (ICC > 0.99) but limited convergence with survey measures. Divergence varies systematically: business associations express more AI risk concern in text vs. surveys (+1.0 effect size), while public authorities and nonbusiness groups show smaller/negative divergences. Divergence shows spatial autocorrelation across European countries. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability.
AI.conclusion: LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence, necessitating validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when using LLMs as measurement instruments.

title: REARL: A Closed-loop Autonomous Driving Simulation Enhancement Framework with Real Traffic Data and Large Language Models
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Corresponding author: Yiwen Sun. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 62503015)
summary: Accurate simulation is crucial for autonomous driving development, yet capturing real-world traffic complexity remains challenging. Existing simulators that rely on predefined rules or static data playback struggle with dynamic traffic. CRITICAL uses real traffic data and a large language model (LLM) to adjust the initial simulation configuration, but the simulated distribution still diverges from real traffic as the rollout evolves. We propose REARL, a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework that integrates real traffic data with LLMs. Real traffic data are clustered, and each cluster center is used as a representative scenario that provides typical real-world traffic patterns for the LLM. A timed sliding-window detector then monitors discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between pairs of vehicles. If a metric exceeds a threshold, the LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making; otherwise the existing controller is kept. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a traffic snapshot and modulates the simulated vehicle with reference to that real action. In a controlled HighD highway setting, compared with the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based learning baseline, REARL reduces the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and the MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, while achieving a time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane change rate of 0.0708.

AI.tldr: REARL is a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework for autonomous driving that uses real traffic data clustering with LLMs to dynamically adjust simulation parameters when discrepancies from real-world patterns are detected.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving simulators using predefined rules or static data playback struggle to capture real-world traffic complexity and dynamic behaviors. While CRITICAL uses real data and LLMs to adjust initial configuration, simulated distributions still diverge from real traffic over time.
AI.method: 1) Cluster real traffic data and use cluster centers as representative scenarios for LLM. 2) Use timed sliding-window detector to monitor discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing. 3) When metrics exceed thresholds, LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making and selects matching real vehicles from traffic snapshots to modulate simulated vehicles.
AI.result: In HighD highway setting, REARL outperformed CRITICAL and PPO baselines: reduced Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067, MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, achieved time headway of 22.8575, and lane change rate of 0.0708.
AI.conclusion: REARL's closed-loop approach effectively bridges the gap between simulation and real traffic by dynamically adapting to detected discrepancies, providing more realistic autonomous driving simulation with LLM-guided adjustments.

title: Physical knowledge on historical data matters more than enforcing physical constraints on the forecast
summary: Time series forecasting has seen signicant advancements with the emergence of new deep learning models. However, forecasting time series in applications involving physical processes remains a major challenge. Despite the apparition of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN), recent models do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior. To this end, we propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) which predicts, along the target, unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast target. This approach enhances the model robustness and results interpretation using domain knowledge. Our method is easily adaptable to any physical model using several equations, each having its own set of unobservable variables, to describe it-self. As a case study, we incorporate physical equations used for groundwater levels predictions by the physical model called Gardenia. This model uses transfers equations between reservoirs, optimized with data assimilation, to simulate the evolution of groundwater levels. Evaluation includes several well known neural network models and the Gardenia model compared on twelve real world datasets. In addition, we study the impact of each component through an ablation study. Our model outperforms other models on ve out of the twelve datasets and our ablation study underlines the importance of having a physical background in our time series forecasting task. Finally, the coherence of the physical variables predicted by our neural network is assessed by a domain expert.

AI.tldr: Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) for time series forecasting with physical processes that predicts both target and unobservable intermediate physical variables, outperforming traditional models and PINNs.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning models for time series forecasting in physical processes fail to estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables that are crucial for domain experts to understand target behavior, despite the emergence of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).
AI.method: Proposes Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) that predicts target variables along with unobservable intermediate physical variables on both historic data and forecast targets, incorporating physical equations and domain knowledge. The method is adaptable to any physical model with multiple equations and tested on groundwater level predictions using Gardenia model equations.
AI.result: PIRNN outperforms other neural network models and the Gardenia physical model on 5 out of 12 real-world datasets. Ablation study confirms importance of physical background, and domain expert validation shows coherent physical variable predictions.
AI.conclusion: PIRNN successfully integrates physical knowledge into time series forecasting, providing both accurate predictions and interpretable intermediate physical variables that enhance model robustness and domain expert understanding.

title: Digital Twins for Opinion Dynamics: A Generative LLM Framework for Social Networks
summary: The study of opinion dynamics in social networks is one of the key challenges in computational social science with direct relevance to understanding political polarization, misinformation, and health responses. Current approaches focus on simplified mathematical models that ignore linguistic and contextual factors related to belief updates or use Large Language Model (LLM)-based simulations that have not been validated against real data. We present a framework based on the concept of a digital twin to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks. The approach fills the gap by cloning a real-world Twitter network, assigns a set of attributes for agents (such as persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, and influence), and employs Mistral-7B to perform opinion update based on memory and social exposure. To evaluate the proposed approach, we validate it against two real Twitter datasets (COVID-19 discourse and U.S elections 2020). The results show that the capability of the proposed framework reproduces opinion trajectories and reduces individual prediction error by more than 50% compared to the best-performing classical baseline (Mistral-7B achieves Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.150 and 0.121 on the COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets, respectively). We observe similar improvements in structural alignment (Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180) and polarization dynamics (Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115) on the two datasets, respectively. Additionally, the ablation studies confirm that agent attributes, memory, and social exposure all contribute to the framework's predictive fidelity in reproducing opinion trajectories, with agent attributes being the most critical contributor. Overall, our results demonstrate that grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics.

AI.tldr: A digital twin framework for opinion dynamics that clones real Twitter networks, uses Mistral-7B for opinion updates, and significantly outperforms classical baselines in reproducing opinion trajectories.
AI.motivation: Current opinion dynamics models either use oversimplified mathematical approaches that ignore linguistic factors or LLM-based simulations that lack validation against real-world data, creating a gap for realistic social network simulation.
AI.method: Creates digital twins of real Twitter networks, assigns agents with persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, and influence attributes, and uses Mistral-7B for opinion updates based on memory and social exposure.
AI.result: Reduces individual prediction error by >50% compared to best classical baseline, achieves MAE = 0.150 (COVID-19) and 0.121 (US Election), improves structural alignment (Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180), and better captures polarization dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks creates a realistic simulation framework that can reproduce complex social dynamics, with agent attributes being the most critical factor for predictive fidelity.

title: TRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives
summary: Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrievalaugmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Biblioth{è}que nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical archives, achieving state-of-the-art performance on French historical documents with economical operation costs.
AI.motivation: Historical archives present unique retrieval challenges including OCR-degraded documents, heterogeneous genres/sources, and the need for strong source traceability for scholarly/institutional use. These requirements aren't well-served by existing RAG systems.
AI.method: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework developed within the DECIDON project. It focuses on accountable source discovery through corpus-aware agent design without requiring model training or complex graph construction, operating as a hosted inference service.
AI.result: On the HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic benchmark (1,752 French historical questions), TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines. It costs approximately $0.02 per question and shows largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions.
AI.conclusion: For large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches, offering both high performance and economic feasibility for heritage institutions.

title: Amortizing Physics-Informed Neural Solvers via Graph Hypernetworks
comment: Accepted at the Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG), 2026
summary: Amortizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs requires describing each equation to a reusable solver. Coefficient vectors encode numerical parameters in predefined slots, leaving operator and cross-field assignments implicit. We make these relationships explicit in an operator graph, with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals and coefficients retained as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Meta-training and target-specific adaptation use governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. We compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning by solution accuracy within a fixed adaptation budget. In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy, with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, meta-training sees uncoupled and one-way systems; after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph's mean final error is 35.7% below the term set and 67.7% below the coefficient vector. In a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient vector performs best. These results support extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships for physics-based solver adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using operator graphs to explicitly represent PDE relationships for amortized PINNs, improving adaptation performance on complex multi-field systems compared to coefficient-vector or term-set approaches.
AI.motivation: Amortizing PINNs across related PDEs requires effective equation description to reusable solvers. Traditional coefficient vectors leave operator and cross-field relationships implicit, limiting adaptation to unseen equations, especially those with complex inter-field couplings.
AI.method: Proposes an operator graph representation with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals, keeping coefficients as term attributes. Uses a graph hypernetwork to generate diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Both meta-training and target-specific adaptation use only governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels.
AI.result: In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction, term-based descriptors (both DeepSets and graph) improve high-reaction accuracy over coefficient vectors. In two-field Fisher-KPP with unseen two-way coupling, graph representation achieves 35.7% lower final error than term-set and 67.7% lower than coefficient vector after adaptation. However, in fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma, coefficient vector performs best.
AI.conclusion: Results support extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships for physics-based solver adaptation, particularly beneficial for complex multi-field systems with unseen coupling patterns during meta-training.

title: From "Who Is This User?" to "What Does This Purchase Mean?": A Deployed Pipeline for Semantic User Profiling at Bank Scale
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, IEEE International Conference on Data Mining 2026 (ICDM)
summary: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories binds the inference budget linearly to user count, which becomes prohibitive at applied scale. We re-cast attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern. The pipeline runs in three phases: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding, Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, and Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. In Profile, a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates. Because inference runs over patterns rather than users, the budget grows with the pattern count rather than the user count. On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history directly in AUC across the evaluated attributes, and the prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. The pipeline is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/profiling-agent-open-ecommerce.

AI.tldr: A per-transaction-pattern LLM inference method that reduces inference costs by orders of magnitude while maintaining accuracy comparable to per-user inference.
AI.motivation: Traditional per-user LLM inference on transaction histories becomes prohibitively expensive at scale due to linear cost growth with user count. Current approaches bind inference budget directly to the number of users, making them impractical for large-scale applications with millions of users.
AI.method: Three-phase pipeline: 1) Resolve phase abstracts item names with optional web grounding, 2) Profile phase uses single LLM call per pattern to infer categorical labels, free-text attributes, and prevalence estimates, 3) Tag phase clusters free-text attributes into queryable database. Inference shifts from per-user to per-transaction-pattern basis.
AI.result: On Open e-commerce corpus, achieves statistical parity with per-user LLM inference (AUC indistinguishable). Prevalence estimates provide discriminative signal. Deployed at major Japanese bank profiling tens of millions of users with ~1000x reduction in LLM inference targets versus per-user pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Per-transaction-pattern inference dramatically reduces computational costs while maintaining accuracy, making large-scale attribute profiling practical for real-world applications like banking. The method enables cost-effective profiling of millions of users with minimal accuracy trade-offs.

title: One Intervention per Component is Enough: Towards Identifiability in Linear Stochastic Dynamics from Steady State
summary: We study the problem of recovering the parameters of a multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process from steady-state observational and interventional data. In many applications, such as large-scale gene perturbation experiments, only stationary "snapshot" measurements are available, making standard stochastic differential equation estimation methods that rely on time-series trajectories inapplicable. We first establish an identifiability result: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) of the drift graph suffices to recover all OU process parameters generically up to a global scaling factor. This holds provided that the SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and certain spectral nondegeneracy assumptions hold. We propose a recursive learning algorithm that orders SCCs topologically and, for each component, isolates its marginal dynamics and solves a linear system derived from the steady-state moment equations, leveraging parameters recovered for upstream components. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose a regularized least-squares estimator that jointly minimizes residuals of the steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data. Experimental results validate our theoretical findings in recovering parameters of the underlying OU process.

AI.tldr: A method to recover Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process parameters from steady-state observational and interventional data when only stationary measurements are available, establishing identifiability conditions and proposing a recursive learning algorithm with regularization.
AI.motivation: In many real-world applications like large-scale gene perturbation experiments, only stationary "snapshot" measurements are available rather than complete time-series trajectories. This makes standard stochastic differential equation estimation methods inapplicable, creating a need for methods that can recover process parameters from steady-state data alone.
AI.method: First establishes identifiability conditions: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) of the drift graph suffices to recover parameters generically up to a global scaling factor, assuming SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and spectral nondegeneracy holds. Proposes a recursive learning algorithm that orders SCCs topologically, isolates marginal dynamics for each component, and solves linear systems from steady-state moment equations using parameters from upstream components. Also introduces a regularized least-squares estimator that jointly minimizes residuals of steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data.
AI.result: Theoretical identifiability results are established showing parameters can be recovered generically up to a global scaling factor. Experimental results validate the theoretical findings in recovering parameters of the underlying OU process from steady-state data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables parameter recovery for multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes using only steady-state observational and interventional data, overcoming limitations of traditional time-series methods. The identifiability conditions and recursive algorithm provide a theoretical foundation for practical applications where only stationary measurements are available.

title: Beyond Depth Truncation: Controlled Evaluation of Depth Utilization in Recursive Language Models
summary:
Depth-recurrent language models iteratively apply a small layer stack, decoupling per-token compute from distinct parameter count. To determine whether such a model genuinely utilizes its depth, both recurrence and layer-pruning literatures rely on a shared evaluation: truncating depth at inference time, plotting quality against retained depth fraction, and reading off the slope. While cheap and training-free, this metric suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously. Depth truncation concurrently reduces the number of block applications, decreases the volume of distinct computation performed, and pushes the readout head onto an out-of-distribution residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the second.
  We propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite that disentangles these three quantities. DCP comprises three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact of the measurement protocol, and a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control, running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures, since in a dense network repeating a layer yields an entirely different model rather than the same model in an alternative configuration.

AI.tldr: Depth Control Protocol (DCP) is a diagnostic suite that disentangles multiple confounding factors in depth-recurrent language model evaluation, moving beyond flawed single-scalar slope metrics.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods for depth-recurrent language models conflate multiple factors when measuring depth utilization. Traditional depth-truncation metrics extract a single scalar that simultaneously reduces block applications, decreases distinct computation volume, and creates out-of-distribution residual streams, making it impossible to isolate the actual contribution of depth utilization.
AI.method: Proposes Depth Control Protocol (DCP) with three positive controls isolating each factor while varying others, a negative control using dense transformers to rule out measurement artifacts, and a controlled training intervention for causal verification. The key control involves running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration - only feasible in weight-sharing architectures.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in abstract, but the method enables disentangling the three conflated factors that traditional depth-truncation metrics fail to separate.
AI.conclusion: DCP provides a more rigorous diagnostic framework for evaluating depth utilization in recurrent language models by separating the confounding effects that traditional single-scalar metrics conflate, with particular applicability to weight-sharing architectures.

title: Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation
comment: No
summary: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.

AI.tldr: GS-Power-UCT is a graph-based MCTS algorithm that shares states reached at the same planning depth in stochastic MDPs, improving sample efficiency while maintaining convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Tree-based MCTS wastes simulations in stochastic MDPs by duplicating the same state when reached through different trajectories, leading to inefficient use of computational resources.
AI.method: Introduces Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT) which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. Also proposes two variants: GS-Power-UCT-F (one node per physical state) and GS-Power-UCT-F⁺ (with adaptive horizon to control bias).
AI.result: Proves convergence rate O(n^{-1/2}) matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based MCTS with state sharing at same depths improves sample efficiency in stochastic MDPs while maintaining theoretical convergence guarantees, with variants offering trade-offs between sample sharing and horizon bias control.

title: MaSCoD: A Multi-Agent Framework for Structural-Context-Guided Candidate Causal Graph Generation
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. We propose MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. We evaluate MaSCoD on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication. MaSCoD exhibits a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Across all six dataset-backbone settings, Full, which supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1, which instead constructs them within the judgment procedure, while also increasing false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over all evaluated baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, rather than uniformly across settings. Partial ablations showed that supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, stage-wise analysis showed that the Full-No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs. These findings support structural pre-organization as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control and motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment.

AI.tldr: MaSCoD is a multi-agent LLM framework for causal discovery that pre-organizes candidate third variables and structural patterns before direct-edge judgment to address premature omission of relevant causal relations.
AI.motivation: Current LLM applications in causal discovery rarely treat premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. There's a need for frameworks that better control for omission of relevant edges in candidate graph generation.
AI.method: Proposes MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. Evaluated on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs datasets using GPT-5.4 as primary backbone with GPT-4o for replication. Compares "Full" (supplies structural hypotheses before judgment) vs "No Phase 1" (constructs them within judgment).
AI.result: MaSCoD shows dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. "Full" achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than "No Phase 1" across all settings, but also increased false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and Sachs with GPT-4o, but not uniformly. Partial ablations showed supplying both information components didn't always outperform single components. Stage-wise analysis revealed retention gap already present after direct-edge judgment.
AI.conclusion: Structural pre-organization should be an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control in LLM-based causal discovery. Findings motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment procedures.

title: CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
summary: Predicting cellular responses to perturbations supports the study of gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies. Despite advances in single-cell perturbation modeling, existing models typically optimize surrogate losses that do not directly reflect the biological criteria used for evaluation, so better data fitting need not yield better biological predictions. To address this mismatch, we introduce \textbf{CellRFT}, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that uses biological evaluation as direct training feedback. CellRFT uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations and integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate CellRFT's applicability across different pretrained models and effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction, reveal that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others, and show that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized, offering a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior, with the potential to inform evaluation design. Code will be made available.

AI.tldr: CellRFT is a reinforcement learning framework that uses biological evaluation metrics as direct training feedback to improve single-cell perturbation prediction models, bridging the gap between model optimization and biological relevance.
AI.motivation: Existing single-cell perturbation models optimize surrogate losses that don't directly reflect biological evaluation criteria, creating a mismatch where better data fitting doesn't necessarily yield better biological predictions.
AI.method: CellRFT uses reinforcement learning with policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable biological evaluations of generated cell populations, integrating multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments show CellRFT works across different pretrained models, improves perturbation prediction, reveals complex interactions between biological criteria, and demonstrates that optimizing complementary rewards can benefit criteria beyond those directly targeted.
AI.conclusion: CellRFT offers a way to directly align model training with biological evaluation metrics, potentially informing evaluation design and providing insights into how biological criteria shape model behavior in single-cell perturbation prediction.

title: Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics
summary: LLM-based AI agents process user requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, often involving the invocation of remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. This execution model can make the optimization of agent serving difficult because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks inter-mix across requests. However, the current agent ecosystem runs without much consideration of resource dynamics, which results in significant waste of the precious resources. This paper analyzes the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. To this end, we characterize the latency with respect to the resource dynamics of processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. Our measurements show that agents have a wide range of behaviors depending on tasks, so that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. We also find that running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in resource dynamics such as CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Furthermore, we uncover that faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Based on these observations, we demonstrate new optimization opportunities that exploit the resource dynamics of tasks: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation. Our results show that the latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks improves $\sim$5.4$\times$, and the average latency across multiple tasks is reduced $\sim$32% compared to native agents.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes resource dynamics in LLM-based AI agent serving, identifies task-dependent bottlenecks, and proposes CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation optimizations to reduce latency.
AI.motivation: LLM-based AI agents process requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, involving remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. The current agent ecosystem lacks consideration of resource dynamics, leading to significant waste of precious resources. There's a need to optimize agent serving as latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks intermix across requests.
AI.method: The paper analyzes resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. It characterizes latency with respect to resource dynamics when processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently, measuring agent behaviors and identifying task-dependent bottlenecks in CPU, disk I/O, and memory.
AI.result: Measurements show agents have wide-ranging behaviors depending on tasks, with even the same tool showing substantial differences in resource dynamics. Running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks. Surprisingly, faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Two optimization techniques are demonstrated: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates significant optimization opportunities by exploiting resource dynamics of tasks. The proposed optimizations improve latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks by ~5.4× and reduce average latency across multiple tasks by ~32% compared to native agents, showing the importance of resource-aware scheduling in AI agent serving.

title: Past, Future, All at Once: Mitigating Stability-Plasticity Dilemma via Post-hoc JANUS Rectification
summary: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks inevitably suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While existing works attempt to mitigate this on the basis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, they adopted an overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality condition. In this paper, we introduce a purely post-hoc and tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality, which is the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to the first order. By projecting parameter updates into the JAcobian NUll Space (JANUS), our method significantly recovers compromised historical knowledge without interfering with the underlying fine-tuning process. To overcome the local validity of the Jacobian approximation, we further propose a Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that utilizes the JANUS shift to dynamically verify the valid trust region and adjust step sizes. Coupled with our proposed ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level singular value decomposition compression techniques, JANUS also achieves great temporal and spatial efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that JANUS seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigating the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation.

AI.tldr: JANUS is a post-hoc weight rectification framework that projects parameter updates into Jacobian null space to prevent catastrophic forgetting while maintaining downstream task adaptation, achieving both parameter space orthogonality and computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning foundation models suffers from catastrophic forgetting, and existing methods use overly restrictive subspace orthogonality conditions that don't fully preserve historical knowledge.
AI.method: A post-hoc, tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that projects parameter updates into Jacobian Null Space (JANUS) with Multi-step Adaptive Rectification for local validity, plus ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level SVD compression techniques.
AI.result: JANUS seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigates the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation, with great temporal and spatial efficiency.
AI.conclusion: JANUS achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality (necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance) through post-hoc Jacobian null space projection, offering an effective solution to catastrophic forgetting in foundation model fine-tuning.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Agentic AI for Networked Low-Altitude UAVs
comment: Agentic AI, neuro-symbolic AI, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), autonomous decision-making, networked UAV systems
summary: Networked low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) need reliable and adaptive decision-making capabilities to operate under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, while many existing agentic systems remain limited by hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This article investigates neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework for combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction to support more reliable and adaptive UAV autonomy. We first examine its capability foundations in data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer, and then develop a reference architecture integrating task and goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. An urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim illustrates how a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing the mission. The results illustrate the potential of NSAAI to support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. We further discuss key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

AI.tldr: NSAAI (neuro-symbolic agentic AI) combines neural grounding with symbolic reasoning to create more reliable, adaptive UAV autonomy that handles uncertainty, intermittent connectivity, and enables reusable skills with evidence-based decision-making.
AI.motivation: Networked UAVs need reliable and adaptive decision-making under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity. Existing agentic systems have limitations including hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization.
AI.method: Developed a neuro-symbolic agentic AI framework combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction. Created a reference architecture with task/goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification/meta-cognition, skill execution/network interaction, and shared knowledge/memory. Implemented and tested in LAESim using an urban fire-inspection case.
AI.result: Demonstrated that UAVs can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse verified image-delivery skills, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing missions. Showed NSAAI supports reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution.
AI.conclusion: NSAAI shows potential for enhancing UAV autonomy through combination of neural and symbolic approaches. Key research directions include uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge/skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation for further development.

title: EPIG-Tree: Compute-Optimal Branching for Gradient-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures
summary: Reward-based reinforcement learning for language models, exemplified by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), collapses an entire stochastic trajectory into a single scalar reward. This is clean and scalable, but it explores and allocates reward inefficiently: a trajectory may contain many causal decisions, recovery attempts, and environment-randomness events, yet every token or action inherits one trajectory-level advantage. We study tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. Our central claim is that branches should be placed not where the policy is merely uncertain, but where an additional branch most reduces uncertainty about the policy gradient per unit of compute. From a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable, we derive two allocation laws: new branches reduce decision uncertainty, while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The resulting EPIG-Tree score allocates branches using the already computed rollouts. It estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty, along with a suffix law $n_e \propto w_e \|\nabla_θ\log π(a_e|h_e)\| σ_e / \sqrt{c_e}$. Empirically, EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, winning in all nine dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep and recovering the reference gradient direction near-perfectly, and it improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration relative to entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO, while branch placement is secondary to token-level credit assignment. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), overtaking flat GRPO, which saturates early at 0.790, and entropy branching as training proceeds, confirming that the gradient-estimation advantage transfers to a stateful, large-action setting.

AI.tldr: EPIG-Tree improves policy gradient estimation by intelligently allocating computational branches based on uncertainty reduction about the gradient, outperforming standard methods like GRPO in various environments.
AI.motivation: Standard reward-based reinforcement learning methods like GRPO inefficiently allocate reward by collapsing entire trajectories into single scalar rewards, failing to properly credit individual decisions and actions within complex trajectories.
AI.method: Proposes tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem, using a law-of-total-variance decomposition to derive allocation laws: branches reduce decision uncertainty while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The EPIG-Tree score estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty for branch allocation.
AI.result: EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, wins in all 9 dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep, improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration, and achieves highest final win rate (0.850) in online multi-turn Wordle, outperforming flat GRPO and entropy branching.
AI.conclusion: Intelligent compute allocation for policy gradient estimation through uncertainty-based branch placement significantly improves efficiency and performance over standard methods, with demonstrated advantages in stateful, large-action settings.

title: Customizable and Jointly Optimized Route Planning: A Deep Architecture Enabling Differentiable Shortest-Path Search
summary: With the widespread use of online navigation and ride-hailing services, achieving optimal route planning for diverse user preferences has recently attracted increasing attention. Classic graph algorithms for pathfinding use heuristic cost functions to define edge weight, thus providing no optimality guarantee of route quality. Prior data-driven approaches equating ground truth of the optimal route with user trajectory, which is however moderately influenced by the navigation service, suffers from the feedback loop problem. To address these issues, we propose a deep architecture that is able to jointly optimize cost functions and route-ranking model towards any route preference. First, we run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes, deeming it as the complete candidate set. Exploiting the property of such a set, we design a neural network structure that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Second, we define route preference as a task of constrained optimization of route attributes, and propose a novel loss function that optimizes a single-objective variable, with other variables strictly under constraints. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that our architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.

AI.tldr: A deep learning architecture that jointly optimizes cost functions and route-ranking models for personalized route planning, addressing feedback loop problems in navigation services by using Pareto optimal routes and constrained optimization.
AI.motivation: Online navigation services struggle with optimal route planning for diverse user preferences. Classic graph algorithms use heuristic cost functions without optimality guarantees, and prior data-driven approaches suffer from feedback loop problems by equating user trajectories (influenced by navigation services) with ground truth optimal routes.
AI.method: 1) Offline collection of Pareto optimal routes using multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm as complete candidate set; 2) Neural network that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in end-to-end differentiable manner; 3) Route preference modeling as constrained optimization of route attributes with novel loss function that optimizes single-objective variable while keeping others strictly under constraints.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show the architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both route quality and customizability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed deep architecture successfully addresses limitations of existing approaches by jointly optimizing cost functions and route-ranking models, providing a more effective solution for personalized route planning that overcomes feedback loop problems and offers superior route quality with customization capabilities.

title: Dynamic Generalized Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport
summary: Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

AI.tldr: TP-DATE introduces a dynamic Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport framework for continuous trajectory reconstruction in spatial transcriptomics that preserves tissue structure while matching expression patterns.
AI.motivation: While static Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport has been used for structure-aware alignment in spatial transcriptomics, there's a lack of general dynamic formulations for reconstructing continuous trajectories that preserve tissue structure alongside expression patterns.
AI.method: Develops TP-DATE framework that generalizes GW-OT dynamically via Quadratic-form OT through path actions, proves static-dynamic equivalence, and introduces travelling-pair flow matching with interacting conditional paths marginalized into a single vector field.
AI.result: TP-DATE demonstrates better preservation of spatial structure and improved continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction on both synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: TP-DATE provides a comprehensive dynamic extension of structure-aware optimal transport for spatial transcriptomics, enabling more accurate reconstruction of continuous developmental trajectories while preserving tissue architecture.

title: E-AVI: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Assessment for Automated Video Interviews
summary: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal content, acoustic delivery, and visual behavior, yet numerical predictions alone provide limited inspectable support. We present E-AVI, an evidence-grounded framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool further supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway. Together, these results demonstrate that our proposed E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

AI.tldr: E-AVI framework improves automated video interview assessment by extracting timestamped multimodal evidence and using evidence attention for scoring, feedback, and QA.
AI.motivation: Current automated video interview assessments provide only numerical predictions with limited inspectable support, lacking transparency and actionable insights for interviewers.
AI.method: Proposes E-AVI framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence (verbal, acoustic, visual), integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring, and uses shared evidence pool for feedback and QA.
AI.result: Outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation on RecruitView and private hospitality datasets; ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses demonstrate predictive contributions and utility.
AI.conclusion: E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis, enhancing transparency and utility of automated video interview systems.

title: Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression
comment: 20 pages, 9 tables, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility materials to be released separately
summary: A memory can answer a current query correctly while discarding distinctions required by a later update. We investigate this failure with a paired-history audit: two histories have the same current answer, receive a shared future update, and require different subsequent answers. A pilot evaluates 24 history pairs across six synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. A deterministic frontier selector obtains strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; a structured writer obtains 62 successes with one unresolved outcome and 56/96. The configured four-outcome joint contrast has finite-sample identification intervals of [0.521, 0.542] and [0.292, 0.313], not confidence intervals. A record-level audit distinguishes retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance without changing those original scores. It finds 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories, while all 14 GLM frontier reveal failures contain correct values in the wrong wrapper. Tombstone removal produces 16/16 exact replay failures in the targeted mechanism. Identifier renaming then exposes a separate flaw: original frontier late-reference adequacy falls from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. We provide and test a label-equivariant repair, but it preserves only 2/8 original late-reference answers: eliminating a naming shortcut does not solve unknown future relevance. These results support a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis, not general superiority of the repaired algorithm. Paid pilot evidence, retrospective diagnostics, and new offline tests are reported separately; no independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory failures in AI systems where a memory answers current queries correctly but discards distinctions needed for future updates, using paired-history audits to expose these limitations.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the problem where AI memory systems can provide correct answers to current queries while failing to preserve distinctions necessary for handling future updates correctly, creating a latent failure mode.
AI.method: The method uses paired-history audits: two histories that have the same current answer receive a shared future update but require different subsequent answers. The study evaluates synthetic mechanisms with different memory conditions, model backends (DeepSeek and GLM), and includes deterministic frontier selectors, structured writers, tombstone removal, and identifier renaming tests.
AI.result: Results show high success rates for deterministic frontier selectors (96/96 on DeepSeek, 82/96 on GLM), lower for structured writers (62 successes), and reveal specific failure patterns. The audit distinguishes different failure types (retained-state adequacy, response delivery, answer-schema compliance) and exposes naming shortcut limitations through identifier renaming tests that reduce late-reference adequacy from 8/8 to 94/320.
AI.conclusion: The paper supports a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis rather than claiming general superiority of any repaired algorithm. It acknowledges limitations: no independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed, and eliminating naming shortcuts doesn't solve unknown future relevance problems.

title: Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models
summary: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

AI.tldr: AI chatbots give different political responses about the Ukraine war depending on the language used, with patterns that align with global geopolitical divisions.
AI.motivation: People increasingly use AI chatbots for news about world events, but it's unclear if these systems provide consistent political answers across different languages. The researchers wanted to investigate whether language influences how AI models assess geopolitical conflicts like the Ukraine war.
AI.method: Researchers tested three major AI models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) by asking them to evaluate 20 statements about the Ukraine war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. They analyzed how responses varied across languages and grouped them by countries' official languages, comparing results with real-world political indicators like public opinion, UN votes, and aid to Ukraine.
AI.result: The study found that the balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs significantly across languages. When grouped by countries' official languages, response patterns align with worldwide political divisions: more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favorable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in UN votes, and less aid to Ukraine. This pattern was consistent across all three models and robust to removal of individual statement pairs.
AI.conclusion: Language can significantly influence how AI chatbots respond to geopolitical questions, potentially reflecting and spreading geopolitical biases. This suggests that information warfare may shape the training text used for AI models, which then reproduces these biases across different language contexts, creating a feedback loop that could reinforce existing political divisions.

title: Evaluating Explanation Methods by the Predictors They Induce
summary: Explanations of machine learning models are usually judged by criteria that are hard to compare. We propose a simpler test: if an explanation really describes how a model uses its features, it should be possible to rebuild the model's predictions from it. We turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, and measure how well that predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. Nothing is fitted, so the score reflects the explanation itself. The test applies to any explanation that can be written as a function of the features; we demonstrate it on partial dependence plots (PDP), accumulated local effects (ALE), SHAP and LIME. We prove that summing partial dependence curves gives the best possible additive summary of a model when its features are independent, and that this fails when they are dependent. Across 13 real datasets and 9 synthetic designs and four model families, which method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence: where features are independent SHAP is slightly worse than PDP, exactly as the theory predicts; on dependent real data SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer a damaged explanation to an intact one.

AI.tldr: A new test for evaluating ML explanations: measure how well explanations can reconstruct model predictions by summing feature effects, without any fitting.
AI.motivation: Current methods for evaluating ML explanations use criteria that are hard to compare and don't directly test whether explanations accurately describe how models use features.
AI.method: Propose a simple test: convert explanations into predictors by summing feature effects, then measure how well these predictors reproduce model predictions on unseen data (no fitting involved). Apply test to PDP, ALE, SHAP, and LIME explanations.
AI.result: 1) Summing PDP curves gives optimal additive summary when features are independent. 2) Performance depends on feature dependence: SHAP slightly worse than PDP with independent features, but SHAP leads on dependent real data. 3) Some existing quality metrics prefer damaged over intact explanations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed test provides a practical, no-fitting-required evaluation of explanation fidelity; shows that explanation quality depends critically on feature dependence; and reveals flaws in some existing evaluation metrics.

title: FedeRICo: Federated Region-Influenced Coupling for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Urban traffic forecasting often relies on information distributed across stakeholders who may be unable to share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints, motivating federated spatial-temporal approaches. In such federated settings, each client observes traffic over a distinct sensor subgraph with its own spatial topology and temporal dynamics, leading to significant heterogeneity across clients. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods typically rely on model parameter aggregation and provide limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries. This introduces two key limitations. Specifically, parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains tends to dilute client-specific representations, while road network partitioning breaks the propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose FedeRICo, a federated traffic forecasting framework that combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture in which a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimisation without destructive parameter interference. To recover cross-client spatial dependencies, boundary messages are extracted through a trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients. Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

AI.tldr: FedeRICo: A federated traffic forecasting framework that uses gradient-level collaboration and boundary-aware residual communication to handle client heterogeneity while recovering cross-client spatial dependencies.
AI.motivation: Federated traffic forecasting faces challenges due to privacy/commercial constraints preventing raw data sharing. Clients have heterogeneous spatial topologies and temporal dynamics in their sensor subgraphs. Existing methods have limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries and parameter aggregation tends to dilute client-specific representations.
AI.method: Proposes FedeRICo with dual-branch architecture: global branch captures transferable forecasting structure via gradient alignment across clients; private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. Uses trend-residual decomposition to suppress periodic structure and communicate only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients.
