SkillAA contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment. With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting. These results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation.

AI.tldr: SkillAA is a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models that uses a unified skill graph to enable attribution-guided repair and scoped validation through contrastive analysis of successful vs failed executions.
AI.motivation: Existing skill methods lack structured routing from observed failures to editable locations, and skill graphs underutilize semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for targeted skill retrieval, updating, and validation.
AI.method: SkillAA represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph structure. It contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes, and updates only selected local structure.
AI.result: With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA achieves 81.5% on SearchQA, 66.7% on LiveMath, and 91.2% on DocVQA, attaining the highest observed mean in every main setting.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation for skill optimization in frozen language models.

title: A Learning Algorithm for Threshold Boolean Networks with Prescribed Fixed Points
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, to be published in 20th International Meeting, CIBB 2025, Revised Selected Papers
summary: We present a learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with a prescribed set of fixed points. The proposed method employs a custom differentiable loss function that jointly enforces fixed point preservation, penalizes spurious attractors, encourages binary outputs, and promotes sparsity through L1 regularization. Applied to the FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana, the approach achieved perfect reconstruction (i.e., all 10 desired fixed points and no spurious ones) in 5 out of 30 independent runs, recovering on average 8.53 $\pm$ 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. In contrast, standard methods such as the Perceptron and Logistic Regression recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced between 8 and 31 spurious ones. An additional analysis varying the sparsity coefficient ($λ$) confirmed that the method's performance and the structural properties of the inferred networks remain robust within a practical range (up to 0.01) of regularization strengths. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed algorithm in capturing meaningful network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints.

AI.tldr: A learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks that preserves prescribed fixed points while minimizing spurious attractors through custom differentiable loss functions and L1 regularization.
AI.motivation: Standard methods for learning threshold Boolean networks (like Perceptron and Logistic Regression) can successfully recover desired fixed points but often introduce many spurious attractors, which can significantly alter the network's dynamical behavior and interpretation.
AI.method: A custom differentiable loss function that jointly enforces: 1) fixed point preservation, 2) penalty for spurious attractors, 3) encouragement of binary outputs, and 4) sparsity promotion through L1 regularization. The approach is applied to infer threshold Boolean networks with prescribed sets of fixed points.
AI.result: Applied to the FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana: achieved perfect reconstruction (all 10 fixed points, no spurious ones) in 5/30 runs; average performance was 8.53 ± 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. Standard methods recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced 8-31 spurious attractors. Performance remained robust across practical regularization strengths (λ up to 0.01).
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm effectively captures meaningful network dynamics under prescribed constraints, demonstrating superior performance over standard methods by preserving desired fixed points while minimizing spurious attractors, with stable performance across practical regularization settings.

title: How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning Information and Release Control in Stateful LLM Agents
summary: Agent harnesses supply planning guidance, organize execution, and check completion. We study how these components affect success, erroneous acceptance, and cost in two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in $τ^2$-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) with shuffled policy text matched in word count (Sham), isolating the contribution of guidance content. Across 265 matched cells, Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90\% task-clustered bootstrap interval, 1.15--13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61\% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17\% of correct ones, at less than one cent of additional cost per episode. Which component matters more depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: at low liability the planning gain dominates; at high liability the verifier's avoided false passes dominate---and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.

AI.tldr: Agent systems combining supply planning guidance and execution verification improve task success rates, especially for complex tasks, with cost-effective terminal verification reducing erroneous acceptances.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how different components of agent systems—specifically planning guidance and execution verification—affect performance metrics like success rates, erroneous acceptance of invalid results, and operational costs in real-world applications like retail and airline operations.
AI.method: The researchers conducted experiments in two retail settings and an airline pilot program using a τ²-bench framework. They compared prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) against shuffled policy text with matched word count (Sham) to isolate the effect of guidance content. They also implemented a read-only terminal verifier and analyzed 265 matched cells to evaluate performance differences.
AI.result: Fixed planning guidance improved oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90% CI: 1.15-13.36 points), with greater benefits for higher-complexity tasks. The terminal verifier rejected 61% of oracle-invalid episodes while only withholding 17% of correct ones, adding less than one cent per episode cost. The relative importance of planning vs. verification depends on loss assignment for erroneous acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Both planning guidance and execution verification contribute to agent system performance, but their relative value depends on risk tolerance. For low-liability scenarios, planning provides major success benefits; for high-liability situations, verification is crucial for avoiding false passes. Notably, a standalone verifier captures most false-pass benefits of full planning-plus-verification systems at much lower cost.

title: Improving Generalization and Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation
summary: Current offline reinforcement learning (ORL) algorithms tend to overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness performance when deployed to real environments, thus compromising their effectiveness. Existing methods typically enhance in-distribution generalization and robustness by leveraging regularization techniques widely used in computer vision. However, due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts, these methods still suffer from notable limitations in in-distribution generalization and robustness, making it difficult to achieve stable performance in complex environments. To address this issue, we theoretically analyze the error bounds of the behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation, revealing that the error scales positively correlated with the distance between states. Based on this insight, we propose a method called $\bf{B}$oundary-$\bf{A}$ware $\bf{D}$ata $\bf{A}$ugmentation (BADA), which leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling the generation of synthetic data that more faithfully preserves the original data distribution. We first conduct qualitative studies in a toy environment, showing that BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets further demonstrate that BADA attains state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.

AI.tldr: BADA (Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation) improves offline RL generalization by using neighboring states to create interpolation boundaries for synthetic data generation, preserving original data distributions better than existing regularization methods.
AI.motivation: Current offline RL algorithms overfit training data and perform poorly in real environments due to limited in-distribution generalization and robustness. Existing methods using computer vision regularization techniques fail because low-level physical signals are highly sensitive to distributional shifts.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis reveals error bounds of behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation scale with state distances. BADA leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries for synthetic data generation that better preserves original data distributions.
AI.result: Qualitative studies in toy environments show BADA generates mixed samples that preserve policy smoothness and accurately reconstruct multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: BADA effectively addresses offline RL's generalization limitations by boundary-aware data augmentation, outperforming existing methods in preserving data distributions and achieving robust performance in complex environments.

title: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/NVlabs/SoL-Pi . Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/SoL-Pi/
summary: As coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, their work expands from isolated predictions into long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency therefore becomes important for scaling recursive self-improvement. We take an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. At this scale, the process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. In other words, estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 relative to Pi.

AI.tldr: SoL-Pi is an optimized coding agent system that achieves comparable performance to Pi while reducing token usage by 44-49% and API costs by about one third through four efficiency mechanisms, enabling more scalable automated research loops.
AI.motivation: As coding agents evolve from simple code completion to continuous autonomous operation, token efficiency becomes crucial for scaling recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems, since unattended operation creates long trajectories of reasoning and feedback that can be costly.
AI.method: Takes an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across numerous diverse environments. The process yields four reusable mechanisms that survived selection: action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading, collectively forming SoL-Pi.
AI.result: On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. Estimated hourly savings are $8.75-$13.50 relative to native Codex/Claude Code harnesses, and $4.36-$5.71 relative to Pi.
AI.conclusion: The SoL-Pi system successfully enables more efficient automated harness discovery with production-level outcomes through token-efficient mechanisms that transfer beyond their original development setting, making recursive self-improvement more scalable and cost-effective.

title: SAGG: Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating for Robust Multimodal Learning under Heterogeneous Corruption
comment: Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Multimodal gradient balancing methods modulate encoder gradients with a shared scalar per modality, implicitly assuming that corruption is uniform across the training batch. In practice, corruption is sample-heterogeneous: within a single mini-batch, different samples may have different modalities corrupted. We prove that under this heterogeneous corruption model, any batch-level sample-agnostic linear estimator with a shared modulation parameter incurs an irreducible bias with respect to the clean-data gradient, and that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy within a natural distribution-free estimator class. Motivated by this result, we propose Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG), which makes a binary retain-or-discard decision per sample via an online feature-norm quality test and incorporates a truncation mechanism for variance control. We prove that SAGG-based SGD converges at the standard O(1/sqrt(T)) rate to stationary points of the clean loss without a corruption-dependent error floor, and derive a certified robustness radius for the independent-encoder architecture that connects per-modality Lipschitz constants to the classification margin. Experiments on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under Gaussian noise injection, partial modality missing, and natural contribution imbalance show that SAGG consistently outperforms ten existing methods, with the largest gains in high-corruption regimes where batch-level bias is most severe.

AI.tldr: SAGG (Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating) is a new multimodal learning method that addresses heterogeneous corruption by making per-sample binary decisions on whether to retain or discard gradients, outperforming existing batch-level methods in corrupted settings.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal gradient balancing methods use a shared scalar per modality, assuming uniform corruption across batches. However, in practice, corruption is heterogeneous - different samples within the same batch can have different corrupted modalities, causing irreducible bias in current methods.
AI.method: Proposes Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG) which makes binary retain-or-discard decisions per sample via an online feature-norm quality test. Includes a truncation mechanism for variance control. Theoretical analysis shows sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy within the class of distribution-free estimators.
AI.result: SAGG-based SGD converges at standard O(1/sqrt(T)) rate to stationary points of the clean loss without corruption-dependent error floor. Derives certified robustness radius for independent-encoder architecture. Experiments on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under various corruption types show SAGG consistently outperforms 10 existing methods, with largest gains in high-corruption regimes.
AI.conclusion: Batch-level gradient modulation suffers from irreducible bias under heterogeneous corruption, while sample-level adaptation via binary gating (SAGG) provides unbiased estimation and superior practical performance, especially in high-corruption scenarios.

title: FreqCondNorm: Towards Cross-domain Predictive Maintenance through a Frequency-Conditioned Transformer Foundation Model
summary: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labelled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). We propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling. On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

AI.tldr: A Transformer-based architecture (FreqCondNorm) uses frequency-conditioned normalization to handle heterogeneous time-series data in predictive maintenance, achieving strong fault diagnosis transfer across sampling frequencies but limited improvements for remaining useful life prediction.
AI.motivation: Deep learning predictive maintenance models struggle with transferability across different machines and operating conditions, particularly when dealing with scarce labeled data and signals spanning wide sampling frequency ranges (1 Hz to ~100 kHz).
AI.method: FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture with a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series data. The model is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling.
AI.result: Achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (6.4 percentage points improvement over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT for fault diagnosis, demonstrating strong transfer capability across different sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: FreqCondNorm effectively addresses the challenge of handling heterogeneous time-series data with varying sampling frequencies for fault diagnosis, showing strong transfer capabilities. The lack of improvement in remaining useful life prediction suggests a mismatch between the pretraining objectives and RUL tasks that requires further investigation.

title: Hypernetwork-Parameterized Spatially Adaptive Neural Operators for PDE Learning
summary: Spatially heterogeneous partial differential equations (PDEs) exhibit location-dependent dynamics arising from variations in geometry and physical coefficients. Existing neural operators improve localized modeling through multiscale features, attention mechanisms, or domain decomposition, yet their update rules often remain spatially shared. Hypernetwork-based methods adapt parameters across PDE instances but typically generate only one global parameterization per instance. Consequently, shared operators may underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions, with these localized errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout. We propose a spatially adaptive neural operator (SANO), which replaces this spatially shared parameterization with a spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters. SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing their update rules to vary across space, and partition-of-unity weights assemble the overlapping local predictions. Experiments on one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks show that SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.

AI.tldr: SANO: A spatially adaptive neural operator that generates location-dependent operator parameters instead of spatially shared ones, improving accuracy in heterogeneous PDEs with varying geometries and coefficients.
AI.motivation: Existing neural operators use spatially shared parameterizations that underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions in heterogeneous PDEs, with errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout. Current hypernetwork methods only generate global parameterizations per PDE instance, not location-specific adaptations.
AI.method: SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, allowing update rules to vary across space, with partition-of-unity weights assembling overlapping local predictions.
AI.result: Experiments on 1D, 2D, and 3D PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks show SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.
AI.conclusion: SANO's spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters provides superior modeling of spatially heterogeneous PDEs compared to existing approaches with spatially shared parameterizations.

title: Refuse, Decompose, Refresh: A Claim-Safe Protocol for Closed-Loop AI Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 0 figures, 3 tables. The reproducibility artifact is linked in the paper
summary: An AI evaluation can be perfectly reproducible and still support the wrong claim. This risk is acute in closed-loop systems: policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace. We propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions. Refuse: abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support. Decompose: report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as one PASS/FAIL label. Refresh: treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence. We instantiate the protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Rather than a universal threshold, we contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims.

AI.tldr: Proposes a claim-safe evaluation protocol for AI systems that emphasizes abstention when evidence is insufficient, separates different types of failures, and treats distribution shifts as opportunities to refresh reference data rather than evidence of faults.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluations can be perfectly reproducible yet still support wrong claims, especially in closed-loop systems where policy decisions affect which states are visited and which failures leave measurable traces. There's a need for evaluation protocols that ensure claims are properly supported by evidence.
AI.method: A three-action protocol: Refuse (abstain when clean reference or matched runtime comparison lacks support), Decompose (separate protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses rather than using single PASS/FAIL labels), and Refresh (treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate/recompute reference maps rather than fault evidence). Implemented in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development/heldout seeds.
AI.result: In preregistered heldout with 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows: 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted, 54/55 remained runtime-admitted (showing abstention as part of result). Stable false admission was 0/20 components. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction with significant difference. Drift logs showed why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered different alarm rates across regimes, with only middle regime matching frozen detector reference.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims, rather than proposing universal thresholds. The protocol ensures claims are properly supported by evidence in AI system evaluations.

title: ZeroHAT: Behavior-Conditioned Zero-Shot Human Activity Trace Generation
summary: Human activity traces record individuals' timestamped visits to points of interest and are essential for applications such as mobility prediction and urban simulation. However, accessing large-scale HATs is challenging due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Synthetic HAT generation offers a promising way to make such data available and has attracted growing interest from both industry and academia. Although many efforts have been devoted to this topic, most of them rely on real data from a region to generate synthetic data for the same region, which is infeasible for the many regions where real HATs are unavailable. To fill this gap, we propose ZeroHAT, a behavior-conditioned framework that generates synthetic HATs for a target region in a zero-shot manner by transferring behavioral patterns learned from real HATs in source regions and adapting them with publicly available contextual information about the target region. ZeroHAT has three key novel components: (i) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor; (ii) a cross-region behavioral cloning module; and (iii) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. We evaluate ZeroHAT on a ten-city benchmark, where extensive experiments show that ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.

AI.tldr: ZeroHAT is a zero-shot framework that generates synthetic human activity traces for regions without real data by transferring behavioral patterns from source regions and adapting them using publicly available contextual information.
AI.motivation: Accessing large-scale human activity traces (HATs) is challenging due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Existing synthetic HAT generation methods require real data from the target region, making them infeasible for regions where real HATs are unavailable.
AI.method: ZeroHAT uses a behavior-conditioned framework with three novel components: 1) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor, 2) a cross-region behavioral cloning module, and 3) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. It transfers behavioral patterns from source regions and adapts them using publicly available contextual information about target regions.
AI.result: On a ten-city benchmark, ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.
AI.conclusion: ZeroHAT enables zero-shot synthetic HAT generation for regions without real data, overcoming the limitation of existing methods that require target region data, and demonstrates superior performance in both downstream utility and data fidelity.

title: EviRec: Continual Evidence Learning for Dual Cold-Start POI Recommendation
summary: Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a core task in location-based services, yet most existing methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog. Through a large-scale data-driven analysis of 10 U.S. cities, we identify substantial POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, motivating the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation. To address this setting, we propose EviRec, a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates how much historical evidence should be trusted separately for each candidate POI. EviRec scores each visible candidate from three complementary views: a matching view based on the user's recent mobility profile, a transition-memory view that captures repeated mobility routines, and a lifecycle view that reflects candidate maturity. Because a near-zero transition score may indicate either irrelevance or insufficient observation, EviRec qualifies the evidence using each candidate's observation state and applies a reliability gate to adaptively route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence. We evaluate EviRec on a full-year, five-city POI check-in dataset containing more than 30,000 users and 684,200 trajectories. Experimental results show that EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains concentrated on cold-start queries. In particular, EviRec improves NDCG@10 by 20.4\% on Dual-New cases over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses further confirm that these gains arise primarily from candidate-specific reliability gating while largely preserving previously learned mobility routines.

AI.tldr: EviRec is a continual evidence-learning framework for POI recommendation that addresses dual cold-start problems by adaptively routing between different evidence sources based on candidate-specific reliability estimates.
AI.motivation: Most POI recommendation methods assume fixed user populations and POI catalogs, but real-world data shows substantial POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, creating continual dual cold-start challenges.
AI.method: EviRec uses a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates trustworthiness of historical evidence per candidate POI. It scores candidates from three views: matching (recent mobility), transition-memory (repeated routines), and lifecycle (candidate maturity). A reliability gate adaptively routes between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence based on observation state.
AI.result: EviRec outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on a large-scale dataset (30k+ users, 684k+ trajectories), with 20.4% NDCG@10 improvement on Dual-New cases. Gains primarily come from candidate-specific reliability gating while preserving learned mobility routines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed EviRec framework effectively addresses continual dual cold-start POI recommendation by adaptively combining different evidence sources based on candidate-specific reliability estimates, showing significant improvements particularly for cold-start scenarios.

title: Limits of Confidence in Diffusion
summary: Discrete diffusion, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, generate a sequence by writing multiple token positions per step, drawing each from a per-position distribution and choosing which positions to write from those same distributions. For domains of general interest (pixels, phonemes, or words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens. We show that a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given the tokens already fixed, that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position distributions do not determine whether a group is dependent: two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals while differing in which combinations of values occur. On ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task whose joint distribution is available in closed form, we verify that every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent, and measure the generated distribution to be $29\times$ the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics are $1.0$.

AI.tldr: Discrete diffusion samplers using per-position token distributions cannot capture token dependencies, causing distribution mismatches even when per-sample metrics appear perfect.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses limitations of discrete diffusion samplers (remasking and uniform-state) that generate sequences by writing multiple token positions per step using per-position distributions. In real domains (pixels, phonemes, words), tokens have inherent dependencies that these methods fail to capture.
AI.method: The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that per-position distributions can only match the training distribution when positions are conditionally independent. They demonstrate that two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals but differ in which value combinations occur. They validate this on ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task with known joint distribution, testing dependency in groups of undetermined positions.
AI.result: Experimental results show that every group of two or more undetermined positions written by confidence ranking is dependent. The generated distribution has 29× the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics score 1.0 (perfect), revealing a fundamental mismatch between distribution-level and sample-level evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion samplers using per-position token distributions are fundamentally limited in capturing dependencies between tokens, leading to distributional discrepancies that are invisible to per-sample metrics but measurable through distribution-level evaluation.

title: Sharp Reconstruction Bounds for Autoencoders Using the Same Forward Map
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables
summary: We study reconstruction in autoencoders that apply the same forward map before and after setting the observed coordinates to zero. For equal odd input and hidden dimensions $d\geq 3$, among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms whose Jacobian singular values lie in $[m,M]$, we show that the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is $\max\{1-M(M-m)/2,0\}$, with affine maps attaining this sharp bound at every prescribed depth. A translated radial rotation can nevertheless reconstruct any prescribed ball exactly with singular values arbitrarily close to one, motivating additional conditions for a finite-data bound. We test this prediction on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan. At input scale $0.05$, the mean theoretical bound is $0.155$, about $84\%$ of the mean normalized training error $0.185$ across four spatial regions, two depths, and three seeds. At this scale, adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error below $6\times10^{-6}$.

AI.tldr: Autoencoder reconstruction analysis showing theoretical error bounds for orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, with affine maps achieving sharp bounds, and practical validation on LiDAR forest data.
AI.motivation: The paper studies reconstruction properties in autoencoders that use a specific forward map structure (applying same forward map before and after zeroing observed coordinates). It aims to understand theoretical reconstruction error bounds and validate them on real-world data.
AI.method: Mathematical analysis of autoencoders with equal odd input/hidden dimensions (d≥3) among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms. Derives theoretical bounds on reconstruction-derivative error, shows affine maps attain sharp bounds. Then validates on real LiDAR forest data (798,452 points) at different scales, depths, and spatial regions.
AI.result: Proves least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is max{1-M(M-m)/2,0} with sharp bound attained by affine maps. Shows translated radial rotations can reconstruct prescribed balls exactly. On LiDAR data, theoretical bound (0.155) matches ~84% of actual training error (0.185). Adding one hidden coordinate reduces reconstruction error below 6×10⁻⁶ at scale 0.05.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes theoretical foundations for autoencoder reconstruction errors, demonstrating that affine maps achieve optimal bounds among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms. Practical validation on LiDAR data shows theoretical predictions closely match empirical results, suggesting the framework is useful for understanding and designing autoencoders in real-world applications.

title: PAA: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra: A Generative and Complete Probabilistic Extension of Allen's Interval Relations
comment: 41 pages, 7 figures. Open-source implementation at https://github.com/HRI-EU/probabilistic-allen-algebra
summary: Allen's interval algebra is a qualitative calculus for temporal relations, but its thirteen base relations are crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries. This is inadequate for temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions such as "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning. We develop the probabilistic Allen algebra (PAA): a generative and complete extension in which relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries rather than assigned as scores. Time points are Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, and point-interval and interval-interval relations to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates such as precedence, overlap, and containment are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and thirteen relations reduce to five and then three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions such as "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

AI.tldr: Develops Probabilistic Allen Algebra (PAA) - a generative, complete extension of crisp Allen's interval algebra that handles temporal uncertainty through probability distributions over interval boundaries.
AI.motivation: Traditional Allen's interval algebra uses crisp predicates that are inadequate for real-world temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain, and expressions like "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning.
AI.method: Extends Allen algebra probabilistically by modeling time points as Gaussian distributions and intervals as having Gaussian midpoints with truncated-Gaussian durations. Relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries. Contact relations receive positive measure through tolerance bands, and the system preserves Allen's taxonomy while decomposing relations into correlation-aware temporal primitives.
AI.result: Creates a probabilistic framework where relation probabilities come from multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. The system is scale-invariant, separates graded expressions from contact relations, recovers crisp Allen algebra as tolerance vanishes, and preserves the hierarchy as intervals collapse to points. All results are Monte-Carlo validated with an open, tested Python package.
AI.conclusion: PAA provides a rigorous, generative probabilistic extension of Allen's interval algebra that naturally handles temporal uncertainty while preserving the original algebra's structure, offering practical utility through an open-source implementation for applications involving uncertain temporal information.

title: COMPASS: Ordered Clustered Routing at 100K Scale
summary: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order, giving rise to the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP). Optimizing each cluster independently seems natural, but misses non-local dependencies. We introduce the COMPASS algorithm for OCTSP, which combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers. COMPASS has no quality ceiling and its solutions keep improving with compute. It exploits the clustered structure, and can reach exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. Empirically, COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. Unlike common large-scale routing solvers, COMPASS consumes general distance matrices and is not limited to coordinate inputs. We demonstrate scaling to 100K synthetic nodes and to 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. To our knowledge, the latter is the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.

AI.tldr: COMPASS algorithm solves large-scale Ordered Clustered TSP by combining search with learning-accelerated routing, scales to 100K nodes, handles asymmetric distances, and can find exact solutions with exponential time only in cluster size rather than instance size.
AI.motivation: Large-scale routing problems often involve visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order (Ordered Clustered TSP). While optimizing each cluster independently seems natural, this approach misses important non-local dependencies between clusters, leading to suboptimal solutions.
AI.method: COMPASS algorithm combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers. It exploits the clustered structure of the problem, can reach exact solutions in time exponential only in cluster size rather than instance size, and has no quality ceiling (solutions improve with more compute). Unlike many routing solvers, it works with general distance matrices, not just coordinate inputs.
AI.result: COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods, scales to 100K synthetic nodes and 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. The 28.5K-node solution is the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: COMPASS provides an effective approach for large-scale Ordered Clustered TSP that can handle massive real-world instances with asymmetric distances, offering both practical scalability and theoretical advantages through its clustered decomposition approach.

title: Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks
summary: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

AI.tldr: AI collaboration can feel like "ours" when we lead the process, but disowning occurs when we just approve AI suggestions - ownership depends on collaborative dynamics, not just output quality.
AI.motivation: As AI becomes integrated into everyday tasks, we need to understand how it affects our sense of ownership and contribution when machines share in producing what we make, examining what preserves or erodes felt authorship.
AI.method: Exploratory qualitative survey where participants described two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not, analyzing narratives about collaborative experiences.
AI.result: Felt ownership depends on collaboration process: people disown work when merely approving AI suggestions but retain ownership when leading, iterating, or rewriting; ownership can extend to vision-driven tasks even with AI execution; loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension erode ownership; disclosure practices often decouple from actual pride.
AI.conclusion: AI development should support people's sense of authorship by designing collaborative processes that enable leadership, iteration, and comprehension rather than passive approval, and understanding disclosure motivations separate from actual ownership experiences.

title: Minimax-Optimal Online Contract Design with Unrestricted Bounded Contracts
summary: We study repeated contract design when a principal observes outcomes but not the actions that generate them. The principal may use any bounded outcome-contingent payment vector, and the agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in those payments. For every fixed number $m\ge2$ of outcomes, the minimax regret over $T$ rounds is of order $T^{m/(m+1)}$, up to logarithmic factors. The upper bound allows arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. Its key is an effective-dimension reduction that the benchmark can be normalized even when fixed tie-breaking is not shift invariant, after which revealed preference yields a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates. A learning policy built on a Lipschitz parametrization of this map attains the rate using only observed outcome categories. The lower-bound construction accounts for how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions. It shows that each additional contractible outcome creates a precise and unavoidable increase in the worst-case cost of learning.

AI.tldr: Repeated contract design with hidden actions: minimax regret scales as T^(m/(m+1)) for m outcomes, showing each additional outcome increases learning cost unavoidably.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses repeated contract design where the principal observes outcomes but not the agent's actions (moral hazard). Key challenge: agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in payments, complicating learning. Need to understand fundamental limits of learning optimal contracts over time.
AI.method: 1. Studies minimax regret over T rounds with m outcomes; 2. Upper bound: uses effective-dimension reduction where benchmark can be normalized even without shift-invariant tie-breaking; 3. Revealed preference yields monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates; 4. Learning policy built on Lipschitz parametrization of this map using only observed outcome categories; 5. Lower bound: construction showing how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions.
AI.result: For fixed m ≥ 2 outcomes, minimax regret over T rounds is Θ(T^(m/(m+1))) up to logarithmic factors. Upper bound works for arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity without smoothness/monotone-surplus assumptions. Each additional contractible outcome creates precise unavoidable increase in worst-case learning cost.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes fundamental trade-off in learning optimal contracts: more observable outcomes paradoxically make learning harder with higher minimax regret. The dimension-reduction technique and Lipschitz-based learning policy provide practical approach, while lower bound shows inherent complexity cannot be avoided.

title: Deep Noir: Autonomous Steering Discovery via Architectural Chronometry in Transformer Models
summary: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual. We introduce Deep Noir, a framework that uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters. Across three scales (1B x 3, 2-3B x 2, and 7-9B x 4), our engine achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam at 1B (standard deviation 4.7; 39 runs), with gains increasing to 21 to 42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment, it achieves a 13.1 percentage-point improvement with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. On sentiment, RepE without head masking fails to improve over baseline, while Deep Noir improves all models (p less than 0.01). We further show that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases monotonically with steering magnitude. This finding is relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

AI.tldr: Deep Noir is a framework that autonomously discovers optimal steering parameters for LLMs using Logit Lens convergence and causal attribution, achieving significant performance improvements across multiple model scales and architectures while exposing predictable security vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Current activation steering methods require manual identification of where and how strongly to steer LLMs at inference time, which is inefficient and limits scalability across different models and tasks.
AI.method: Uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters across different model layers and attention heads. The framework operates across three model scales (1B, 2-3B, and 7-9B parameters) with multiple architectures.
AI.result: Achieved 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam detection at 1B scale (39 runs, std dev 4.7), with gains increasing to 21-42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment analysis, achieved 13.1 percentage-point improvement without code changes. Demonstrated consistent improvements across all models (p < 0.01) where RepE without head masking failed.
AI.conclusion: The mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. However, steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases with steering magnitude, which is important for agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

title: Learning Principal-Agent Contracts for Equitable Smallholder Carbon Farming under Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures
summary: Agricultural soils are a major untapped carbon sink. Carbon farming is emerging as a promising practice for tapping this potential. Smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture across South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, are key to scaling climate mitigation via carbon farming. It is ironic that real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach them. We study this important gap through the lens of contract design. An aggregator offers a single pooled contract to a heterogeneous population of smallholder farmers who have private adoption costs (adverse selection) and exert unobserved effort (moral hazard), with agronomic outcomes evolving over multiple seasons. We formulate this evolving contracting problem as a POMDP and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximising contract. We analyse the performance of the aggregator under various conditions. We find that a profit-maximising aggregator does not merely inherit the exclusion of smallholders, it amplifies it. On large farms the aggregator realises 87.7% of achievable adoption, against only 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) costs fall as farm size rises, and the aggregator's pooling contract compounds this gradient rather than offsetting it. A counterfactual that makes MRV costs purely area-proportional eliminates this disparity. Our results and simulation can guide contract and policy design that opens carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

AI.tldr: RL-designed dynamic carbon farming contracts amplify exclusion of smallholder farmers due to disproportionate MRV costs, creating 87.7% adoption on large farms vs 8.2% on smallholdings.
AI.motivation: Agricultural soils represent a major carbon sink, and smallholder farmers are crucial for scaling carbon farming for climate mitigation. However, real-world carbon programs fail to reach them despite their dominance in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
AI.method: The study examines this gap through contract design lens, modeling an aggregator offering pooled contracts to heterogeneous smallholders with private adoption costs (adverse selection) and unobserved effort (moral hazard). They formulate this as a POMDP and use reinforcement learning to learn dynamic profit-maximizing contracts.
AI.result: Profit-maximizing aggregators amplify smallholder exclusion rather than just inheriting it: 87.7% adoption on large farms vs only 8.2% on smallholdings. MRV costs fall with farm size, and pooling contracts compound rather than offset this gradient. Counterfactual analysis shows making MRV costs purely area-proportional eliminates the disparity.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight how current contract designs worsen inequality in carbon farming access. Results can guide contract and policy design to open carbon income opportunities for smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

title: Q&A on Any Spreadsheet Requires Interpreting Its Grid Structure
summary: Semantic cell annotation improves chunking interpretability for spreadsheets in LLM-driven RAG systems, aiding answer generation through enriched context rather than improved retrieval accuracy. We propose a novel framework of splitting any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation. Our framework beats the state of the art, yet it faces a hard ceiling. Spreadsheets are fundamentally two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles. Because classification models are restricted to finite, pre-defined classes, they cannot perfectly capture this structural nuance, even with human-level annotation. We show that addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification. Instead, the field must develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text. Text chunks would be easier for downstream RAG to interpret and generate from.

AI.tldr: A framework using semantic cell annotation improves spreadsheet chunking for LLM RAG systems, but faces inherent limitations due to spreadsheets' 2D unstructured nature requiring dimensionality reduction rather than classification approaches.
AI.motivation: Spreadsheets present a challenge for LLM-driven RAG systems because they are fundamentally two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles, making traditional chunking approaches inadequate for proper interpretation.
AI.method: Proposed a novel framework that splits spreadsheets into interpretable chunks using semantic cell role annotation, which beats state-of-the-art methods but reveals inherent limitations of classification-based approaches.
AI.result: The framework outperforms existing methods but hits a hard ceiling because classification models with finite, pre-defined classes cannot perfectly capture the structural nuance of spreadsheets, even with human-level annotation.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification to develop dimensionality-reduction techniques that directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text for easier RAG interpretation and generation.

title: The Bias of Nonlinear Two-Time-scale Stochastic Approximation under Constant Step-Sizes
summary: Two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) is a fundamental tool for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control. However, finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. In this paper, we study nonlinear TTSA with step-sizes $α\ggβ$. Under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions, we upper bound the mean-squared error and the bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria. Our bounds scale as $O(α+β^2/α^2)$, which we prove to be tight when $β\leα^{3/2}$. The analysis separates the contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling, thereby clarifying the origin of the $β^2/α^2$ term. Our results reveal qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting previously studied, showing that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects that are absent in the linear case.

AI.tldr: Nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation with step-sizes α≫β achieves O(α+β²/α²) error bounds, proving this rate is tight when β≤α³/², revealing qualitative differences from linear TTSA settings.
AI.motivation: Finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation schemes under constant step-sizes remain difficult to obtain, despite TTSA being fundamental for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control.
AI.method: Study nonlinear TTSA with step-sizes α≫β under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions. Analyze mean-squared error and bias of iterates around their limiting equilibria, separating contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling.
AI.result: Obtain error bounds scaling as O(α+β²/α²) and prove these bounds are tight when β≤α³/². The analysis reveals the origin of the β²/α² term and shows that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects absent in linear TTSA.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation exhibits distinct finite-time behavior from linear settings, with the derived error bounds providing fundamental performance guarantees for practical applications in RL and optimization under constant step-sizes.

title: RAFT: A Stateful Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Effective troubleshooting agents in enterprise customer support depend on retrieving actionable guidance from similar historical cases, yet existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature. We introduce RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents), a stateful RAG framework that abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, surfacing cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; an optional case-level graph links cases through a configurable similarity representation. We evaluate this retrieval layer directly, which, unlike evaluating a full agent system, requires no production deployment. Because public multi-stage troubleshooting data is extremely rare, we pair a synthetic benchmark built from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation with real Apache Jira issues carrying human-created duplicate labels. RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline; the Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories. We release our benchmark, implementation, and the Apache Jira evaluation set.

AI.tldr: RAFT is a stateful RAG framework that improves troubleshooting agent performance by retrieving relevant historical case entries at intermediate states rather than treating cases as static documents.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems for enterprise customer support treat support cases as static documents, overlooking their multi-stage, stateful nature, which limits their effectiveness in retrieving actionable guidance for troubleshooting agents.
AI.method: RAFT abstracts closed historical cases into directed chains of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, matching intermediate states of active cases with similar historical states and returning parent-case trajectories anchored at matched states. Optional case-level graphs link cases through configurable similarity representations.
AI.result: RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress with statistically significant gains. Evaluation using synthetic benchmark from Microsoft Learn documentation and real Apache Jira issues shows the advantage transfers to real case histories.
AI.conclusion: The stateful RAG approach in RAFT significantly improves retrieval accuracy for troubleshooting agents by accounting for the temporal, multi-stage nature of support cases, with promising real-world applicability demonstrated through both synthetic and real data evaluations.

title: SCGFM-ART: Amortized Relational Transport for Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Models
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures
summary: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across severely heterogeneous graph domains. However, severe domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics impede the construction of a unified, domain-agnostic representation space. To address this, we propose SCGFM-ART, a structure-centric GFM framework that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport (ART). The relational atlas serves as a universal coordinate system defined by a finite set of relational landmarks (bases), while ART directly predicts reusable, end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans, bypassing costly runtime Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. Under this formulation, SCGFM-ART decomposes a graph into a unified representation: globally via its relational response coordinates relative to the atlas, and locally via its node-to-role structural correspondences. These correspondences project disparate node attributes into a canonical role space, resolving structural and semantic heterogeneity within a singular alignment interface. Rigorously modeling graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces, we establish coordinate fidelity bounds, prove stability under predicted transport plans, and derive an amortized coverage bound that guarantees our learning objective tightly surrogates ideal relational coverage. Benchmarked across 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks, SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability, securing superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14, respectively. Topological perturbation analyses demonstrate that node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances beyond global coordinates. On real-world benchmarks, the amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time.

AI.tldr: SCGFM-ART is a structure-centric graph foundation model that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas using amortized relational transport, enabling transferable graph representations across heterogeneous domains.
AI.motivation: Current graph foundation models struggle with severe domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics, making it difficult to create unified, domain-agnostic representation spaces for transfer learning across diverse graph domains.
AI.method: The proposed SCGFM-ART framework uses Amortized Relational Transport (ART) to align graphs onto a shared relational atlas defined by relational landmarks. It predicts reusable graph-to-base transport plans end-to-end, bypassing expensive Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. The method decomposes graphs into unified representations: globally via relational response coordinates and locally via node-to-role structural correspondences.
AI.result: SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability across 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks with superior average ranks (2.29 and 1.14). It demonstrates 44.2 to 85.1 times faster inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time, and topological analyses show it retains fine-grained structural nuances.
AI.conclusion: SCGFM-ART successfully addresses heterogeneity challenges in graph foundation models through structure-centric alignment onto a relational atlas, providing efficient, transferable representations while maintaining theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements.

title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents
comment: 43 pages
summary: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, we evaluate 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. We find that: (1) Context management becomes increasingly valuable as the context-window budget tightens, with most of its benefit coming from preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization provides the strongest overall efficiency among the context-management strategies, whereas making elided content recoverable adds machinery that models rarely use and yields no accuracy gain. (3) Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy. (4) Predefined tools improve performance for models with weaker bash proficiency, whereas bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface and achieve substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectory-level analysis explains these effects: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and the action space changes the granularity at which code is written. These findings inform model- and budget-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes coding harness components for autonomous coding agents, finding that context management is crucial with limited budgets, rule-based elision before LLM summarization works best, planning shifts from accuracy aid to cost saver, and simpler bash interfaces benefit stronger models while tools help weaker ones.
AI.motivation: Existing work evaluates coding harnesses as monolithic systems, making it unclear which individual components are effective. The paper aims to enable component-level comparisons to understand how different harness components affect autonomous coding agent performance.
AI.method: The study uses a lightweight coding harness with fixed execution loop while varying three components: planning, action space, and context management. They evaluate 176 matched settings across four models on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, testing five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Context management becomes valuable as context-window budgets tighten, mainly preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Rule-based elision before LLM summarization provides strongest efficiency; recoverable elision adds unused machinery. (3) Planning shifts from accuracy scaffold for weak models to cost saver for strong models with little accuracy change. (4) Predefined tools help weak models, while bash-capable models perform better with bash-only interfaces at lower cost. Trajectory analysis shows context management extends trajectories without changing behavior, planning affects where trajectories stop, and action space changes code-writing granularity.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide insights for model- and budget-aware harness design and offer a modular framework for evaluating future harness components, enabling more targeted improvements to autonomous coding systems based on model capabilities and resource constraints.

title: Seismic Site Response Prediction from Sparse Observations Using Finite-Element-Pretrained Latent Dynamics
summary: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, yet correcting these discrepancies is difficult because records are limited in both sensor coverage and number of events. This study proposes the Transfer-Enabled Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations (FLARE-T) to improve these predictions by learning and calibrating low-dimensional latent dynamics that connect the base acceleration input to acceleration outputs at multiple depths. FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It then trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into the learned coordinates and uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics within them. A short response window initializes each prediction, while the complete base motion drives the response. The framework was evaluated using a layered-soil centrifuge test and the Lotung field vertical array. Test-set results show that FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to the original finite-element models, reducing errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and, at Lotung, for both horizontal components. Two Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters achieved comparable test-set accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration. FLARE-T therefore provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions.

AI.tldr: FLARE-T uses transfer learning to calibrate numerical site-response models using limited field data by learning low-dimensional latent dynamics that connect base acceleration to multi-depth responses.
AI.motivation: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, but correcting these discrepancies is difficult because field records are limited in both sensor coverage and number of events.
AI.method: Proposes FLARE-T which: 1) learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations, 2) trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into learned coordinates, and 3) uses limited field records to calibrate the dynamics within the latent space.
AI.result: FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and response spectra relative to original finite-element models, reducing errors at every sensor for motions of different intensities. Tested on layered-soil centrifuge test and Lotung field vertical array with two different source models achieving comparable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FLARE-T provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions, reducing dependence on precise prior calibration.
